en: At the right moment, one should awaken and break free; having fully understood the bond, what does the Hero say is that bond, or knowing what does one break free? (Sūyagaḍa 1.1)

Whether it be animate or inanimate, having become greedy for food, one may even permit others to take it; thus, one is not released from suffering. One might kill living beings oneself by means of wind, or have them killed by others.

Or if one approves of someone who is killing, one increases one's own enmity. (Sūyagaḍa 3) In whatever family a person is born, or with whomsoever he dwells, that fool is ruined by his attachment to "mine," being infatuated with one another. (Sūyagaḍa 4)

Wealth and even kinsmen—none of this provides protection when one considers the nature of life; thus, through karma alone, one is severed. Transcending these bonds, some ascetics and brahmins [attain liberation]. *Sūyagaḍa 5*
Not knowing this, young men are distracted by sensual pleasures.
(Sūyagaḍa 6) There are five great elements; thus it is held by some here:
earth, water, fire, air, and space as the fifth. (Sūyagaḍa 7)

"These five great elements—of these, one is said to be the self; yet, upon their destruction, the embodied being is destroyed. (Sūyagaḍa 8) "And just as in a single mound of earth, many things are seen,"
"Thus, O friend! In this entire world, the wise are seen through various [means of knowledge]. (Sūy.
9) "Thus some speak, being dull-witted and dependent on worldly undertakings; having themselves committed evil, they undergo intense suffering. (Sūy. 10)
Individual gain is the highest good for both the foolish and the wise;
they do not exist after death, nor do there exist beings who have been reborn. There is neither merit nor evil, nor is there any other world beyond this one. (Sūyagaḍa 1.1.11)
With the destruction of the body, the destruction of the embodied soul occurs. (Sūy.
12) Whether acting or causing others to act, one who acts in every way does not exist; thus the self is a non-doer, yet they are so shameless. (Sūy. 13)
If those speakers were indeed like this, what would happen to them in the world?
Being dull-witted and dependent on violent undertakings, they go from darkness to darkness.
(Sūyagaḍa 1.1.4) There are five great elements; thus it is declared by some here.
Furthermore, some say that the self and the world are eternal;
they do not perish in either way, nor does anything non-existent arise.
All things, having attained a state of necessity, remain so in every respect. (Sūyagaḍa 1.15–16)

When the five aggregates are perishing, fools, burning with the fire of momentary existence, speak of one as distinct from another, and of cause and non-cause. (Sūyagaḍa 1.1.7) Earth, water, fire, and likewise wind, all together...
"The form consists of four elements," so say the knowers. (Sūy.
18) Even while dwelling in a house, or being forest-dwellers and ascetics, those who have adopted this view are liberated from all suffering. (Sūy. 19)

Having understood the seam of the boat, those people are not knowers of the Dharma; those who speak thus are not those who have crossed over the flood. Having understood the seam of the boat, those people are not knowers of the Dharma.
Those speakers who speak thus do not go beyond the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). Having understood the connection between the boat and the shore, those people are not knowers of the Dharma.
Those speakers who speak thus do not go beyond the womb (rebirth). (Sūyagaḍa 21–22)
Those people who, having understood the connection regarding the boat, speak thus, are not knowers of the Dharma; they have not reached the further shore of birth.
(Sūyagaḍa 23) Those people who, having understood the connection regarding the boat, are not knowers of the Dharma...
Those speakers who speak thus do not go beyond suffering. Having understood the connection between the two boats, those people who speak thus are not knowers of the Dharma;
they do not go beyond Māra.
They experience various kinds of sufferings again and again within the cycle of saṃsāra, which is agitated by birth, death, and old age;
going through high and low states, they enter the womb for an endless time. (Sūyagaḍa 26)
Thus spoke the son of the Nāya clan, the Great Hero, the supreme Victor. So I say. Furthermore, for some there is rebirth; living beings are born separately. (Sūyagaḍa 27) Thus I say.

They experience pleasure and pain, or they are afflicted from their very state. (Sūyagaḍa 28) That suffering is not self-made, nor is that pleasure or suffering made by another; it is neither beneficial nor non-beneficial. (Sūyagaḍa 29)
"Beings experience [the results of karma] individually—not what was done by themselves, nor by others—but rather what was acquired by them in that manner. Thus it has been declared by some here.
Speaking in this way, these fools consider themselves wise. (Sūyagaḍa 1.1.30)
Not knowing what is fixed and what is unfixed, those of little intelligence—
some who are thus merely "sitting by" (pāsattha) and are even more arrogant—
though they have so applied themselves, they are not liberated from suffering. (Sūyagaḍa 31–32)
Agitated by the fear of ignorance, they wander here and there. (Sūy.
34) Now, one might release that which binds, or at the time of death, one might be freed from the snare of worldly existence; but the fool does not grant that [release]. (Sūy. 35)
"Having no self-control and lacking true wisdom, wandering through the uneven paths,
he is bound by the snares of worldly existence and meets his destruction there.
(Sūyagaḍa 36) "In this same way, some ascetics are of false view and are ignoble."
Those who are suspicious of what is free from suspicion, and non-suspicious of what is suspicious;
those fools who do not suspect the teachings of the Dharma, being unrefined and unskilled, do not suspect the [harmful] undertakings. (Sūyagaḍa 37–38)

Having cast off all personal exertion, having removed all latent tendencies, being free from falsehood and karma— one who has fallen away from this goal is like a deer that has strayed. (Sūyagaḍa 39) Those who do not recognize this are of false views and are ignoble.
Or like deer caught in a snare, they will surely meet their destruction. (Sūyagaḍa 40) Some brahmins and some ascetics claim that knowledge is inherent in themselves;
yet all living beings in the entire world do not know anything at all. (Sūyagaḍa 41)

Just as a barbarian might repeat what has been said to him by one who is not a barbarian, yet does not understand the underlying reason, so too do those of wrong knowledge speak each their own [opinion], merely repeating what they have heard. (Sūyagaḍa 42)
They do not know the meaning of certainty; they are like the ignorant barbarians. (Sūy.
43) The investigation of the ignorant is conducted through ignorance; being unable to discern even themselves, how could they instruct others? (Sūy. 44)
Just as two creatures lost in a forest, both being deluded and following one another in their ignorance, undergo intense suffering;
so too, a blind man leading a blind man travels a long distance along the wrong path. (Sūyagaḍa 1.2.45)
A creature may enter upon a wrong path, or perhaps follow along a road;
likewise, some who seek liberation, thinking "we are followers of the Dharma," may enter upon what is non-Dharma—they do not speak that which is entirely upright. (Sūyagaḍa 46–47)
Thus, some, with their own conjectures, do not attend upon others; with their own conjectures and their own [limited] insights, they are of evil intellect. (Sūy.
48) Thus, explaining by means of mere reasoning, they are unskilled in what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.

They do not find satisfaction in suffering, like a bird in a cage. (Sūyagaḍa 49) Praising themselves and censuring others, those who are thus distracted therein have wandered through the cycle of existence. (Sūyagaḍa 50)

Furthermore, another view proclaimed [by those who hold to action] is the doctrine of the proponents of activity, a ground for the deliberation on karma, which increases the cycle of existence (saṃsāra):
"One who knows does not act with the body; it is the ignorant one who causes injury. (Sūyagaḍa 51)
When questioned, he reveals the other [person], for that which is unmanifest is indeed blameworthy. (Sūy.
52) There are these three ways of undertaking action by which evil is committed:
through one's own exertion, through the dispatching of others, and through approval in the mind. (Sūy. 53)
These indeed are the three means by which evil is committed;
thus, through the purification of one's state of being, one attains nirvāṇa.
A father, for the sake of food, exerts himself for his son while remaining uncontrolled.
Even while eating, the wise one is not defiled by karma. (Sūy.

55) Those who perceive with the mind, their consciousness does not exist [in that way]; for them there is nothing blameless other than that [state], and they are not practitioners of restraint. (Sūy. 56)
Thus, by means of these views, people who are dependent on the abode of pleasure, thinking [these views] to be a refuge, serve what is evil.
Just as one born blind, having boarded a leaking boat... (Sūy. 1.6.7)
Desiring to reach the further shore, he falters along the way. (Sūy.
58) In this same way, certain ascetics who are of false view and ignoble, though longing for the far shore of *saṃsāra*, wander about within *saṃsāra*. (Sūy. 59)

Thus I say: Whatever food has been prepared, even if it is sought by a faithful person for the sake of his own life, he who eats it—even if it is separated by a thousand [other things]—partakes in that which belongs to both sides. (Sūyagaḍa 60)

Not understanding that very [truth], unskilled in the uneven path, they perish like fish in a whirlpool when the water approaches. By the power of the water, they meet their destruction once it has dried up. (Sūy. 61)
By the ḍhaṅkas and the kaṅkas, those who are intent on meat are tormented. (Sūy.
62) In this same way, certain ascetics, seeking pleasure while remaining [in their practice], will be struck down repeatedly, like the fish of Vaisalī. (Sūy. 63)
This is indeed another ignorance;

here, some have declared that this world has its origin in the gods, while others say it originates in Brahmā. Some say the world was created by Īśvara, and others likewise by Prajāpati. (Sūyagaḍa 1.1.64)
Endowed with both soul and non-soul, and accompanied by pleasure and pain—thus was it said by the Great Sage that the world was created by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū).
Māyā was praised by Māra; therefore, the world is without consolation. (Sūyagaḍa 65–66)
Some brahmins and some ascetics say that the world was created from an egg;
they speak thus because they do not know the truth, speaking falsely. According to their own doctrines, they claim the world was made. (Sūyagaḍa 1.1.67)
They do not understand that truth; it is never subject to destruction. (Sūy.
68) Having understood that the arising of what is unpleasant is indeed suffering, how can those who do not understand this arising practice restraint? (Sūy. 69)

The self is pure and free from evil; this has been declared by some here [in this world]. Yet, due to the fault of playfulness, one may fall into transgression therein. Here, the sage who is restrained becomes one who is subsequently free from evil.

Just as rainwater becomes pure and free from impurities once again in autumn, so too does the wise man, having reflected upon these things, become subdued through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Each of those who proclaim themselves teachers has separately proclaimed his own various doctrines concerning the future life. (Sūyagaḍa 71–72)
In their respective stations, they have indeed attained perfection and not otherwise;
oh, here itself they are masters of their own will, endowed with all desires fulfilled! Those perfected ones are free from disease; thus it has been declared by some here.
Men who are obsessed with their own views place only their own success first and speak harshly.
Unrestrained, they will wander again and again through beginningless time, attaining for kalpas the status of Asuras and Kibbisas.
Thus I say:
O living beings! These are no refuge—those fools who imagine themselves wise, having abandoned their former associations; they may become teachers of what ought to be done. (Sūyagaḍa 1.7.6)
Having fully understood that knowledge, a sage should not be infatuated with them, nor should he be drawn toward them or attached to them; rather, he should proceed with moderation.
(Sūyagaḍa 1.7.77) Furthermore, some here have declared that [householders] possess both possessions and violence.
Free from possessions and free from harmful undertakings, let the monk wander as a refuge. A wise man should seek his food among what has been prepared;
he should go about for alms with what is given, being without greed and fully liberated, avoiding all humiliation.

One should examine popular opinion; here, that which has been proclaimed by some is born of perverted understanding, inconsistent with other accounts, and following after them. [Yet others say: "The world is infinite, eternal, permanent, and does not perish. (Sūyagaḍa 1.1.2.80)
"The world is finite according to the doctrine"—thus the wise one perceives deeply. (Sūy.
81) "He understands it to be immeasurable; thus it has been taught by some here"—"everywhere there is a limit"—thus the wise one perceives deeply. (Sūy. 82)
Whatever beings there may be, whether moving or stationary, they exist within the cycle of existence; that which makes them moving or stationary is their own conduct.
The vast activity of the world leads to various divergent paths.

All [beings] experience undesirable suffering, therefore all are to be spared from harm. This indeed is the essence for the knower: that he does not injure anything. Having understood this much, one should follow the principle of non-violence.

Having lived the life and being free from worldly attachments, the sage, having thoroughly guarded against the influx [of karma], remains constantly restrained in his conduct, posture, and bed, as well as in his food and drink.
(Sūyagaḍa 86) By means of these three states, the sage is ever restrained.
One should discern the high, the burning, the hidden, and that which is neutral. (Sūy.

87) But the sage who is always self-restrained, who has closed the five gates of influx, and who is white [pure], a mendicant neither attached to nor detached from worldly things, should wander forth until liberation. (Sūy. 88)
Thus I say. [Veyāliya:
Awaken! Why do you not awaken? For awakening is indeed difficult to attain after death.
The nights do not return, nor is life easily obtained again. (Sūy.
89) See how the young and the old, even those still in the womb, pass away; just as a weaver takes up a ball of thread, so too does life break off at the exhaustion of its duration. (Sūy. 90)
One is plundered by deceptions and by loved ones; a good rebirth after death is not easily obtained.
Having perceived these dangers, one should desist from violent undertakings and listen well.
Regarding this world, beings wander separately; living creatures are plundered by their own karmas.
One who takes up [the burden] through his own actions cannot escape it when it has not yet been exhausted. (Sūy.
92) Gods, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Asuras, those who roam the earth, and reptiles; kings, men, merchants, and Brahmins—even they, being afflicted by suffering, must abandon their stations. (Sūy. 93)
Beings, greedy for sensual pleasures and attached to them, are companions of their own karma;
in due time, they perish like a palmyra tree when its bonds are severed—thus, at the exhaustion of its lifespan, it breaks apart.
(Sūyagaḍa 94) And even he who may be very learned, a righteous brahmin, or a mendicant...

"Stupefied by his own actions, he is tormented intensely by those very karmas. But look at him who has risen through discernment; even while not yet having crossed over here, he speaks with certainty: 'Will you know the near shore or the far shore? You are being tormented by karmas in the midst of the stream. (Sūyagaḍa 95–96)
Even if one wanders naked and emaciated, even if one eats only at the end of the month—
if one is here corrupted by deceit and the like, one will enter the womb again and again.
By evil karma, O Puruṣādānīya, the life of humans has its limit.
In this world, people who are intoxicated by sensual pleasures and lack self-restraint fall into delusion. (Sūy.
98) Live with victory and remain disciplined; the paths involving living beings are difficult to traverse. Therefore, follow the very instruction rightly proclaimed by the heroes. (Sūy. 99)
Free from passion, heroic, and fully awakened, they have desisted from all forms of deceitful conduct and crushing;
they do not kill living beings in any way. Having desisted from evil, they are extinguished. It is not only I who am being destroyed; living beings in the world are also being destroyed.
Thus, one should dwell with companions; being free from anger, one should endure when assailed. (Sūy.

101) Having shaken off the mortar-like [impurities] like plaster, one should emaciate the body through fasting. Here, one should go forth in non-violence alone; this is the Dharma proclaimed by the Sage. (Sūy. 102)
Just as a bird covered in dust shakes off and scatters the clinging grey powder,
so does the ascetic Brahmin, through diligent application, destroy his karma.
[He sees] the mendicant who has risen for the practice of alms-gathering, the ascetic established in his proper station.
The young and the old entreat him; even if they wither away, people do not obtain [what they seek]. (Sūy.
104) If they utter piteous cries, if they weep for the sake of their sons, they are unable to make the steadfast monk, who has risen [in renunciation], turn back. (Sūy. 105)

Even if they are led away by desires, even if they are bound and taken home, and even if they do not wish for life itself, they cannot be made to remain [in the world] if they have attained that [state]. Their mothers, fathers, sons, and wives will grieve for them as they possess them with attachment. (Sūy. 106)
Do not nourish yourself, for by nourishing you, you will also abandon the other world. (Sūy. 107) Attached to various things through various means, unrestrained men fall into delusion;
seized by the uneven with the uneven, those evildoers become even more arrogant. (Sūy. 108)

Therefore, O wise one, look with discernment; being desisted from evil, calmed, humble, and a hero, follow the great path—the certain way leading to liberation, which is the road of the Vaitālīya. Having entered this path, be restrained in mind, speech, and body. (Sūyagaḍa 1.6.22)
Having abandoned wealth, kinsmen, and worldly undertakings, one should wander well-restrained.
Thus I say.
Just as a snake sheds its skin, so does he cast off passion; having understood this, the sage does not become intoxicated.
A brahmin who, by means of another's food, brings about his own welfare while being a source of reproach to others, is a mere glutton.

He who despises other people wanders extensively through the cycle of existence; yet, having obtained this very [human] state, the sage, understanding it here, does not become intoxicated. (Sūyagaḍa 111–112)
Whether one be a leader or even a messenger sent by another, he who has entered the path of silence should never feel shame;
rather, he should always practice the doctrine with equanimity in any pure form of self-restraint as a wandering ascetic. (Sūyagaḍa 1.13)
The wise one, being concentrated and detached, passed away while still alive.
Having looked far ahead, the sage [regarded] the Dharma of the past as well as that of the future.
Thus, O Brahmin, when questioned with harsh words, he remained unprovoked and conducted himself according to the doctrine.
Always victorious when fully wise, the sage should proclaim the Dharma with equanimity;
always subtle and untainted, the Brahmin should neither be angry nor conceited.
(Sūyagaḍa 1.16) When one is well-restrained amidst the praise of many people, that man is independent of all things.
He who is always free from agitation brought forth the Dharma of Kāśyapa.
(Sūy. 117) Many living beings exist separately; each seeks its own moment of existence.
The wise one, established in the state of silence, practiced restraint therein. (Sūy. 118)
The sage who has reached the further shore of the Dhamma stands at the end of all violent exertion;
those who possess the sense of "mine" grieve for him, yet they do not obtain their own possessions.
The wise man knows that [possessiveness] brings suffering in this world and suffering upon suffering in the next world.
"Knowing that this [world] is indeed subject to destruction, who would dwell in a household?

Having understood the great entanglement, as well as the homage and worship found here—which are subtle thorns difficult to extract—one who possesses discernment should abandon intimacy. (Sūyagaḍa 1.2.2.120–121)
A monk, devoted to ascetic practice and vigor, guarding his speech and restrained within himself, should dwell alone in a place, a seat, or a bed, remaining concentrated.
He should not long for anything, nor should he be attached; being self-controlled, he should frequent an empty house as his dwelling.
When questioned, he should not utter a word; he should neither cut [grass] nor spread out a bed of straw. (Sūy.
123) Where the sun has set and there is no commotion, the sage should endure both the level and the uneven ground.
There may be wandering ascetics or even terrifying beings, or perhaps there may be *śirīṣa* spiders. (Sūy. 124)
Whether from horizontal [beings], humans, or celestial beings, he should endure the three kinds of afflictions;
the great sage, having gone to an empty dwelling, should not lose his hair-pores [i.e., his composure].
He should not long for life, nor should he be one who seeks honor.
Terrors enter into the interior of a monk who has gone to an empty house.
For the protector who is well-disciplined and who fears a solitary seat, that [state] is called equanimity (sāmāiya), provided he does not manifest himself out of fear. (Sūy. 126–127)

For a wise sage who consumes food boiled in hot water and stands firm amidst the heat, association with women is unwholesome; likewise, there is a lack of concentration for one who has gone thus [to such association].
For a monk who has committed an offense and speaks harshly with accusation, [there is no peace].
The wise man should avoid many faults and should not engage in contentious disputes. (Sūy.

129) They say that he who rejects cold water, who makes no promises, and who avoids even a drop [of forbidden food], observes the *sāmāyika* vow—namely, he who does not eat food belonging to a householder. (Sūy. 130)
Life, they say, has no fixed measure; nevertheless, the foolish person acts with arrogance.
The fool is destroyed by his own evils—having understood this, the sage does not become intoxicated.
Driven by desire, these beings fall away; they are full of deceit and obscured by delusion.
The Brahmins flee from the rain; they endure the cold and heat with their speech. (Sūy.
132) Just as an unvanquished gambler, skilled in dice, having taken a loaded die, does not play for the past, nor for the future, nor even for the present. (Sūy. 133)
Thus, in this world, the Protector has proclaimed the unsurpassed Dharma;
the wise man, regarding it as beneficial and supreme, should grasp it and abandon the rest, just as one leaves behind husks to take the grain.
This, O Uttara, is declared for the sake of human beings; thus have I heard regarding the "village-dharmas."

Those who have abstained and exerted themselves, following the Dharma of Kāśyapa—those who practice this well-proclaimed teaching according to the great sage’s doctrine—they have truly exerted themselves and have risen up;
they support one another through the Dharma. (Sūyagaḍa 1.3.5–6)
One should not look back at one's former home, desiring to shake off worldly attachments;
those who are not troubled by such things know the supreme equanimity.
A restrained monk should neither act as a witness nor should he mediate for others.
Having understood the unsurpassed Dharma, one should not engage in bodily actions nor harbor pride.

A Brāhmaṇa should not offer praise for what is concealed, nor should he boast or proclaim himself; rather, he should possess well-discerned discernment toward those by whom the purified, cleansed, and washed [Dharma] has been humbly embraced. (Sūyagaḍa 1.3.8–9)

Free from anger, patient, well-restrained, established in the Dharma, and possessing the vigor of ascetic practice, one should wander with senses composed; for one’s own welfare is attained only with difficulty.
Surely this was not heard by you in the past, or perhaps it was not practiced accordingly.
This was declared by the Sage, the Knower, who sees everything in the world.
Having thus understood this great distinction in the Dharma, many people, following the will of their teacher, have become restrained and have crossed over the great flood. (Sūyagaḍa 1.4.141–142)
Thus I say:
For the monk whose karma is restrained, whatever suffering has been encountered from non-restraint is shed through self-discipline; having abandoned death, the wise proceed on. (Sūy. 143)
Those who are satisfied with requests for favors are declared to be equal to those who have crossed over [the flood].
Therefore, look upward; having seen that sensual pleasures are fraught with disease, the kings here maintain the supreme [dharma] as proclaimed by the merchants. (Sūyagaḍa 144)
Thus have the supreme great vows been declared, along with the abstention from eating at night. But those men here who pursue pleasure, who are obsessed with sensual desires and infatuated by them—
reckless like a miser— they do not understand the higher concentration.
Just as a bull, when exhausted by the yoke and weakened by the weight of its load, becomes feeble within, lacking strength, and being unable to pull, sinks down in exhaustion;
even so, the wise man, understanding the pursuit of sensual desires, should abandon attachment to them this very day. (Sūyagaḍa 1.4.7)

One who desires should not desire sensual pleasures, whether they be obtained or unobtained. (Sūy. 148) Lest one become a non-virtuous person later on, one should transcend [the world] and discipline oneself. The non-virtuous person grieves; he thunders and laments greatly. (Sūy. 149)

"Behold, this life is indeed fleeting; the youth of a hundred-year lifespan quickly perishes. Like crows in a temporary dwelling, men who are greedy and infatuated with sensual pleasures do not awaken.
Those here who are dependent on violence, who wield weapons against themselves, and who are exclusively destructive—" Sūy. 150.
He shall go to the world of the dead, toward the demonic quarter for a long time. (Sūy.
151) They say that life has no fixed limit, yet even so, the foolish person acts with impudence;
seeing what purpose is served by the present, does he not see the world beyond? (Sūy. 152)

One who has not seen yet sees through those who have seen; indeed, one who has not seen gains the vision of faith through the deluding karma that has been committed. Suffering again and again in delusion, one should become disenchanted with praise and honor. (Sūyagaḍa 1.6.24)
Thus, being guarded by his companions and restrained toward living beings as toward himself,

even if a man dwells in a house, he who is gradually restrained toward living beings and is well-restrained everywhere according to the doctrine shall go to the world of the gods. (Sūyagaḍa 1.5.154–155)
Having heard the instruction of the Blessed One, one should apply oneself there to the truth;
having everywhere subdued greed, the monk should gather pure alms.
Knowing everything, he should abide [in restraint], established in the Dharma and energetic in his spiritual practice.
One who is self-controlled, disciplined, ever-striving, intent on the self, and established in the highest goal—[such a one does not rely on worldly things]. (Sūy.
157) Wealth, offspring, and kinsmen—the fool considers these to be his refuge, thinking, "These are mine;
I belong to them. Yet they are no protection, no refuge is found there. (Sūy. 158)
Whether in the face of approaching misfortune, or when suffering has already arrived, the wise man does not regard as a refuge the destiny and rebirth of a solitary being.
All living beings are fashioned by their own karma; they are subject to suffering that is unavoidable. (Sūyagaḍa 1.5.2.19)
Deceitful people, terrified by fear and afflicted by birth, old age, and death, wander about.

Having understood that this very moment is fleeting, and that enlightenment is said not to be easily obtained, one should endure it with such composure; thus spoke the Jina and his remaining disciples.
In former times there were monks, and even now there are those who are well-disciplined;
they are said to possess these qualities, following the Dharma of Kāśyapa.
One should not kill living beings in any of the three ways; for one's own benefit, free from worldly motives, and self-restrained.
Thus have the infinite ones been perfected; so too are those who are present now and those yet to come in the future.

Thus spoke he, the one possessed of unsurpassed knowledge, the one possessed of unsurpassed vision, the bearer of unsurpassed knowledge and vision—the Arhat, the Blessed One, the Son of the Jñātṛ clan, as declared at Vaiśālī. (Sūyagaḍa 163–164)
Thus I say.
[The Understanding of Afflictions] One considers oneself brave as long as one does not see a conqueror.
Like Śiśupāla against the great Arhat, he fought those of firm resolve.
Brave men were born at the head of the battle; when the combat had arrived, the mother did not recognize her son as he was distinguished by victory. (Sūyagaḍa 165–166)

In this way, even when unassailed and unskilled in the conduct of a monk, one considers oneself a hero as long as one does not practice austerity. When, in the winter months, the cold wind touches him... (Sūy. 1.6.7)
There the dull-witted despair, like Kṣatriyas deprived of their kingdom. (Sūy.
168) When scorched by the heat of summer in a palace that is very cool, there the dull-witted despair, like fish in a shallow pool. (Sūy. 169)

"Constantly begging for alms is painful; it is difficult to satisfy, leads to weariness, and results in misfortune"—thus have various people said. Not paying heed to these words, whether in villages or in cities... [Sūyagaḍa 1.70]
In that regard, the weak-spirited despond, like cowards in battle. (Sūy.
171) Some hungry monk is bitten and mangled by a dog;
therein the weak-spirited despond, like living beings scorched by heat. (Sūy. 172)
Some speak thus:
"These are those who have come to the crossroads, intent on service; these are the 'Evañjīvinas' (those who live by such means).
Some practice asceticism, naked and carrying alms-bowls.
Shaven-headed, with limbs ruined by itching, covered in filth and lacking composure—thus some have gone astray;
ignorant themselves, those dull-witted ones, obscured by delusion, go from darkness to darkness. (Sūy. 1.1.74–75)
Bitten by gadflies and mosquitoes, and unable to endure the touch of grass, I have not seen the next world; at most, there may be death. [Sūy.
176] Tormented by the plucking of their hair, they are devoted to the practice of celibacy.

In this regard, the dull-witted falter like fish that have entered a net. In the practice of self-inflicted violence, some who possess perverted dispositions and have fallen into a state of passion are destroyed by ignoble men. (Sūy. 177–178)
At the frontier, some fools bind a well-behaved monk, thinking him to be a spy or a thief; they strike him with whips, or with their fists, or even with stones.
(Sūyagaḍa 1.2.3.17) There, he is covered with sticks, or with fists, or else with fruits.
The fool does not remember his own faults, just as a woman does not recall her wayward course when she has gone astray.
O people! These are all-pervasive afflictions, harsh and difficult to endure;
like elephants entangled in a snare, the weak-spirited have returned home under their power. (Sūyagaḍa 1.8.18–19)
Thus I say: Subtle are the attachments of the monks, which are difficult to overcome; therein some despond, and are unable to exert themselves. (Sūy. 182)
Seeing us, some of the leaders weep as they surround us:
"O dear one! You have been raised by us; O dear one, whose are you that you abandon us? "Your father is old, dear one; these young women are your sisters. (Sūyagaḍa 183)
"O father! Why do you abandon your own brothers and sisters?
Support your mother and father; in this way the world will be [righteous].
Indeed, O father, this is the worldly custom for those who protect their mother. (Sūy. 184–185)
"O Father! Your daughter-in-law is gentle in her speech; your sons, O Father, are young, and your wife is new—let her not go to another man.
Come, Father, let us go home; let us not work together with them. (Sūyagaḍa 1.8.6)
"Let us see her seed as well; let us first go to our own home.
O father! Having gone, one may return again; by that [act] one does not cease to be a śramaṇa. Who is able to prevent you from moving against your will? (Sūy. 187–188)
"Whatever property we have, dear one! even all that gold and business assets—we shall give all that to you. Thus they entreat him, moved by compassion. (Sūy.
Unbound by attachments, he then abandons the household life. (Sūy.
190) Just as a creeper growing in the forest entwines a tree, even so do kinsmen bind him with a lack of composure. (Sūy. 191)

He is not bound by attachments, like an elephant that slips away from its pursuers during the onset of a new rut, or like a boar that escapes from close range. These attachments of men are as difficult to cross as the depths of the underworld. (Sūyagaḍa 192)
How many suffer here, being infatuated by excessive attachments?
Having fully understood that, a monk should recognize that all attachments are great influxes;
having heard the unsurpassed Dharma, he should not long for worldly life. (Sūy. 193–194)
There are whirlpools here, O Kāśyapa, which have been proclaimed by the Buddha; where the Buddhas advance, there the unawakened ones sink.
Kings and royal ministers, Brahmins, or even Kshatriyas—Sūy. 195.
They invite the monks who live in accordance with the Dharma with worldly enjoyments:
"O Great Sage! Enjoy these excellent pleasures—by means of elephants, chariots, and carriages, and by traveling to pleasure gardens; we shall honor you! (Sūyagaḍa 196–197)
"O long-lived one! We shall provide you with these enjoyments: clothing, perfumes, ornaments, women, and beds; we shall honor you. O virtuous ones!
Whatever discipline you have practiced in the state of a mendicant—" (Sūyagaḍa 198)
"For one living in a house, everything is available in that way. (Sūy.
199) "For you who have been wandering for so long, where now is there any fault?"—in this way he entices him, like a pig with wild rice. (Sūy. 200)
Chastised by their conduct as monks, yet unable to endure it there, the dull-witted become despondent, like the weak in a garden.
Unable to endure even the coarse ascetic practices, they are tormented by their penances.
There the dull-witted falter, like old oxen in a garden.
Having received such an invitation, they become infatuated and greedy for women; addicted to sensual pleasures and being urged on, they go back home. (Sūy. 202–203)
Thus I say:
Just as in the midst of battle, a coward turns his back and seeks a bracelet, a thicket, or a hiding place—for who knows defeat? (Sūy. 204)
"Of all moments, this moment is such a moment;

we are being defeated, we are falling away!"—thus the coward ponders. In this way, some ascetics, perceiving themselves to be weak... [Sūy. 205]... Thus indeed do some ascetics, having recognized their own lack of strength...
Seeing the danger that lies ahead, one should disregard this worldly renown.
Who knows the transformation [of destiny]? Whether women or water, when driven by circumstances, we shall not speak [of them as obstacles], for there is nothing that is preordained.
Thus they examine [the world], yet those who examine it remain caught in doubt, like travelers unacquainted with the path.
But those who are leaders among the wise, like heroes at the time of battle, [remain steadfast]. *Sūyagaḍa 208*
They do not strike their backs; what could be worse than death? (Sūy.
209) Thus having risen, the monk should cast off the bonds of the household;
having abandoned worldly undertakings in every direction, he should wander for the sake of his own self. (Sūy. 210)
Some revile that monk who lives in accordance with the holy life;
those who revile him in this way are themselves lacking in internal composure. Bound together by a common purpose, they are mutually infatuated. (Sūyagaḍa 2.1.11)
"Give alms to the sick; whatever you have, give it away. (Sūy.
212) "In this way, you who remain full of passion, living in mutual dependence, having lost your true splendor and integrity, are far from reaching the further shore of saṃsāra. (Sūy. 213)
If they should address them thus: "O monks who are experts in liberation, by speaking in this way you are indeed serving a dual path;
you eat from their feet, or [you accept food] brought for the sick. (Sūy. 214)
Having consumed that water containing living beings, or whatever has been prepared for his sake, he suffers intense torment from the heat [of his fever].
Though he scratches himself excessively, being distracted and lacking composure, it is better for one who is not ill not to scratch at all. (Sūy. 215–216)
Instructed by him who was free from worldly attachment, those wise ones realized:
"This is not our own path; it is speech and action that were not properly examined.
Such as this is this speech, which, like a bamboo at its tip, will only lead one to ruin.

It is proper for householders to eat food brought to them, but not so for monks. That which is called the "proclamation of Dharma" involves violence and is not purified; indeed, it was previously established by such [wrong] views. (Sūy. 218–219)
Failing to strive by means of all appropriate methods, they then reject right speech;
thus, overcome by passion and hatred and struck down by falsehood, they become once again arrogant. (Sūy. 220)
When reviled, they seek refuge [in patience] like crags in a mountain. (Sūy.
221) One who is composed in self should perform many virtuous practices; whatever does not cause conflict with others, that one should practice. (Sūy. 222)
Having taken up this Dhamma proclaimed by Kāśyapa,
a monk, being composed and free from illness, should provide for one who is ill.
Having understood the excellent Dhamma, he who possesses right view is fully extinguished.
Having warded off obstacles, you should wander forth until final liberation.
Thus I say.
The great men of old, whose wealth was their austerity, have said this.
Through water they attained perfection; therein the weak man desponds.
Namī Vaidéha did not eat, while Rāmōttara did eat; likewise the seer Bāhu ate water, as did Nārāyaṇa.
Āsile, Dēvile, Cēva, Dīvāyaṇa, and the great seer Pārāsara, having eaten water, seeds, and green vegetables—these were formerly great men who were declared here as authoritative. (Sūy. 227)
"Having eaten and drunk, they have attained perfection"—this is what I have heard.
But in this matter, the dull-witted falter like donkeys whose strength is exhausted; they crawl backward, like those who move on their haunches in a state of confusion. (Sūy. 228–229)
In this regard, some indeed say: "Pleasure is found through pleasure;
therein lies the noble path and the supreme state of concentration.
Do not disregard this, lest you destroy much [merit] with a little.
Those who do not seek liberation from this [bondage] suffer like those carrying iron;
they persist in the taking of life, being unrestrained in false speech, persisting in taking what is not given, in sexual intercourse, and in possessiveness. (Sūy. 231–232)

Thus some unrefined fools, having fallen under the sway of women and turning their backs on the teaching of the Jina, proclaim themselves to be "near" (pāsattha), just as one might squeeze a boil or a tumor for a mere moment. (Sūy. 233)
Thus, regarding women who speak [flatteringly], what fault could there be in that?
Just as the one named Mandhātā drank water even when it was still, so too, regarding women who speak [flatteringly], what fault could there be in that? (Sūy. 234–235)
Just as the tawny crane drinks water silently, so too [should one behave] among women who speak seductively; what fault could there be in that? (Sūy.
236) Thus, some who are "nearby" (pāsatthā), holding wrong views and lacking nobility, act in this manner.

Overcome by sensual desires like young women longing for their lovers, they do not see the future; seeking only the present, they suffer later when their life-span and youth have perished. (Sūy. 237–238)

Those wise ones who have completed their course so that they do not suffer remorse later, being liberated from bondage, do not long for life. Just as the Vaitaraṇī river is considered difficult to cross here in this world, Sūy. 239.
Thus, in this world, women are difficult to overcome for those who are full of delusion.
But those by whom association with women and their honors have been cast behind them, having rejected all this, they remain in perfect composure. (Sūyagaḍa 240–241)
These merchants shall cross over the flood where living beings are despondent, being tormented by their own karma;
having fully understood this, the monk should wander, well-restrained and self-controlled. (Sūy. 242)
One should avoid false speech and renounce taking what is not given.

Whether above, below, or across, toward whatever beings there may be, whether mobile or stationary, one should practice restraint everywhere; this is declared to be peace and nirvāṇa. (Sūyagaḍa 243–244)
Having taken up this Dhamma proclaimed by Kāśyapa,
a monk, being composed and free from illness, should attend to one who is ill.
Having understood the excellent Dhamma, he— possessing right view— is fully extinguished.
Having warded off obstacles, you should wander as a mendicant until final liberation.
Thus I say.
[The Comprehension of Women]
"Having abandoned mother and father, as well as former associations, I shall wander alone with a companion, having desisted from sexual intercourse and dwelling in solitude.
[The woman replied: "That subtle enticement by a disguised person—women are dull-witted. (Sūyagaḍa 247)
They even know the stratagem by which some monks become attached:
they sit on lotus roots in concealment; they constantly smear their bodies with fragrant substances; they even bite themselves below; and they scratch their arms, heads, and armpits. (Sūy. 248–249)
When women invite him with suitable beds and seats, he should recognize these very things as such, as well as various kinds of palaces;
he should not fix his gaze upon them, nor should he entertain any rash impulses toward them. (Sūyagaḍa 250)
One should not even dwell in their company; thus the self is well-guarded. (Sūy.
251) Having been addressed and informed, one invites the monk with words;
he should recognize these very things as various kinds of sounds. (Sūy. 252)
Having approached with many mental bonds, piteous and humble, they speak sweet words and entice him with various tales.
Just as one might lure a fearless lion wandering alone with meat, so do they approach from the side. (Sūyagaḍa 253)
Women bind even a certain self-restrained mendicant there;

they bend him further toward themselves, just as a wheelwright bends a felloe by means of a sequence [of heating], or as a deer caught in a snare, though struggling, is not released from it. (Sūy. 254–255)
Then he regrets it afterwards, like one who has eaten milk-rice mixed with poison;
thus, having adopted detachment, cohabitation is not fitting for the wise man.
Therefore, one should avoid women, knowing them to be like a thorn smeared with poison.
He who has mastery over his senses does not even enter noble families for the sake of an assault. (Sūy.
257) Those who are greedy for this kind of alms-seeking are among the unvirtuous; even if he is a learned ascetic, such a monk should not dwell together with women. (Sūy. 258)
An ascetic should not form intimate attachments with sisters, daughters-in-law, nurses, or even female slaves, nor with grown women or young maidens.
Furthermore, upon seeing a relative or a friend, he may at times feel affection.

Beings are greedy for sensual pleasures; they think, "This man is one who protects and nourishes us. (Sūy. 260) Even upon seeing an ascetic who remains indifferent [to worldly affairs], some become angry there, or because food is not provided, they become suspicious of the fault of women. (Sūy. 261)
They form intimacies with those women, having fallen away from the practice of meditative concentration; therefore, such ascetics do not attain their own welfare through their seated assemblies.
Having abandoned many households, some have entered into a state of association with householders.
The lazy proclaim only the path of stability;
they boast of their vigor in the assembly, yet they commit evil deeds in secret.
Those who know them recognize them as such: "This man is deceitful and a great rogue. (Sūyagaḍa 263–264)
One's own evil deed does not vanish; even when exhorted, the fool persists in his ways.
Do not act with disregard for the Veda; when reproved, he becomes weary and resentful once more.
Even those who have risen above [worldly life] remain devoted to the nurture of women—men who are exhausted by the pursuit of female company.
Many women fall under the power of those who are attached to the fifty [sensual objects]. (Sūy.
266) [They endure] even the cutting off of hands and feet, or the excision of flesh from the thighs; they undergo the torment of heat, being split open and drenched with salt water. (Sūy. 267)
Some, tormented by their own evil deeds, endure the cutting off of ears and noses and the cutting of the throat;
yet they do not say, "I will never do this again. This is what has been heard thus from some, for even the female gender has been well-explained [in the scriptures].
Having spoken thus, they either act accordingly through their speech or through their deeds. (Sūy.
269) One thinks one thing in the mind, speaks another with the voice, and acts yet another through deed;
therefore, a monk should not place his trust in them, knowing that women are full of deceit. (Sūy. 270)
A young woman, having put on variegated ornaments and garments, might say to a monk:
"I shall practice the religious life under a tree; explain the Dharma to me, O Venerable One!
Or, through her profession of faith, she might say: "I am a female lay follower and a fellow-practitioner of the monks. (Sūyagaḍa 271)
Just as a wise man, though skilled, might perish when trapped in a jar of oil;
just as a fire enveloped in a jar of oil, once quickly heated, goes to its destruction—so too do ascetics go to their destruction through living in association with women. (Sūy. 272–273)
They commit evil karma; when questioned, they indeed say thus:
"I do not do evil," or "This one marked me. This is the mark of a fool's dullness, and that he denies what he has done again and again. (Sūy. 274)
One who desires honor and is despondent commits double the sin. (Sūy.
275) They say that a naked ascetic, worthy of being beheld and self-restrained, should accept an invitation for clothing, a bowl, food, or drink. (Sūy. 276)
In this way, one should understand wild rice; one who is bound by the snares of the senses should not desire to return to the household life, for the dull-witted man falls back into delusion.
Thus I say. (Sūyagaḍa 277)

One should never take delight in sensual pleasures; rather, one who desires enjoyment should eventually become dispassionate toward them by hearing about the enjoyments of the ascetics, just as some monks consume [their food]. But if a monk, having fallen into that very snare, becomes infatuated and remains attached to sensual desires...
Having broken open [the head] and then having pulled out the hair, they strike with their fists. (Sūy.
279) "O Keśin, if you, as a mendicant, do not dwell together with women, I shall pluck out your hair; otherwise, you must wander [alone] without me. (Sūy. 280)
Now, when he has been found, they send him, saying: "Go and fetch alābu-cuttings of that kind, and bring back vaggū fruits.
Wood is for cooking meat, or there will be a fire tonight.
"Have sandals made for me; come now, massage my back. (Sūy.
282) Look after my clothes; bring me food and drink.
Permit me [to use] perfume, a broom, and a barber. (Sūy. 283)
Give me collyrium and ornaments, a cock, and lodhra along with lodhra flowers; bamboo, palāśīya, and pills;
as well as koṣṭha, tagara, and aguru, all ground together with usīra. (Sūyagaḍa 284)
"Take oil for the mouth, bilva fruits for the storehouse, and Nandi-cuṇṇa powder for the protection [of the goods];
know the parasol and the rain-garment, the weapon for the sake of good cutting, and have a dark-blue cloth dyed. (Sūyagaḍa 285–286)
Know that the beautiful fan is for the sake of cooling the body; the myrobalan fruits, the water-vessel, the cosmetic box, and the ointment-stick are for me.
Know the fan to be for the sake of fanning. (Sūy. 287) And bring the tweezers, the comb, and the Ceylonese sandalwood paste.
"Provide a mirror and offer tooth-cleansing wood.
Know that betel-nut, betel-leaf, a needle, thread, a storehouse, and a loom are required; as well as a good mortar and pestle, and a vessel for straining alkaline water. (Sūy. 288–289)
"O venerable one! Dig a pit for the outcaste, a pit for the water-carrier, a latrine, and a well for my daughter;
and a trough for the cowherd’s calf, and a small water-jar with a drum for the young girl. (Sūy. 290)
Know that [they seek] a dwelling, a residence, and food. (Sūy.
291) And for the sake of a couch with new cloth, for the sake of footstools and bridges, or for the sake of a longing for a son, they become slaves under command. (Sūy. 292)
When the fruit has arisen, take it or else abandon it; for some who nourish their children become like oxen carrying a burden.
Even kings, having risen [from their thrones], act as nurses supporting a child. (Sūyagaḍa 293)
Even though they are well-restrained in mind, they remain like swans that are constantly preoccupied with their plumage. (Sūy.

294) Thus, for many previous lives, those who have devoted themselves to the pursuit of enjoyments—whether as slaves, or like sacrificial victims, or like messengers, or like mere cattle—they are not truly anyone at all. (Sūy. 295)
Thus indeed one should avoid solicitation, intimacy, and cohabitation with those of such a kind; for these sensual pleasures are blameworthy and are declared to be such.
A monk should not touch a woman, nor an animal, nor should he himself grasp anything with his hand. (Sūy.
297) The wise one of perfectly pure conduct, the knower, should avoid actions performed by others through mind, speech, and body; as a homeless ascetic, he endures all sensations. (Sūy. 298)
Thus spoke that hero, whose passion and delusion were shaken off; therefore, O monk, being inwardly purified and well-liberated, you should wander for the sake of final liberation.
Thus I say. (Sūy. 299)
[Regarding the lack of knowledge concerning hell:
"I shall ask the omniscient great seer: 'How are the hells ahead characterized by torment?
O Sage, you who know, speak to me who do not know: How indeed do the foolish go to hell? (Sūy. 300)
Thus questioned by me, the great-souled Kāśyapa, who possesses swift wisdom, spoke this:
"I shall explain the difficult path of suffering and evil, which is rooted in the past and characterized by wicked deeds.
Whatever fools here, seeking worldly life, perform sinful and cruel actions... (Sūy. 301)
They fall into hells of terrible form, thick with darkness, and of intense torment. (Sūy.
302) Those living beings who, for the sake of their own pleasure, harm mobile creatures and those that are stationary;
who injure them and become takers of what is not given; they do not learn anything of what leads to the welfare of the self. (Sūy. 303)
The fool who is arrogant, a reviler of many living beings, and lacking in self-restraint, meets with slaughter;
at the time of his end, he goes to hell, falling headlong and entering a miserable state.
(Sūyagaḍa 304) Having heard the cries of those who are being harmed, "Kill! Cut! Pierce! Burn!"—he enters that evil destination.
Those hell-beings, their consciousness shattered by fear, wonder: "In which direction indeed shall we go? (Sūy.

305) As they approach ground that is like a blazing, glowing mass of embers, being burned, they cry out piteously; there they remain for a long duration, screaming at the top of their voices. (Sūy. 306)
If they have heard that the Vaitaraṇī is difficult to cross, with currents as sharp as a razor's edge, yet they cross that difficult Vaitaraṇī, being driven by spears and struck by weapons;
those of evil conduct are pierced by stakes, having approached a boat from which they have utterly abandoned themselves. (Sūyagaḍa 307)
But others, having been pierced with long three-pronged spikes, are driven down into the earth.
Having tied heavy stones to the necks of some, they cause them to sink into vast waters.
Others are tossed about in the mud of lotus-stalks, in sand, and in glowing embers; there they are made to roll and are roasted. (Sūy. 308–309)
That which is called "sunless" is a place of great terror, a vast and blinding darkness difficult to traverse, extending upwards, downwards, and across all directions, where a fire burns.
In that cave where the fire blazes intensely, the one who lacks knowledge is consumed, his wisdom lost. (Sūyagaḍa 310)
And always [they experience] that pitiable state of existence, which is deeply degrading and characterized by extreme suffering. (Sūy.
311) Having ignited four fires, there the doers of cruel deeds torment the fool;
staying there and being tormented, they are like fish caught in a living fire. (Sūy. 312)
Tranquility is indeed a great relief, for those hell-beings who have performed evil deeds are bound by their hands and feet and, with axes in hand, they cut them like planks.
Again, while their limbs are smeared with blood and excrement, broken and crushed, they are being turned over.
The hell-beings see them quivering like living fish on a red-hot iron plate.
Yet they do not turn to ash there; enduring the intensity of their experience through sharp, piercing agony, they suffer as miserable beings here for their own evil deeds. (Sūyagaḍa 314–315)
And there, in that place of intense whirling, they cast themselves into a fiercely blazing fire;
they find no peace in that perilous place, yet they continue to practice penance, tormented by their own unworthiness.
A sound like that of a city on fire is heard there, as words are uttered from those who have been brought to that state of suffering.

Those whose karma has arisen, being themselves subject to arisen karma, torment themselves again and again. O evil ones, they deprive living beings of their lives; I shall explain that to you exactly as it is:
there, the foolish are tormented by all the punishments resulting from their own past deeds. (Sūy. 317–318)
Being tormented, they fall into hell, into that place of intense heat which is full of foulness;
there they remain, devouring foul things, being overcome by their karma, and are devoured by worms.
Furthermore, it is a place of constant, total heat, intensely oppressive, and of a nature of extreme suffering.
Having thrown him into cauldrons and divided his body, they heat his head with fire. (Sūy.
320) They cut the fool’s nose with a razor; they also cut both his lips and his ears;
having pulled out his tongue to the length of a span, they heat it with sharp spears. (Sūy. 321)
Screaming there like cymbals struck together, those fools wail throughout the night;
they drip with blood, pus, and flesh, their limbs scorched by fire and smeared with caustic salt.
(Sūyagaḍa 322) If those children have drunk blood and pus, they become fires of youth with exceeding radiant power.
There are large cauldrons, many fathoms deep, standing upright and filled with blood and pus.

Having thrown the fools into them, they boil them while they cry out in distress, wailing piteously; parched with thirst, they are made to drink molten copper that is hot as fire, and as they are being consumed, they shriek even more piteously. (Sūyagaḍa 323–324)

Having deceived themselves by means of themselves in this world, they remain for hundreds of thousands of previous aeons in those states of existence, having performed many cruel deeds; as the karma was wrought, so is its burden. Having accumulated filth, these ignoble ones are utterly deprived of what is desired and beloved.
Those foul-smelling and entirely harsh touches, consisting of putrid corpses, they inhabit as a result of their karma.
Thus I say.
Furthermore, I shall explain to you, according to the facts, that other state characterized by eternal suffering.
Just as fools who perform evil deeds must experience the karmas they have previously committed (Sūy.
327): Having bound them by their hands and feet, they cut open their bellies with sharp knives;
having seized and torn apart the body of the fool, they pull out his entrails, which were firmly bound within (Sūy. 328).
They stretch out his arms from the root; they burn his wide-open mouth with fire;
they remind the fool of his past pleasures in secret; and when he is enraged, they pierce his back with a goad.
Like this very earth, heated, blazing, and glowing, it becomes like fire for those who step upon it. (Sūyagaḍa 329)
Burning, they cry out piteously, yoked to glowing-hot yokes.
These fools, driven by force, stumble along the ground upon a path of red-hot iron as if it were slippery mud;
as they proceed through that impassable place, they are struck with sticks like sacrificial victims.
Falling headlong into that [hell], they are struck by falling rocks;
it is called Santāpanī, where those of evil deeds suffer for a long duration.
Having been cast into cauldrons, the fools are boiled; even when burnt there, they spring up again.
Being torn apart by birds of prey, they are devoured by other creatures with sharp claws. (Sūy.
333) There is a place called Samūsiya, a smokeless abode, where those tormented by their own suffering wail piteously;
having been cut to pieces and flayed, they are roasted on spits like meat. (Sūy. 334)
There they are impaled, their limbs torn apart, and devoured by birds with iron beaks;
this long-lasting state is called Sañjīvanī, wherein beings who have committed evil deeds are tormented. (Sūy.
335) They cause them to be scorched with sharp spikes, like a captured beast or a deer caught in a snare.
Pierced by spears, they cry out piteously; afflicted on both sides, they suffer extreme misery. (Sūy.
336) There is always a vast, deep pit of water in which those of many cruel deeds stand, burning with fire that requires no fuel.
Bound there, some remain for a long duration, emitting loud cries. (Sūy. 337)

Having begun with great violence, they throw that [being] there while it is crying out piteously; those of evil deeds whirl about there like a drop of clarified butter fallen into the midst of a fire.
Furthermore, it is a place of constant, total heat, intensely oppressive, and of a nature of extreme suffering.
Having bound them by their hands and feet, they attack them as if with clubs against an enemy.
They break the back of the fool with blows; they also split his head with iron mallets.
With their bodies shattered like wood being carved, they subject them to red-hot spikes. (Sūyagaḍa 339–340)

Those who perform cruel and evil deeds are bound and driven like arrows; having mounted a single elephant, two are made to carry it, or even more than that. When the beast is enraged, they are pierced by its tusks.
These fools, driven by force, tread upon the ground which is full of mud, thorns, and vast expanse.
When their bodies are tormented by intense heat and their minds are despondent, they are driven to perform the *koṭṭabali* (the offering of flesh).
In the great torment known as Veyāliya, solitary ascetics are struck down in the sky upon the edge of a mountain;
there, those who have committed many cruel deeds suffer for more than a thousand *muhūrtas*.
Driven along, the evildoers groan, tormented day and night in the vast, solitary, and treacherous hell; there they are struck down by that uneven treachery.
Enraged, their former enemies seize them with clubs and pestles and break them apart. (Sūyagaḍa 3.44)
With their bodies torn apart and vomiting blood, they fall upon the surface of the earth with their heads turned downward.
There, great jackals named Anāśika, impudent and ever-angry, devour those who have committed many cruel deeds; they are not far from there, bound by iron chains.
There is a river named Sayājalā, difficult to cross, with shifting mud and molten iron that is scorching hot;
entering upon that difficult passage, they proceed single-filed in succession.
These painful sensations touch the fool, as he remains there for a long time without interruption. (Sūyagaḍa 347)
There is no protection for one who is being struck; alone, he himself must experience the suffering.

Whatever kind of karma one previously performed, that very same thing follows one in the future life. Having gathered an existence of absolute misery, the sufferer experiences that infinite suffering. (Sūyagaḍa 348–349)

Having heard of these hells, the wise person should not harm anything whatsoever in the entire world; holding a singular vision and being free from possessions, he should awaken and not fall under the sway of the world.
Thus, for animals, humans, and asuras, this cycle of transmigration is fourfold, endless, and results in suffering.
Having understood all this thus, one should await the time [of death] with longing and practice the purified way.
Thus I say.
[Praise of Mahāvīra]
Ascetics, brahmins, householders, and followers of other sects questioned him:
"Who has declared a doctrine that is exclusively beneficial, peerless, and excellent when examined?
And what was his knowledge, what was his vision, and what was the conduct of the son of Naya?"
"O monk, you know this according to its true nature; speak as you have heard it, just as it was settled. (Sūy.

353) "He who knows the essential, who is skilled and well-established, possessing infinite knowledge and infinite vision, the glorious one who stands within the range of the eye—know the Dharma and perceive steadfastness. (Sūy. 354)
Above, below, and in the horizontal directions, whatever living beings there are— whether moving or stationary—
the wise one, having observed them as ever-present, proclaims the balanced Dharma like an island.
He is all-seeing, possessed of surpassing knowledge, free from the scent of impurity, steadfast-minded, and established in his self.
He possesses unsurpassed knowledge throughout the entire world; he has transcended all bonds, is fearless, and is without a body (soul-less).
He is one of vast wisdom, wandering without attachment, a steadfast man who has crossed over the flood, possessing infinite vision.
Like the sun, he shines unsurpassedly; like the lord of Vairocana, he illuminates the darkness.
The leader, the sage Kāśyapa of swift wisdom, is the unsurpassed debtor of the Jinas regarding the Dharma;
like the great and powerful Indra among the gods, he is the distinguished thousand-eyed one in heaven.
His insight is like an inexhaustible ocean, or like the great sea that has no end or shore.
Like Sakka, the lord of the gods, he shines with splendor—free from passion, free from aversion, and liberated.

By his heroism, he is one whose heroism is perfected; like Sudarśana, the best of all mountains, or like the joyous city of the gods, he, endowed with manifold virtues, shines resplendently. (Sūyagaḍa 359–360)
Itself measuring one thousand yojanas [in width], the triple-tiered Paṇḍakavana-Vaijayanta [palace] is ninety-nine thousand yojanas above [the earth] and one thousand yojanas below;
touching the sky and resting upon the earth, it is that which the suns revolve around. (Sūy. 361)

He is gold-colored and has many delights, in whom Mahendra bestows his love. He is a mountain, a great light of sound; he shines with a polished golden hue, supreme among mountains and difficult peaks, like a blazing fire upon the earth. (Sūy. 362–363)
Standing upon the earth like the king of mountains, with his pure radiance shining like the sun,
thus he, possessing the color of gold through his splendor, shines forth as a delightful wreath of light;
even so is the fame of the great mountain Sudarśana proclaimed.
Thus indeed was the ascetic Nātaputta [Mahāvīra] preeminent in birth, fame, vision, knowledge, and conduct.
Like Mount Niṣadha among the great mountains, or like Mount Rucaka among the circular ranges, he was preeminent;
thus was he known as the source of prosperity for the world. Among the sages, he was declared by the wise to be the most excellent. (Sūyagaḍa 365–366)
Having proclaimed the unsurpassed Dharma, he meditates upon the unsurpassed, supreme, and excellent meditation—
pure, utterly white, free from blemish, and white with the purity of complete detachment.
Having purified all karma without exception, that great sage attains the unsurpassed, highest state.
Having attained infinite success, the state, and tranquility through knowledge, conduct, and vision;
just as among trees the *śālmali* is known, or as they call the Nandana grove the best among forests, so too is one who has attained prosperity through knowledge and conduct. (Sūyagaḍa 368–369)
Just as thunder is supreme among sounds, as the moon is of great majesty among the stars,
and as sandalwood is said to be the best among fragrances, even so they say the one without vows is the best among sages.
Just as the self-existent ocean is the best of bodies of water, or as Dharaṇinda is said to be the best among serpents.
Among horses, they call Erāvaṇa the best;
among elephants, they call Airāvaṇa the best; among rivers, the Gaṅgā; among lions, the king of beasts;
and among birds, Garuḍa Veṇudeva. But among those who proclaim liberation, the Son of the Jñāta (Nātaputta) is the best here. (Sūyagaḍa 371–372)
Just as Vīsaṇa is among the Jōhas, or as the lotus is said to be among flowers, just as Daṇḍavakka is the best of Kṣatriyas, so is Vardhamāna the best of the Īśins.
Among gifts, the granting of fearlessness is the best; among truths, they say that which is irreproachable is the best.
In this world, the supreme holy life belongs to you, and the supreme ascetic is the Jñātaputra (the Son of the Jñātās).
Among those established in stability, the Lava-saptamas are the best; among assemblies, the Sudharmā is the best;
and as Nirvāṇa is the best of all states, so there is no knower superior to the Jñātaputra. (Sūy. 374–375)
Shaking off [karmic matter] from the past, free from attachment, and not forming any store of possessions,

the one of swift wisdom has crossed the great flood of existence like an ocean— the Hero who brings fearlessness, possessing infinite vision. Anger, pride, and likewise deceit, with greed as the fourth— these are the internal defects.
Having spoken thus, the Arhat, the Great Sage, neither commits evil nor causes it to be committed. (Sūy.

377) Having understood that the positions of the Agnostics—consisting of the doctrines of action, non-action, and the discourse on skepticism—are all mere assertions, he has established himself in self-restraint for the long journey. (Sūy. 378)

Having abandoned sexual intercourse and eating at night, practicing austerities for the sake of the destruction of suffering, and having understood this world and the world beyond, the Master restrained all evil impulses.
Having heard the Dharma spoken by the Arhats—composed and purified in its eight aspects—Sūy. 379.
"By having faith in that, people will become free from rebirth, like the gods headed by Indra.
Thus I say. [The Discourse on the Censure of the Slothful]
Earth, water, fire, and air; grass, trees, and seeds; and living beings that are mobile;

those born from eggs and those born from wombs; those born from moisture and those designated as born from sap—these bodies have been declared. One should know them within these and observe their suffering.
By these very means, they repeatedly inflict violence upon themselves through their bodies;
thus, wandering again and again along the path of birth, they cause destruction among mobile and immobile beings.
That fool who, throughout various births, commits many cruel deeds, is destroyed by that very act. (Sūyagaḍa 382–383)

Whether in this world or in the next, whether by means of a hundred [pleasures] or otherwise, those who have fallen into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) bind and experience manifold miseries for one after another. (Sūy.
384) Those who, having abandoned both mother and father, would nevertheless initiate fire-rituals while professing the vows of a śramaṇa...

They say that this world is characterized by unwholesome conduct, for those who cause injury to living beings do so for their own pleasure. (Sūy. 385) One who kindles [a fire] should extinguish it; one who has extinguished it should not let the fire flare up again. Therefore, the wise man, having discerned the Dharma, should not, as a scholar, initiate any activity involving fire. (Sūy. 386)

The earth is also living beings, and water is also living beings; crawling creatures and those that fly together approach, as well as those dwelling in moisture and those resting on wood—these one burns when one instigates fire.
Plants are living beings that hang down; their food and bodies are likewise distinct.

He who, for the sake of his own pleasure, acts with violence toward many living beings out of recklessness; he who destroys both the potential for birth and growth by being unrestrained in his assault upon seeds—him they call one whose nature is unrighteous in this world, he who harms seeds for his own gratification. (Sūyagaḍa 388–389)
Wombs are filled with those who are tossed about; men—others, princes, youths, the middle-aged, and the elderly—all pass away when their lifespan is exhausted.
Be awakened, O living beings! Having seen this danger, human birth is not obtained by the foolish. (Sūyagaḍa 390)
When the world has become entirely subject to suffering, one undergoes transformation through one's own karma. (Sūy.

391) In this world, some deluded ones proclaim liberation through the avoidance of food and the acquisition of possessions; others through the use of cold water; and still others proclaim liberation through fire-offerings. (Sūy. 392)

"There is no liberation for those who do not avoid [forbidden things] such as looking at women; by not renouncing salt and alkaline substances, they consume liquor, meat, and garlic, and then plan their residence elsewhere. (Sūy.
393) "Those who proclaim that perfection is attained through water, touching water in the evening and in the morning..."

If success were possible through water, many living beings would have attained perfection in water—fish, tortoises, crocodiles, otters, porcupines, and water-demons. Those who proclaim that perfection is achieved through water say what is impossible; the wise declare this to be so. (Sūy. 394–395)
If cold water could remove the impurity of karma, then one might desire happiness;
yet, like a blind man following a guide, the dull-witted destroy living beings in this very way while performing sinful deeds. (Sūy.
396) For if one who is committing sinful actions were to remove that [impurity] with cold water...
Some who destroy living beings with water attained perfection; they spoke falsely, claiming that success comes through water.

(Sūyagaḍa 397) Those who declare that perfection is achieved by means of the burnt offering, while touching the fire morning and evening—for them, perfection would come from touching the fire just as it would for those base meat-sellers who touch the fire. (Sūyagaḍa 398)
Indeed, there is no perfection through what is seen without investigation; they go toward destruction, not understanding.
Know that one should examine with living beings the pleasant sensation, having taken up the true knowledge regarding the mobile and the stationary.
(Sūyagaḍa 399) Beings cry out, are destroyed, and tremble due to their karma; having separately reflected upon the various worlds, the monk [should act accordingly].
Therefore, the wise man, guarding himself, should abstain from it; seeing even a tiny creature, he should withdraw [his hand]. (Sūy.

400) He who consumes what has been acquired contrary to the Dharma, or who bathes by splashing with water, or who washes or tears his garment—he, they say, is far from the state of a Nagaṇiya. (Sūy. 401)
Having fully understood karma regarding water, the wise man should live by using filtered water until final liberation;
he should not consume seeds or bulbs, and he should abstain from bathing and such acts, as well as from women.
"He who runs after families for the sake of alms, they say, is far from being a true ascetic. (Sūy.

403) "He who runs after families for the sake of alms, being greedy for his belly, he has destroyed the Dharma; they say such a person is unworthy of the teachers' community, he who would beg for the sake of food. (Sūy. 404)
Having gone forth, yet living on the food of others, seeking the favor of his mouth and greedy for his belly—
like a great boar greedy for wild grain— he will not be far from his own destruction.
(Sūyagaḍa 405) He speaks pleasant words while serving for the sake of food and drink pertaining to this world.
One who is both a *pāsattha* (one living near the community) and a *kusīla* (lazy) becomes like a *pulāka* (worthless grain that has lost its essence). (Sūy.
406) One should endure with alms-food obtained without prior announcement; one should not seek honor through asceticism.
Remaining unattached to sounds and forms, and having abandoned all domestic ties to sensual pleasures, (Sūy. 407)

Having transcended all attachments, the steadfast one, enduring all sufferings, free from worldly possessions, unattached, and wandering without fixed abode—the monk who brings fearlessness to others is one whose soul is undisturbed.
Born for the sake of the burden, the sage should consume [his food]; the monk should long for detachment from evil.
When afflicted by suffering, one should shake off [the defilements], just as one would subdue the enemy at the head of battle. (Sūy.
409) Even when being struck, remaining firm like a plank, he awaits his final end;
having shaken off karma, he does not fall into deception, just as a cart stops when its axle is worn out. (Sūy. 410)
Thus I say:
energy is to be understood as twofold; it is proclaimed as "energy."
What indeed is the heroism of a hero? And how is this proclaimed?
Some proclaim karma, while others of good conduct proclaim non-karma; by these two positions are mortals seen. (Sūy. 411–412)
They say negligence is karma, and likewise non-negligence is its opposite;
whether it pertains to that state or to a specific place, it applies to the fool or even the wise.
Some, however, while training in the scriptures, [act] for the excessive destruction of living beings.
Some recite mantras while harming living beings;
being deceitful, they practice deception and exert themselves for the sake of sensual pleasures.
These shameless ones, slayers and cutters, pursue their own pleasure. (Sūyagaḍa 414–415)

Whether by mind, by speech, or even by body—whether internally or externally—in both ways they are unrestrained; the hater creates enmities, and through those enmities he becomes further attached to them. (Sūyagaḍa 416)
Violent undertakings and even painful contacts lead those who commit evil deeds toward future existence. Fools, driven by passion and hatred, create much demerit. (Sūy. 417–418)
This has been declared to you as the effort of action belonging to the foolish;
now hear from me about the effort of non-action belonging to the wise.
(Sūyagaḍa 4.19) The self-controlled one is liberated from bondage, with all bonds severed on every side.
The impetuous, sinful karma pierces like an arrow to the very core.
Having adopted the well-expounded path of right conduct, one strives again and again; yet, [the mind] repeatedly dwells upon what is unpleasant and likewise upon impurity.
Established in their respective positions, they will pass away from various stations;
there is no doubt about this, for this dwelling is unstable, [as seen] by the kinsmen and friends.
Having understood this, the wise man should uproot his own greed.
One should enter upon the noble state, which is free from all worldly attachments.
Having understood through one's own intelligence, or having heard it, the essence of the Dharma,
the homeless ascetic, being firmly established, should renounce all evil deeds.
Whatever means one knows for the preservation of one's own life,
a wise person should quickly practice that training even in the midst of it. Just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its own body, [so should one withdraw from worldly attachments].
In this way, a wise person should withdraw evil things through the inner self.
He should withdraw his hands and feet, his mind, and all his senses;
likewise, he should withdraw evil dispositions and such faults of speech. (Sūy. 426–427)
Having fully understood pride and deceit, the wise one has heard this from me here among some: "This is the heroism of a hero—
[regarding] those living beings, whether mobile or stationary, above, below, or across."

One should practice restraint in all things; peace and Nirvana are proclaimed [as the goal]. One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given, nor speak falsehoods with a longing for gain; this is the duty of one who dwells in virtue.
One should not even mentally desire that which passes by;
being restrained in every way and self-controlled, one should thoroughly withdraw from the influx [of karma].
One should avoid evil that has been done, is being done, or will yet come to be.
Those who are self-restrained and have conquered their senses do not approve of all that [the unenlightened do].
As for those unenlightened ones who, though highly esteemed, are heroes yet lack the vision of right conviction—their exertion is entirely fruitless. (Sūyagaḍa 431–432)
And those highly fortunate Buddhas, heroes who perceive with perfect rightness—their exertion is entirely pure, and it becomes fruitless for them in every respect.
Even their austerity is not pure, [if they are] those who have gone forth from great families. (Sūy. 433)
One should not seek praise from those who understand one's birth or complexion. (Sūy.

434) Eating little food, subsisting on alms, speaking little, being easy to follow, patient, inwardly tranquil, self-controlled, free from worldly attachments, and always striving—[this is the life of a sage]. (Sūy. 435)
Having concentrated upon the yoga of meditation, having completely withdrawn the body, and knowing supreme endurance, you should wander as a mendicant until liberation.
Thus I say. (Sūyagaḍa 436)
"What is the Dhamma that was proclaimed by the wise Brahmin?
