Listen to me regarding that straight Dhamma, according to reality, as taught by the Jinas. (Sūyagaḍa 437)
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Chandalas, or even Bokkasas, Eshikas, Veshikas, or Shudras—whoever is dependent on violence and established in possessiveness, their enmity increases. (Sūy. 438)
Sensual pleasures, which arise from exertion, do not bring liberation from suffering.
Having committed an act of violence for the sake of wealth, those who crave sense-objects do not themselves enjoy that wealth; rather, as a doer of deeds, they are tormented by their own actions.
Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and legitimate sons—these are not able to protect you when you are being afflicted by your own karma.
Having understood this matter, one should follow that which leads to the supreme goal. (Sūyagaḍa 441)
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, the monk should practice that which was taught by the Jinas.
Having abandoned wealth, sons, kinsmen, and possessions,
and having cast off the internal stream of sorrow, he should wander about without concern for worldly things.
Earth, water, fire, air, plants, and trees with seeds;
those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, from juices, from fermentation, and from sprouts—having understood this, one should thoroughly know these six classes of living beings. (Sūyagaḍa 444)
Neither by mind, nor by body, nor by speech, is he one who undertakes violence or possesses anything.

Having understood false speech, external objects, and grasping, as well as the various weapons and possessions in this world, one should thoroughly comprehend that through knowledge. (Sūyagaḍa 4.45–46)
Deceit, fear, and sleeping on the bare ground—these are the things to be shaken off in this world; one should thoroughly understand that as true knowledge.
Washing, rubbing [the body], enemas, and purgatives—Sūy. 447.
One should thoroughly understand that knowledge [of worldly arts] which involves vomiting, collyrium, and causing distress; Sūy. 448.
One should thoroughly understand that knowledge [of worldly arts] which involves perfumes, garlands, bathing, as well as cleaning the teeth and the practice of possessing women; Sūy. 449.
One should thoroughly understand that which is designated for oneself, that which is purchased, that which is borrowed, that which is brought [as alms], that which is stale, and that which is unfit;
as well as food that causes haste, food mixed with eye-salve, and food involving the act of killing for the sake of greed. (Sūyagaḍa 450)
One should thoroughly understand that science of massage and ointments; (Sūy.
451) one should thoroughly understand that science of stretching, of performing services, of answering questions, of making requests, and of accepting alms from a householder. (Sūy. 452)
One should not train in the art of Aṭṭhāvaya, nor should one practice divination and the like, nor hand-to-hand combat and trade; one should thoroughly understand that science.
One should also avoid sandals, umbrellas, flutes, and fanning with a yak-tail fan.
One should thoroughly understand that science of serving others and mutual service. A sage should never void excrement or urine upon green plants,
nor should he ever wash himself by scooping up water with his hands.

One should never eat food or drink belonging to another, nor wear the clothes of another even if one is naked; one should thoroughly understand that as true knowledge. One should avoid couches, thrones, and seats within the homes of householders.
One should thoroughly understand that science [of worldly existence], whether it be inquiry or seeking refuge. (Sūy.

457) One should thoroughly understand that science [of worldly existence]: fame, renown, and praise; whatever honor and worship there may be; and all the sensual pleasures in the entire world. (Sūy. 458)
"A monk should thoroughly understand that knowledge by which he may sustain himself here with such food and drink as is provided by others. Thus spoke the Nirgrantha, the Great Hero, the Great Sage.
He who possesses infinite knowledge and vision should teach the Dharma as it is found in the Sūtra.
When speaking, he should not speak falsely, nor should he utter secret or vital secrets; he should avoid the position of a deceiver and explain only after careful reflection. (Sūyagaḍa 460–461)
In this regard, this is the third speech: that which one regrets after having spoken, and that which is secretive, should not be spoken; this is the command of the Nigaṇṭhas.
One should not utter mocking speech, friendly speech, or abusive speech.
One should never speak unpleasantly, saying "you, you" in every way.
A monk should always be free from bad conduct and should avoid social intimacy; for in such company there are pleasant-seeming obstacles, which the wise should recognize. (Sūy. 463–464)
Except for an unavoidable circumstance, he should not sit in another's house;
he should not play with village girls, nor should the sage laugh excessively.
Unenvious toward magnificent things, practicing self-restraint, he should wander as an ascetic.
Being vigilant in his conduct, he should endure whatever he encounters there.
When being struck, he should not become angry; when being reviled, he should not retort.
With a serene mind, he should endure it and should not raise a clamor. (Sūy. 466–467)
Having obtained desires, one should not long for more;
one should always delight in solitude and learn from the teachers in the presence of the Buddhas.
Being desirous of learning, one should attend upon those who possess right insight and are well-disciplined in their studies.
Those heroes who rely on their own wisdom, who are steadfast and have conquered their senses; who do not look for a lamp even in their own homes—those men are worthy of offerings.
Those heroes are liberated from bondage and do not crave further life.
Not greedy for sounds or tactile sensations, and not dependent on worldly undertakings—
all that has been spoken at great length transcends the conventional agreement (samaya).
Having thoroughly understood both excessive pride and deceit, the wise man [should remain detached].
A sage should direct all forms of reverence toward *nirvāṇa*. Thus I say.
[Samādhi]
First, having reflected upon the Dharma with wisdom—straight and composed—listen to this:
a monk who is free from attachment, attained to composure, and without a basis for rebirth, should wander among beings.
Above, below, and across the quarters, toward whatever creatures there are, whether moving or stationary.
Restraining both hands and feet, one should not take what is not given from others. (Sūy.
474) Having well-expounded the Dharma and being free from doubt, the monk who practices in the Lāḍha country should be self-reliant toward all beings;
seeking life in this world, he should not create acquisitions, nor should the learned ascetic monk create attachments. (Sūy. 475)
With all his senses stilled toward living beings, the sage should wander, completely liberated from all sides;
he should perceive creatures and various beings, who are tormented and consumed by suffering.
While the fool commits acts against these, he becomes entangled in evil karmas. (Sūyagaḍa 476)
One who is excessively talkative performs evil karma; one who is silent also performs karma.
One who lives in fear performs evil; indeed, the wise have declared that absolute concentration is peace.
The Buddhas have taught that through concentration one should delight in solitude, remaining steadfast in the soul by abstaining from the taking of life. (Sūyagaḍa 477–478)
One should observe the entire world with equanimity; one should not do anything pleasing or displeasing to anyone.
Rising up, yet becoming dejected and once again despondent, one merely seeks honor and the desire for praise.
Seeking food prepared specifically for oneself, one wanders at will and remains despondent.
The fool, being attached to women and to various possessions, creates attachments; obsessed by enmity, he accumulates stores. Having passed away from here, he goes to a miserable and difficult state.
Therefore, the wise man, having discerned the Dharma, should wander as a sage, liberated from everything. (Sūyagaḍa 480–481)

One who desires to live in this world should not commit evil; wandering without attachment, speaking with reflection, and having subdued greed, one should not engage in talk that causes harm to others.
One should not desire food prepared for oneself, nor should one cultivate intimacy with those who do so. (Sūyagaḍa 1.6.27)
Shaking off [the body] while observing the noble path, having abandoned attachment and looking back no more, one should strive for this state of solitude.
Thus, liberation is not false; behold! This is the liberation from falsehood.
Another is free from anger, devoted to truth, and ascetic. (Sūyagaḍa 483–484)

O noble one, the monk who refrains from sexual intercourse with women and likewise from possessiveness toward high and low objects of the senses has undoubtedly attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Having overcome both aversion and attachment, the monk [endures] the touch of thirst as well as the touch of cold.
One should endure heat and the bite of insects; one should tolerate what is fragrant and what is foul.
Guarded in speech and having attained meditative composure, one should wander as a mendicant, having mastered the *leśyās*.
One should neither seek a house nor cause one to be built; one should abandon the state of association with worldly beings.

Those people who are proponents of non-action (akriyāvādins), when questioned by others, point to asceticism (dhuta) while remaining attached to worldly undertakings; being bound by the world, they do not know the Dharma that is the cause of liberation.
Furthermore, in this world, the Māṇavas hold various individual inclinations and maintain distinct doctrines regarding action and non-action.
For the fool who, having been born, commits violence against the body, enmity increases as he remains unrestrained.
Not understanding the exhaustion of his own lifespan, that dull-witted man, acting with recklessness, clings to the notion of "mine.
While being consumed by the night and the day, the deluded one suffers amidst miseries as if he were ageless and immortal. (Sūyagaḍa 489–490)
Abandon all wealth and offspring, as well as those who are kinsmen, those who are dear, and friends;

even their lamentations lead only to delusion, for other people carry away that wealth. Just as small deer, while wandering, keep far away from a lion out of apprehension, [so should one avoid worldly attachments].
Thus, having scrutinized the nature of things, the wise man should avoid evil from afar.
But the intelligent man, awakening to the truth, should withdraw himself from evil; perceiving that sufferings are born of violence, he should live as one who has reached the state of nirvāṇa.
The sage who has attained the self should not speak untruth; this is Nirvana, the complete concentration.
He should not do it himself, nor cause others to do it, nor approve of another who is doing it.
He should remain pure and born [in the dharma], he should not revile others, and being free from delusion, he should not be attached. (Sūyagaḍa 494)
Possessing fortitude and liberated, one should wander as a mendicant neither for the sake of honor nor seeking praise.

Having gone forth from the home, free from longing, having cast off the body and severed the ties of worldly causes, the monk should wander, liberated from the cycle of existence, desiring neither life nor death. (Sūyagaḍa 495–496)
Thus I say.
Which path has been proclaimed by the wise Brahmin?
Having entered upon the straight path, one crosses over the flood that is so difficult to cross.
You know that unsurpassed, pure path which brings liberation from all suffering; tell us of it, O Great Sage, just as a monk [knows it]. (Sūy. 497–498)
If no one should ask you—whether gods or humans—as to which path they should follow, how would you explain it to them?
If anyone should ask you, whether gods or humans... [Sūy. 499]
One should counteract those [faults]; hear from me the essence of the path.
This most formidable [path] was proclaimed by Kāśyapa in due succession—taking which, as in the past, merchants cross the ocean.
Some have crossed over, some are crossing, and others will cross in the future;
having heard this, I shall explain it. O people, listen to me!
Earth-living beings are distinct entities, and water-living beings possess similar qualities.
Wind-beings are separate entities; so too are grasses, trees, and those possessing seeds.
Furthermore, there are mobile creatures; thus the six classes of beings have been declared.
To this extent alone consists the aggregate of living beings; no other category exists.
Having examined with all appropriate methods that the wise man perceives all things as undesirable suffering, he therefore does not harm anything.
This indeed is the essence of the knower: that he does not injure anyone. (Sūyagaḍa 505)
One should understand the vow of non-violence to be just this much:
one should know the renunciation toward all beings, whether moving or stationary, above, below, and across; this is declared to be peace and nirvana. (Sūyagaḍa 506–507)
Having overcome hatred, one should not come into conflict with anyone,
whether by mind, speech, or even by body, down to the smallest degree.
Thus restrained, that wise and steadfast one should practice the alms-round with moderation.
Always restrained in seeking food, and avoiding improper seeking;
one who is well-restrained should not accept such food or drink as that which involves the injury of living beings or is prepared specifically for his sake. (Sūyagaḍa 509–510)
One should not practice foul deeds; this is the duty of one who is established in virtue.
Whatever one might desire, that is not permitted in every respect. One should not sanction the act of killing, guarding oneself and having conquered the senses.
There are certain positions held by the faithful in villages or in cities:
having undertaken such speech, one might say "merit exists" or "merit does not exist"—this is a source of great fear. (Sūyagaḍa 512–513)

If living beings, whether mobile or stationary, are killed for the sake of giving, then for the purpose of protecting them, one should not say, "It exists. [One should not say it exists] regarding those for whom such food and drink are prepared. (Sūy. 514)
They create an obstacle to the gains of others; therefore, one should not say "there is nothing. (Sūy.
515) Those who praise giving desire the destruction of living beings, and those who prohibit it cause the deprivation of their livelihood. (Sūy. 516)
They do not speak of either of these two: "it exists" or "it does not exist.
Having cast off this influx of karma, they attain nirvana.
The Buddhas regard nirvana as supreme, just as the moon is among the stars. (Sūyagaḍa 5.17)
Therefore, the sage who is always self-controlled and restrained should aim for *nirvāṇa*.
For living beings who are awakening and being tormented by their own karma, that island is called a good refuge;
it is said to be a place of firm support. (Sūy. 518–519)
He who is always guarded in his senses, self-controlled, with the stream [of craving] severed and free from intoxicants,
proclaims the pure Dharma, which is perfect and incomparable. Not understanding that very [Dharma], those who are unawakened yet imagine themselves awakened— Sūyagaḍa 520.
Those who think "the Buddhas are deluded" are at the extreme; they are not composed.
Having eaten seeds, water, and whatever has been prepared for their sake, they practice meditation while being ignorant and lacking composure. (Sūy. 521–522)
Just as the ḍhaṅkas, kaṅkas, kulalas, maggukas, and sihis brood over their prey for fish, so too is their meditation the lowest and most defiled;
even so are some ascetics, those of wrong view and ignoble conduct. (Sūyagaḍa 5.2.3)
They meditate on specific objects [of sense], like cranes or those of impure character.
Having abandoned the pure path, some here who are foolish,
having gone onto a wrong path, thus bring about their own suffering and destruction.
Just as a blind man who has boarded a leaking boat desires to reach the other shore but perishes midway, so too are some ascetics who hold wrong views and are ignoble. (Sūy. 526)
Those who have entered the stream of the kasiṇa are approaching great danger.
But having taken up this Dhamma proclaimed by Kāśyapa, one may cross over this most terrible flood; thus, one should wander as a seeker of the self.
Having desisted from the ways of the village, one should wander as a mendicant, exerting strength by taking oneself as the standard for all those who exist in the world.
Having thoroughly understood both excessive pride and deceit, the wise man [should act accordingly].
Having rejected all this, the sage should be intent upon *nirvāṇa*.
He should be intent upon the dharma of the virtuous and reject the dharma of evil.
A mendicant who possesses the vigor for exertion should not harbor anger or pride.
Those Buddhas who have passed away and those Buddhas who are yet to come—
their foundation is this [teaching], just as the earth is the support for all living beings. Now,
when one has undertaken the vow, various high and low sensations may touch him.

One should not be struck down by them, just as a great mountain is not shaken by the wind. Restrained, possessed of great wisdom, steadfast, and practicing the acceptance of alms, one should remain withdrawn and await the [proper] time; such is the teaching of the Kevalins.
Thus I say.
[The Assembly] These are the four assemblies, which the proponents of doctrines speak of separately.
The third [view] maintains that there is action and non-action; the fourth, they say, is ignorance. (Sūy.
535) Those ignorant ones, though they may be skilled, are not well-established; they do not cross over doubt.
Being unskilled, they speak with those who are unskilled, saying, "There is no method of inquiry," and thus they speak falsely. (Sūy. 536)

Thinking "this is truth" and "this is untruth," and declaring "this is good" and "this is not good," many such people here are indeed deceptive; even when questioned, they conceal their true disposition.
They say, "We are free from mental constructs," yet they illuminate their own purpose in this way.
Those who, regarding the future, are wavering and indeterminate, and who proclaim non-action, are proponents of non-doing (akriyāvādins).
Having grasped their speech with a confused state of mind, he becomes one who is deluded and speaks without proper reflection.
They have declared this dual-sided position and this single-sided position, as well as the sixfold basis of action (chalāyatana-karma).
Thus they speak, not understanding; these many men who profess various forms of non-action and are full of deceit, wander through the cycle of existence which has no end. (Sūy.
540) The sun neither rises nor sets; the moon neither waxes nor wanes.
The waters do not flow and the winds do not blow; the world is indeed barren and fixed. (Sūy.

541) Just as a blind man, even with a lamp, does not see forms despite their presence, so too those who deny action—whose wisdom is obstructed—do not perceive action, even though it exists. (Sūy. 542)
Having mastered these eight branches—the year, dreams, bodily marks, omens, the body, portents, and the eightfold [astrology]—many people in this world know things yet to come. (Sūy.
543) Some of those omens turn out to be true, while for some others, that knowledge fails them.
Not practicing the state of knowledge, they have declared liberation through knowledge alone. (Sūy.

544) Having examined the world in this way, those ascetics and brahmins declare that suffering is created by oneself and not created by another; they have declared that knowledge and conduct are the means of liberation. (Sūy. 545)

These leaders in this world are indeed guides for the eye; they teach the path that is beneficial for living beings, and they have declared it to be eternal in the world—that [path] in which, O man! beings are well-established.
Whether they be Rākṣasas, or those belonging to Yama, or gods, Gandharvas, or [other] classes of beings.
Those who move through the air and those born from the earth undergo reversal again and again. (Sūy.

547) Know that which they call the flood, the water without a further shore, to be the difficult-to-cross whirlpool of existence; therein, despondent because of the snares of the sense-objects, they wander through both worlds. (Sūy. 548)
Fools do not exhaust karma through karma; the wise and intelligent ones exhaust karma through non-action.
Having transcended the nature of greed, being contented, they do not commit evil.
Those Tathāgatas know the past, present, and future states of the world as they truly are.
They are leaders who cannot be led by others; indeed, those Buddhas have brought an end to existence.
They neither act nor cause others to act, detesting the injury of living beings.
Always alert, the wise do not falter; some wise ones even become capable of discernment.
Whether it be small creatures or large creatures, he perceives them as his own self throughout the entire world;

seeing this great world as something to be shunned, the awakened one should wander heedfully among those who are heedless. Those who, having understood themselves and others, become sufficient for themselves, become sufficient for others.
One should always abide in that state of the light of knowledge who explains the Dharma after having investigated it thoroughly. (Sūy.

553) He who knows himself and the world, who knows the course of rebirth and the lack thereof, who knows the eternal and the non-eternal, and who knows birth, death, and transmigration—[he is a true sage]. (Sūy. 554)
"Alas! The delusion of beings is such that they do not know influx or restraint;
but he who knows suffering and its exhaustion, he is worthy to proclaim the doctrine of action (kiriyāvāda).
Not being attached to sounds or forms, and not feeling aversion toward tastes or smells..."
Neither desiring life nor longing for death, guarding his intakes and liberated from the cycle of existence— thus I say. [The Discourse on the True Doctrine]
I shall now proclaim this traditional teaching: the various kinds of birth of man, the conduct of the virtuous and the conduct of the non-virtuous; I shall explain peace and the lack of peace.
Having obtained the Dharma from those who have arisen by day and by night, who have come thus [to enlightenment].
Not enduring the assault upon their concentration, they speak such harsh words to the Teacher. (Sūy.

558) Those who, while instructing others in purification, should explain it according to their own personal bias, are not established in many virtues; he who speaks falsely out of suspicion toward knowledge [is likewise]. (Sūy. 559)

Those who, when questioned, practice deception and indeed seek to deceive for the sake of gain—those wicked ones here consider themselves to be virtuous; being full of guile, they go toward infinite destruction.
He who is prone to anger, who speaks what is harmful to the world, and who incites one who is already alienated—Sūy. 560.

Like a blind man taking up a staff, the doer of evil deeds runs on without having desisted. (Sūy. 561) He who speaks with hostility and utters what is unknown [to him] does not attain equanimity when he has fallen into reproach;
yet one who offers assistance, who is modest, and whose vision is directed toward solitude, is not of a deceitful nature. (Sūy. 562)

Even if he is a person of delicate and refined nature, born of noble lineage, and naturally upright, if he does not change even when instructed extensively, he remains the same once he has incurred blame. (Sūy.
563) Furthermore, one who considers himself "possessed of wealth" might, without investigation, engage in speech based on mere calculation.

Intoxicated by his own power, O friend, he looks upon other people as mere puppets. He perishes through his one-sided arrogance; there is no ground for pride in a noble lineage for one who would exalt himself out of a desire for honor, while failing to understand the higher state of those possessing superior wealth.

Whether he be a Brahmin, a Kshatriya, a Vaishya, an Ugraputra, or a Licchavi—if such a person has gone forth as a renunciant and subsists on what is given by others, yet is arrogant regarding his lineage and bound by pride—neither his birth nor his family is his protection; nothing other than well-practiced knowledge and conduct is his refuge. (Sūyagaḍa 566)

Having gone forth, he who pursues the activities of a householder will not reach the further shore of liberation. (Sūy. 567) The mendicant who is free from possessions and lives a life of great austerity—yet who seeks honor and follows after praise—is one who does not understand this very livelihood; such a person repeatedly falls into delusion. (Sūy. 568)

The monk who is eloquent, one who speaks well, who is eminent and learned, whose wisdom is profound and whose self is well-cultivated—if such a person should disparage another person with his speech, he will not thus attain meditative absorption (samādhi).
This applies to the wise monk who would act with such arrogance. (Sūyagaḍa 569)
Or again, those who, anointed with the intoxication of gain, revile other people like ignorant children;

a monk who casts away the intoxication of learning, the intoxication of asceticism, the intoxication of lineage, and the fourth, the intoxication of livelihood—he is wise and a supreme person. (Sūy. 570–571)
Having discerned these intoxications, the wise ones do not indulge in them;
those great seers, possessing the most steadfast dharma, have transcended all lineages and proceed toward both high and low destinies.
Entering villages and towns, the mendicant should be one who has heard the truth and has seen the Dharma.
He who, knowing what is permissible food and what is impermissible food, is not greedy for either food or drink;
the mendicant who has overcome both aversion and attachment—whether among the multitude or wandering alone—should explain [the truth] through solitary reflection:
that for a single living being there is only coming and going. (Sūyagaḍa 5.1.10–11)
Having understood it for oneself, or even having heard it, one should indeed speak the Dharma that is beneficial to living beings.
Those who are wise in the Dharma do not practice those things which are censured and involve worldly motives.
One might fail to understand the true nature of certain things through mere reasoning; thus, by lacking faith, one may fall into a state of ruin.

One should avoid transgressing the time limit for life and should not obstruct the aims of others when they have obtained [the means]. Having discerned both karma and desire, the wise one should completely subdue the nature of the self.
Beings are destroyed by forms that bring fear; therefore, having grasped true knowledge, one should [protect] the mobile and immobile beings. (Sūy. 576–577)
Seeking neither honor nor praise, he should not do anything pleasing or displeasing to anyone;
avoiding all that is purposeless, the monk should remain undisturbed and free from passions. Observing the doctrine as it truly is, he should lay down the rod toward all living beings.
Neither desiring life nor desiring death, one should wander free from delusion and liberated from the cycle of existence. Thus I say.
[The Knot]
Having abandoned worldly ties, one training here should rise up and dwell in pure celibacy;

performing the instruction, one should train well in discipline; he who is wise should not indulge in negligence. Just as a young chick that has not yet grown its wings, thinking itself capable of entering the nest... (Sūy. 580)
Just as a hawk or other bird might carry off a young tree that has not yet produced leaves and whose growth is incomplete,

so too did many of evil character carry off that novice who had not yet touched the Dharma, even though he considered himself a dweller in the forest— just as they would carry off the shadow of a tree that has not yet grown leaves. (Sūyagaḍa 581–582)

A man desiring the final goal should seek composure; knowing that liberation is for those who do not dwell [in worldly things], he should, while illuminating the conduct of the steadfast one, not cast his gaze outward, being one of swift wisdom. (Sūy.
583) He who is well-joined with the good in standing, sitting, reclining, and even in exertion...
One should speak separately when explaining the *āyapaṇṇa* (the scriptures concerning the self) regarding the assemblies and the restraints.
Having heard sounds, even those that are terrifying, the one free from taints (*anāsava*) should wander amidst them;
the mendicant should not indulge in negligence nor in sleep, having crossed over doubt in every way. (Sūy. 584–585)
If, when instructed by one who is young or old— even by a junior who is equal in vows—
one does not properly attain stability in that [teaching], he will be led away into the shoreless [world].
Even if one has strayed, when instructed according to the doctrine by one who is young or old, and even when urged on, [one should remain steadfast].
Whether it be a female slave who has risen up, or householders instructed according to their custom—Sūy.

587—one should not be angry with them, nor should one revile them, nor should one say anything harsh; rather, one should comply, thinking, "They will act accordingly. This is indeed better for me; one should not be negligent. Sūy. 588.
Just as those who are not deluded instruct a person lost in the forest regarding the path that leads to his welfare, so too it is for me a blessing that the wise instruct me correctly. Therefore,
that deluded one should perform with particular devotion the worship due to the one who is undeluded.
In this regard, the Hero, having understood the matter in such a way, correctly brings it to its conclusion.

Just as a guide in the darkness of night does not know the path while he cannot see, but comes to know the path when it is illuminated by the rising of the sun, so too [does one understand the truth]. (Sūyagaḍa 590–591)
In this way, even though the novice has not yet been questioned about the Dharma, he does not know the Dharma while remaining unawakened;

but later, through the word of the Jina, he becomes wise and sees [the truth] with his own eyes, as when the sun rises—[beings] above, below, and across the quarters, those who are mobile and those who are stationary. (Sūy. 592)
One should always wander among them with self-restraint, remaining unshakable and free from mental resentment. (Sūy.
593) At the proper time, one should inquire with equanimity regarding living beings; one should explain the conduct of the diligent seeker.
That which causes fear should be entered separately; this is the analytical, absolute concentration. (Sūy. 594)
Firmly established in these three ways, the protector [of beings]—those who see the three worlds declare that peace lies in the cessation of these very things;
they do not indulge in the attachment of negligence. Having reflected upon this goal, that monk becomes wise through his realization.
Grasping is bondage, while purification is freedom; having approached [the truth] through purity, one attains liberation. (Sūy.
596) Having comprehended the Dharma, they proclaim it; indeed, those who are awakened become the end-makers.
Having crossed over both [banks], they utter the purified answer for the sake of liberation. (Sūy. 597)
One should neither conceal nor disparage [one's own faults]; one should not indulge in pride, nor should one engage in boasting.

One should not make jokes about others, nor should one proclaim talk of one's own penances. Out of apprehension regarding living beings and out of revulsion [for worldly life], one should not maintain one's lineage through the power of mantras. (Sūyagaḍa 598)
A person should not desire anything among living beings, nor should he cultivate unwholesome qualities (Sūy. 599).
He should not harbor even a laughable thought toward evil doctrines; he should recognize that which is harsh therein as base.
He should not be trivial, nor should he boast; he should be free from worldly attachment and devoid of passions, O monk (Sūy. 600).
A monk should not entertain doubt regarding what is doubted; he should explain it through analytical exposition.

With speech arising from the Dharma, he should explain it according to the principles, like a well-winged bird. Following after [the truth], he should recognize what is false; in that manner, he should speak gently and without harshness.

One should not speak anything that causes harm anywhere, nor should one utter words that are obstructive or protracted. One should speak with moderation, speaking complete and full sentences; having listened attentively, being one who perceives the goal of tranquility, a monk should employ pure speech according to the command, forming his intention for the avoidance of evil. (Sūy. 602–603)

One should learn well what has been declared; striving, one should not transgress the proper time. Such a person, possessing right vision, should not disparage right vision; knowing how to speak, he maintains that composure. He does not disparage [the teaching], nor does he speak with concealment; he does not distort the scripture or its meaning. He is a protector. *Sūyagaḍa 604*
Devoted to the Teacher and speaking with due consideration, they correctly master what has been heard. (Sūy.

605) He who possesses pure scriptures and ascetic practice, and who finds the Dharma here and there—being patient, skillful, and discerning—he is worthy to speak that state of concentration. (Sūy. 606)
Thus I say.
[Regarding] the past,
the present, and the future, O Knower.
The Tathāgata considers all [this] as such regarding the destruction of the veil of vision (darśanāvaraṇa).
He knows that which is incomparable through the destruction of doubt; he is the teacher of the incomparable, and for him there is no [obstruction] here or there. (Sūyagaḍa 607–608)
In every respect well-expounded, that which is true is always declared as such; endowed with truth, one should practice moderation toward all beings.
One should not cause harm to living beings; this is the duty of the virtuous.
Having fully understood the world as a mere dwelling place, one should cultivate this life.
One whose self is purified by the application of cultivation is like a boat in the water;
like a boat that has reached the shore, he is freed from all suffering. (Sūyagaḍa 610–611)
The wise man indeed breaks [the cycle], knowing what is evil in the world;
he breaks off evil karmas, not performing new karma.
For one who does not perform [new karma], there is no [further] karma; such a person truly understands what is called "karma. (Sūyagaḍa 612)
Having understood this, that great hero does not undergo rebirth;
the great hero does not undergo rebirth for whom there is no past karma.
Like the wind passing through a net, he leaves behind women, who are dear in this world.
Those people who do not serve women are indeed liberated from the beginning;
those people, released from bondage, do not long for life. Having cast life behind them, they reach the end through their karma. (Sūy. 615)
Those who, through their actions, have become face-to-face with the truth, instruct others on the path. (Sūy.

616) Instruction for individual living beings: The one possessed of wealth, the one worthy of honor, the seeker, the one free from desire, the self-controlled, the steadfast, and the one who has desisted from sexual intercourse. (Sūy. 617)

One should not take even wild rice that has been cut off at the source, provided it is unpolluted, untainted, always firm, and has reached its natural state of perfection. One who knows how to consume what is perfect should not conflict with anyone. (Sūyagaḍa 6.18)
With mind, with speech, and indeed with body, the one who possesses vision [should act].
For that alone is the eye of men who brings an end to doubt;
as the razor moves along the edge, so the wheel rolls along its rim. (Sūyagaḍa 619–620)
The wise cultivate the extremes; by that,
they bring an end here in this human state, having perfected the Dharma—
like the gods who have reached their goal, according to what I have heard.
And this has been heard by me from some among non-humans; they do not [speak] thus.
Some here make an end of sufferings; for others, however, there is accumulated enmity. This accumulation is difficult to overcome.
For one who is being pierced by this [suffering], awakening is difficult to attain again;
likewise, those who proclaim the Dharma established in truth are difficult to find. (Sūy.
624) Those who declare the pure Dharma, which is complete and incomparable...
What talk can there be of birth for that which is without rebirth? (Sūy.
625) How and when do the wise Tathāgatas arise?
These Tathāgatas are free from worldly attachment; they are the unsurpassed eyes of the world. (Sūy. 626)
That unsurpassed state has been proclaimed by Kāśyapa;
having performed that, some who have attained tranquility reach the final goal as wise ones.
Having acquired the energy for exertion directed toward the destruction [of defilements], the wise one proceeds.
He shakes off karma previously committed and does not create new karma.

The Great Hero does not create [new karma]; he faces toward the dust accumulated through successive stages, and having cast off karma—which is considered the very essence of dust—he is liberated. (Sūy. 628–629)
That which is the doctrine of all the saints, that doctrine establishes one as a "wound-extractor";
having established it, they have crossed over and become gods, or they were heroes in the past, and those of good conduct will be so in the future. (Sūyagaḍa 630)
"Those who have crossed over have made manifest the end of the path that is difficult to comprehend.
Thus I say. (Sūy. 631) [Verse]

The Blessed One said: "Thus he may be called 'tamed,' 'vigilant,' and 'one who has cast off worldly activity'—whether he is called a Brāhmaṇa, a Śramaṇa, a Bhikṣu, or a Nirgrantha. [The disciple asked: 'Venerable sir, how indeed does one become tamed, vigilant, and one who has cast off worldly activity—whether called a Brāhmaṇa, a Śramaṇa, a Bhikṣu, or a Nirgrantha? Pray, tell us that, O Great Sage! [The Blessed One replied: 'One who is abstinent from all sinful actions; who is free from attachment, hatred, quarreling, slander, calumny, backbiting, aversion and passion, deceitful falsehood, and the thorn of false belief; who is restrained, self-controlled, patient, and ever-vigilant; who neither becomes angry nor is arrogant—he may be called a Brāhmaṇa.'"

In this regard, a śramaṇa who is independent and free from worldly motives—having desisted from grasping, transgression, falsehood, external things, anger, pride, deceit, greed, affection, and hatred—should be one who has previously abstained from every form of grasping that is a cause of his own faults; such a person, being self-controlled, steadfast, and having cast off the body, may be called a śramaṇa.

In this regard, a monk who is humble, disciplined, modest, self-controlled, diligent, and one who has cast off his body; who, having shaken off various kinds of hardships and obstacles, is established in the purity of internal application; who is steadfast, reflective, and subsists on what is given by others—he is called a "monk."

In this regard, there are certain Nigaṇṭhas who are solitary, possessors of singular knowledge, awakened, whose taints are severed, well-restrained, well-disciplined, and true to their vows; who have attained the state of self-exertion, are wise, and have cut off the stream of suffering on both sides; who do not seek honor, respect, or gain, but are established in the Dharma, knowers of the Dharma, and committed to the path of liberation; who move with equanimity, being self-controlled, diligent, and having cast off the body—such a one may be called a "Nigaṇṭha.
Know this to be exactly so, O Venerable Sirs. Thus I say.
[Puṇḍarīka]

I have heard, O Venerable One, that this was thus declared by the Blessed One: "In this world, indeed, there is a chapter named 'The White Lotus' (*Puṇḍarīka*), and its meaning is explained as follows: Suppose there were a lotus pond, abundant with water, abundant with mud, and abundant with lotuses; it would be filled to capacity, possessed of white lotuses, beautiful, lovely to behold, charming, and exquisite. In various places throughout that lotus pond, many excellent white lotuses would grow—standing in succession, upright, radiant, endowed with color, fragrance, flavor, and texture; they would be beautiful, lovely to behold, charming, and exquisite."

In the very center of that lotus pond, there grew one great, excellent white lotus (*paumavarapōṇḍarīya*), which was gradually tapering, upright, beautiful, endowed with color, fragrance, taste, and touch; it was pleasing, lovely to behold, handsome, and perfect in form. And throughout every part of that lotus pond, in various places here and there, many other excellent white lotuses grew—gradually tapering, upright, beautiful, and so forth, up to being perfect in form. Furthermore, in the very center of that lotus pond, there grew one great, excellent white lotus—gradually tapering, and so forth, up to being perfect in form.

Then a man, having come from the eastern direction, stood on the bank of that lotus pond and saw that great, single, excellent white lotus—gradually tapering, upright, and so forth, up to being beautiful. Then that man spoke thus: "I am a man who knows the field, skilled, wise, experienced, intelligent, not foolish, one who has set out on the path, who knows the path, who knows the course of the path, and who knows the progress upon the path; I shall pull out this excellent white lotus. Having said this, the man advanced toward the lotus pond. As far as he advanced, so far was the great water and the great mud left behind, yet he did not reach the bank nor the excellent white lotus; he sank in the mud of the pond, midway between this shore and the further shore. This is the first type of person.

Furthermore, there is a second type of person: A man comes from the southern direction and, standing on the bank of that lotus pond, sees that great, singular, excellent white lotus—gradually developed, beautiful, and so forth, up to "exquisite. He also sees a certain man here who has left the near shore but has not yet reached the excellent white lotus; he is neither on this side nor on the far side, but is sitting in the mud in the middle of the pond. Then that man spoke thus to that man:

"Alas! These men are ignorant of the field, unskilled, unwise, undiscerning, foolish; they are neither seekers of the path, nor knowers of the path, nor travelers of the path, nor do they know how to exert effort. As for this man, I am one who knows the field, who is skilled, and so on, until: 'I shall extract this excellent white lotus. Yet this excellent white lotus must certainly not be extracted in the manner that this man thinks. I am the man who knows the field, who is skilled, wise, discerning, not foolish, a seeker of the path, a knower of the path, a traveler of the path, and one who knows how to exert effort; I shall extract this excellent white lotus. Having said this, that man advanced toward the pond. And as he advanced, the great water and the great mud receded, yet he did not reach the bank; the excellent white lotus was neither on this side nor on the far side, but remained stuck in the mud in the middle of the pond—this is the second type of person.

Furthermore, there is another type of person: a man comes from the western direction and, standing on the bank of that lotus pond, sees that great, single, noble white lotus, which is well-proportioned and beautiful; he sees two men there who have left the near shore but have not reached the far shore, neither able to reach the noble white lotus, sitting in the mud in the middle of the pond.

Then that man spoke thus: "Alas! These men are ignorant of the field, unskilled, unwise, incompetent, lacking intelligence, and foolish; they do not seek the path, they do not know the path, nor do they know the course or the exertion required for the path, since these men think: 'We shall pull out this excellent white lotus,' whereas indeed this excellent white lotus is not to be pulled out in the manner that these men think."

"I am a man, a field-knower, skilled, wise, experienced, intelligent, not foolish, one who knows the path, one who understands the path, one who knows the course and the progress of the path; I shall pull out this excellent, noble white lotus"—having said this, that man approaches that pond. And as he approaches it, he finds the water deep and vast, and so on, until he sits down in the mud within the pond. And that person... [remains] seated there.

Furthermore, there is a fourth kind of person: a man comes from the northern direction and, standing on the bank of that lotus pond, sees that great, single, noble white lotus, which is well-proportioned and beautiful; he sees those three kinds of men there, who have left the bank but have not yet reached it, and are sitting in the mud.

Then that man spoke thus: "Alas! These men are ignorant of the field, and so forth, until: they do not know the course or the progress of the path, since these men think thus: 'We shall pull out this excellent, noble white lotus,' yet this excellent, noble white lotus is certainly not to be pulled out in the manner that these men think. "I, however, am a man who knows the field, and so forth, until: I know the course and the progress of the path; I shall pull out this excellent, noble white lotus. Having said this, that man advanced. As far as he advanced toward that pond, so far did he encounter great water and great mud, until he sat down midway in the pond—the fourth type of person.

Then, monks, there were ascetics living on the bank, seeking liberation and skilled in their practice, who knew the various ways of traversing; coming from one direction or another, they stood upon the bank of that lotus pond and saw that great, single, excellent white lotus, beautiful in every respect. There they saw four types of men who had abandoned the bank but not yet reached it—neither able to come near nor able to see the excellent white lotus—sitting in the mud in the middle of the pond. Then, monks, that ascetic spoke thus:

"Alas! These men are ignorant of the field, and so on, until: they do not know the course or the exertion required for the path, since these men think thus: 'We shall pull out this excellent white lotus. But this excellent white lotus is certainly not to be pulled out in the manner that these men think. I am a monk, rugged, standing on the bank, knowledgeable of the field, and so on, until: I know the course and the exertion of the path; I myself shall pull out this excellent white lotus. Having said this, that monk does not approach the pond; but standing on the bank of that pond, he makes a sound: "Fly up, O excellent white lotus! Fly up! And then that excellent white lotus flies up.

"It has been proclaimed, O venerable ascetic! But its meaning, O Venerable Sir, must still be understood. Thus the monks and nuns paid homage and reverence to the Blessed Ascetic Mahāvīra; having paid homage and reverence, they spoke as follows: "It has been proclaimed, O venerable ascetic! But we do not yet know its meaning, O venerable ascetic. Then the Blessed Ascetic Mahāvīra addressed those many monks and nuns and spoke as follows: "Indeed, O venerable ascetics! I shall explain, analyze, proclaim, and reveal it—along with its purpose, its cause, and its motive—and I shall demonstrate it again and again."

"O venerable ascetic, referring to the world, I have called it that lotus pond; referring to karma, O venerable ascetic, I have called it the water; referring to sensual pleasures, O venerable ascetic, I have called them the mud; referring to people and nations, O venerable ascetic, I have called them those many excellent white lotuses; referring to the king, O venerable ascetic, I have called him that one great excellent white lotus; referring to the heterodox teachers, O venerable ascetic, I have called them those four types of persons; referring to the Dharma, O venerable ascetic, I have called it the mendicant; referring to the ford of Dharma, O venerable ascetic, I have called it the bank; referring to the discourse on Dharma, O venerable ascetic, I have called it the sound; referring to Nirvana, O venerable ascetic, I have called it the emergence; and referring to this very thing, O venerable ascetic, I have said: 'It is thus.'"

In this world, indeed, whether to the east, west, north, or south, there are certain humans who have been born into the world in succession; that is to say—some are noble, some are ignoble; some are of high birth, some are of low birth; some possess large bodies, some possess small bodies; some are fair-complexioned, some are dark-complexioned; some are handsome, some are ugly. Among those humans, there is one king—...born into an exceedingly pure royal lineage, his limbs and minor parts adorned with the constant marks of royalty, highly honored and revered by the multitude, perfected in all virtues, a Kshatriya, intoxicated [with power], consecrated on the head, well-born of mother and father, beloved for his compassion, a maker of boundaries, a sustainer of boundaries, a maker of security, a sustainer of security, a lord of men, beloved by the people, a priest to the people, a maker of prosperity, a maker of welfare, the best of men, the foremost of men, a lion among men, a venomous serpent among men, a white lotus among the best of men, a scent-elephant among the best of men; wealthy, radiant, prosperous, filled with extensive and vast palaces, beds, seats, vehicles, and carriages; possessing much wealth and many kinds of gold and jewels; engaged in the application of political expedients (*āyoga*); having abundant food and drink distributed freely; abounding in many male and female slaves, cattle, buffaloes, and sheep; with full treasuries, granaries, and armories; powerful, with weak enemies; having uprooted thorns, destroyed thorns, crushed thorns, and eradicated thorns, being thornless; having overthrown adversaries, destroyed adversaries, crushed adversaries, and eradicated adversaries, having conquered adversaries and defeated adversaries; free from famine and the fear of pestilence; ruling his kingdom—which is as described in the *Uvavāiya* [Sūtra]—until it is peaceful, free from riots and disturbances, he dwells [there].

That king has an assembly consisting of the *uggas* and the sons of *uggas*, the *bhogas* and the sons of *bhogas*, the *ikkhāgas* and the sons of *ikkhāgas*, the *nāyas* and the sons of *nāyas*, the *kōravvas* and the sons of *kōravvas*, the *bhaṭṭas* and the sons of *bhaṭṭas*, the *māhaṇas* and the sons of *māhaṇas*, the *lēcchaïs* and the sons of *lēcchaïs*, the preachers (*pasatthāras*) and the sons of preachers, and the generals (*sēnāvaïs*) and the sons of generals. Among them, there may be one who is a faithful believer (*saḍḍhī*) and says: "Let the ascetics (*samaṇas*) or the brahmins (*māhaṇas*) debate; let them come there. There, by means of one doctrine or another, they are proclaimed; we shall proclaim it by this doctrine. He says: "Know this, venerable sirs, how this doctrine is well-expounded and well-proclaimed by me: from the soles of the feet upward, to the tips of the hair on the head downward, and across to the edges of the skin—the soul (*jīva*) is this very self (*āyā*). This is the totality of its states (*pajjava*). This soul lives; this [body] does not live for me. While the body exists, it endures; when it is destroyed, it no longer endures. Such is life: after cremation, it is carried out by others. When the body is consumed by fire, the bones become the color of a pigeon. Four men, with the bier as the fifth, return to the village. Thus, since it is non-existent and not perceived—since it is non-existent and not perceived for those [who hold such views]—it is well-expounded by them: 'The soul is one thing, the body is another. Therefore, they do not dispute thus: 'O long-lived one! Is the self long or short? Circular or round? Triangular or quadrangular? Rectangular or hexagonal? Octagonal? Black or blue? Red or yellow? White? Of good smell or bad smell? Bitter or pungent? Astringent or sour? Sweet? Hard or soft? Heavy or light? Cold or hot? Oily or dry? Since it is non-existent and not perceived, for those [who hold such views] it is well-expounded: 'The soul is one thing, the body is another. Therefore, they do not perceive it thus. It is just as if some man were to draw a sword from its scabbard and show it, saying: 'O long-lived one! This is the sword; this is the scabbard. Even so, there is no man who can draw [the soul] out and show it, saying: 'O long-lived one! This is the self; this is the body. It is just as if some man were to pull a reed from its sheath and show it, saying: 'O long-lived one! This is the reed; this is the sheath. Even so, there is no man who can draw it out and show it, saying: 'O long-lived one! This is the self; this is the body.'"

Suppose, for example, a certain man were to extract the bone from the flesh and point it out, saying: "O long-lived one! This is the flesh; this is the bone. In exactly the same way, there is no man who can point it out, saying: "O long-lived one! This is the soul (ātman); this is the body. Suppose, for example, a certain man were to extract an *āmalaka* fruit from his palm and point it out, saying: "O long-lived one! This is the palm; this is the *āmalaka* fruit. In exactly the same way, there is no man who can point it out, saying: "O long-lived one! This is the soul; this is the body. Suppose, for example, a certain man were to extract the butter from the curd and point it out, saying: "O long-lived one! This is the butter; this, however, is the curd. In exactly the same way, there is no man who, having extracted it, can point it out, saying: "O long-lived one! This is the soul; this is the body."

Just as if some man were to extract oil from sesame seeds and point it out, saying, "O venerable sir, this is the oil; this is the dregs," even so, there is no such person [who can do the same for the soul], up to the point of this body. Just as if some man were to extract sugar-juice from sugarcane and point it out, saying, "O venerable sir, this is the sugar-juice; this is the pulp," even so [it is with the soul] up to the body. Just as if some man were to produce fire from a fire-drill and point it out, saying, "O venerable sir, this is the fire-drill; this is the fire," even so [it is with the soul] up to the body. Thus, since that which is not existing and not found among them is well-proclaimed by them—namely, that the soul is one thing and the body is another—that is false.

"Kill him! Strike him! Dig him up! Pluck him out! Burn him! Crush him! Tear him apart! Strip him! Seize him by force! Rob him!"—thinking thus, "In this much alone there is no life after death," they do not perceive it in this way: namely, regarding action (*kiriyā*) or non-action (*akiriyā*), well-done (*sukaḍa*) or ill-done (*dukaḍa*), merit (*kallāṇa*) or evil (*pāva*), good (*sāhu*) or bad (*asāhu*), success (*siddhi*) or failure (*asiddhi*), or hell (*niraya*) or no hell (*aniraya*). Thus, through various undertakings of karma, they undertake various sensual pleasures for the sake of enjoyment. In this way, some who are arrogant, having gone forth, proclaim their own sectarian doctrine; and believing it, trusting it, and delighting in it, [people say]: "Excellent! Well-expounded is the ascetic or the brahmin! Truly, O venerable one, we shall honor you at will, whether with food, drink, soft food, solid food, clothing, a bowl, a blanket, or a broom. Therein, some applied themselves to honoring him, while others remained devoted to honoring him.

Long before, they had this knowledge: "We shall become ascetics, homeless, possessing nothing, without sons, without wives, subsisting on what is given by others, living as mendicants; we shall not commit evil karma through our own exertion. Yet, though they have not themselves desisted from such acts, they themselves commit them, they cause others to commit them, and they approve of others committing them. Thus, they are infatuated with, greedy for, obsessed with, and addicted to the enjoyment of women and sensual pleasures; they are lustful, overcome by passion and hatred. They do not destroy themselves, they do not destroy others, nor do they destroy other breathing beings, creatures, living beings, or sentient beings. Having abandoned their former associations but not having reached the Noble Path, they are neither on this side nor on the far side; they are stranded in the midst of sensual enjoyments. Thus is described the first type of person, who holds the view that the soul and the body are one and the same.

Furthermore, the second type of person is described as consisting of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtika*). Indeed, here in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain men who have been born into the world in successive order; that is to say, some are noble (*ārya*), some are ignoble (*anārya*), and so on, up to some being ill-favored in appearance (*durūpa*). Among them, there is a certain king—just as previously described in detail regarding the Great Himavat mountains and so forth, including the sons of the army commanders. And among them, there is one who possesses faith (*śraddhin*), such that he is willing to send forth ascetics (*śramaṇa*) or brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*) to travel [to other lands]. There, having been established in a particular doctrine, he says: "We shall instruct you in this doctrine. Know this, O Venerable Sirs! How this doctrine of mine is well-proclaimed and well-established."

In this world, indeed, there are five great elements (*mahābhūta*) by which no action is performed—whether it be activity (*kiriyā*) or non-activity (*akiriyā*), well-done (*sukkaḍa*) or ill-done (*dukkada*), auspicious (*kallāṇa*) or sinful (*pāva*), virtuous (*sāhu*) or non-virtuous (*asāhu*), perfection (*siddhi*) or non-perfection (*asiddhi*), or liberation (*niraya*) or non-liberation—even down to a mere blade of grass. One should know that collection of separate elements in their respective places, as follows: earth is the first great element, water the second, fire the third, air the fourth, and space the fifth great element. These five great elements are uncreated, not caused to be created, unmade, not artificial, not derived from a maker, beginningless, endless, fruitful, not dependent on a priest (or a creator), continuous, eternal, and with the soul as the sixth. Furthermore, some say thus: "There is no destruction of what exists, nor the arising of what does not exist. This much is the aggregate of living beings (*jīvakāya*); this much is the aggregate of matter (*atthikāya*); this much is the entire world. This is the extent of the world's creation. Even down to a mere blade of grass, they think: "Whether one buys or causes to buy, kills or causes to kill, cooks or causes to cook—even having bought or caused to buy a human being—know this: there is no fault in this. They do not perceive it thus, as follows: [the existence of] activity or [non-activity], up to liberation or non-liberation. Thus, through various undertakings of karma, they undertake various sensual enjoyments for the sake of food.

Thus those ignoble ones, having fallen into error, proclaim their own doctrine; believing and trusting it, they—neither here nor hereafter—sink down amidst sensual pleasures in the interval. This is declared regarding the second type of person consisting of the five great elements.

Furthermore, there is another type of person who is described as one for whom God is the cause (*īsarakāraṇiya*). Indeed, here in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain men who have been born into the world in succession; that is to say, some are noble (*ārya*), while others are even of ugly appearance (*durūpa*). Among them, there is a certain great king—such as those from Mahāhimavanta up to the sons of army commanders—and among them, there is a certain person who has faith (*śraddhin*). He thinks: "Let the ascetics (*śramaṇa*) or brahmins come at will to travel [to me], so that this Dharma may become well-expounded and well-proclaimed by me."

Indeed, in this world, phenomena (dhammas) originate from man, culminate in man, are led by man, arise from man, are illuminated by man, are fully possessed by man, and they remain only after having overcome man itself. Just as, for example, a boil might arise on the body, grow on the body, and be fully present on the body, yet it remains only after having overcome the body itself; even so, these phenomena also originate from man and so forth, until they remain only after having overcome man himself. Just as, for example, a tumor might arise on the body, grow on the body, and remain only after having overcome the body itself; even so, these phenomena also originate from man and so forth, until they remain only after having overcome man himself.

Just as, for example, a fig tree might be born from the earth, grow within the earth, and be fully supported by the earth, yet it stands having overcome the very earth; even so, the qualities (dhammā) that begin with the person stand having overcome the person itself. Just as, for example, a tree might be born from the earth, grow within the earth, and be fully supported by the earth, yet it stands having overcome the very earth; even so, the qualities that begin with the person stand having overcome the person itself. Just as, for example, a lotus pond might be born from the earth [and so on], yet it stands having overcome the very earth; even so, the qualities that begin with the person stand having overcome the person itself.

Just as, for example, there might be a water-lily born in water that, having grown in the water, remains entirely submerged by the water; even so, the phenomena (dharmas) originating from the person remain entirely submerged by the person. Just as, for example, there might be a bubble on the water born in the water that, having grown in the water, remains entirely submerged by the water; even so, the phenomena originating from the person remain entirely submerged by the person. Furthermore, regarding this twelve-fold collection of scriptures (*gaṇipiṭaka*) taught, proclaimed, and expounded by the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas—namely: *Ācāra*, *Sūtrakṛta*, *Sthāna*, *Samavāya*, *Vivāhapannatti*, *Jñātādharmakathā*, *Upāsakadaśā*, *Antakṛddaśā*, *Anuttaraupapātikadaśā*, *Praśnavyākaraṇa*, *Vipākaśruta*, and *Dṛṣṭivāda*—they say: "All of this is false; this is not true, this is not according to reality; this is the truth, this is real, this is according to reality. Thus they form a conception, thus they establish a conception, thus they maintain a conception. Like a bird in a cage, they do not escape from that kind of suffering. They do not discern it thus: "There is action" (*kriyā*), or up to "there is no liberation" (*aniraya*). Thus, through various undertakings of karma, they pursue various sensual pleasures for the sake of enjoyment. Thus these ignoble ones, having fallen into error and believing thus, are neither on this shore nor on the far shore; they are stuck in the middle, immersed in sensual pleasures. This is the third type of person, declared to be one who holds the cause to be God (*Īśvara*).

Furthermore, the fourth type of person is described as a proponent of destiny (*niyativādin*). Indeed, here in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain men—even down to the sons of army commanders—who possess faith. They think: "Let the ascetics or brahmins come as they please; this Dharma has been well-expounded and well-proclaimed by me."

In this world, indeed, there are two kinds of persons: one person proclaims action (*kriyā*), and one person proclaims non-action (*akriyā*). Both these persons—who proclaim action and who proclaim non-action—are equal, identical, and have fallen into the same condition. But the fool, having fallen into such a condition, discriminates thus: "I am suffering, or I am grieving, or I am wasting away, or I am tormented, or I am afflicted, or I am burning with fever; I did this myself, or another caused me to suffer, grieve, waste away, torment, afflict, or burn with fever; another did this. Thus the fool, whether regarding his own cause or the cause of another, discriminates thus while having fallen into that condition. But the wise man, having fallen into such a condition, discriminates thus: "I am suffering, or I am grieving, or I am wasting away, or I am tormented, or I am afflicted, or I am burning with fever; I did not do this myself, nor did another cause me to suffer, or [the rest] up to burning with fever; another did not do this. Thus the wise man, whether regarding his own cause or the cause of another, discriminates thus while having fallen into that condition. This I say: Whether in the east, west, north, or south, whatever living beings there are—whether mobile or stationary—they undergo such aggregation, they undergo such transformation, they undergo such separation, and they undergo such destruction. They come together through observation, yet they do not discriminate thus: "This is action," or [the rest] up to "this is non-liberation. Thus, through various undertakings of karma, they undertake various sensual enjoyments for the sake of food...

In this very way, those ignoble ones who have gone astray, believing that [view]... thus they are neither on this shore nor on the further shore, but are stuck in the midst of sensual pleasures. This is declared the fourth type of person, the Niyativādin.

Thus, these four types of persons have different inclinations, different desires, different conducts, different views, different tastes, different undertakings, and are possessed of different resolutions; having abandoned their former associations but not having reached the noble path, they are neither on this shore nor on the further shore, but are stuck in the midst of sensual pleasures.

Regarding this, I say: in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain types of people, namely: some are noble and some are ignoble; some are of high birth and some are of low birth; some are well-built and some are small-statured; some are handsome and some are ugly; some are fair-complexioned and some are dark-complexioned; some are beautiful and some are unattractive. Their families and clans are possessed of property, such as small amounts or large amounts. Having come from such families, some have renounced everything and set out upon the mendicant’s life; some, having abandoned their kinsmen and possessions while they still exist, have set out upon the mendicant’s life; and some, having abandoned their kinsmen and possessions when they no longer exist, have set out upon the mendicant’s life.

Those who, having renounced both what exists and what does not exist, both the known and the unknown, and all requisites, have set out upon the mendicant’s life, already know this: namely, that here indeed a man, for his own sake, conceives various notions such as: "The field is mine, the dwelling is mine, silver is mine, gold is mine, wealth is mine, grain is mine, bronze is mine, cloth is mine; my vast collection of riches, gold, gems, jewels, pearls, shells, crystals, corals, and red precious stones—my essence and my prosperity—is mine; sounds are mine, forms are mine, smells are mine, tastes are mine, touches are mine; these sensual pleasures are truly mine, and I too belong to them."

Therefore, the wise person should first recognize within himself thus: "Indeed, some painful illness or affliction may arise for me—undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, impure, unlovely, and offensive; painful and not pleasant. "Alas, O venerable ones! These sensual pleasures might take upon themselves some other painful illness or affliction for me—undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, impure, unlovely, and offensive; painful and not pleasant—so that I might suffer, grieve, burn, be tormented, be afflicted, or be consumed by pain. Deliver me from this other painful illness or affliction—undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, impure, unlovely, and offensive; painful and not pleasant! But even such a thing has never been obtained before: these sensual pleasures are neither a protection nor a refuge. At one time a man abandons sensual pleasures, and at another time sensual pleasures abandon the man. Sensual pleasures are indeed one thing, and I am another. Why then should we be infatuated with one another through sensual pleasures? Having understood this, we shall abandon both ourselves and sensual pleasures. The wise person should know: "This is external; this is even more subject to change," namely: [the following: *Note: The passage ends here, leaving the list of things subject to change incomplete.*

"My mother is mine, my father is mine, my brother is mine, my sister is mine, my wife is mine, my sons are mine, my grandsons are mine, my daughters are mine, my daughters-in-law are mine, my friends are mine, my companions are mine, my kinsmen and well-wishers are mine; these indeed are my relatives, and I too belong to them. Thus, that wise man should first of all understand for himself: "If some suffering or affliction of disease were to arise for me here—undesirable, up to painful, not pleasant—then, O venerable ones, let my relatives take over this suffering or affliction of disease of mine, which is undesirable, up to not pleasant; let me not suffer, or grieve, or up to be tormented; deliver me from this other suffering or affliction of disease, which is undesirable, up to not pleasant. But even thus, it has never been obtained before. Or, if some suffering or affliction of disease were to arise for those venerable relatives of mine—undesirable, up to not pleasant—then, O venerable ones, let me take over this suffering or affliction of disease of these venerable relatives, which is undesirable, up to not pleasant; let them not suffer, or up to be tormented; let me deliver them from this other suffering or affliction of disease, which is undesirable, up to not pleasant. But even thus, it has never been obtained before. One person's suffering is not taken over by another; what is done by one is not experienced by another. Each is born individually, each dies individually, each passes away individually, each is reborn individually, each has individual distress, each has individual perception, each has individual thought, each has individual consciousness, each has individual sensation...

"Indeed, relatives are neither a protection nor a refuge; at some point, a man abandons his relatives, or at some point, relatives abandon a man. Relatives are indeed one thing, and I am another. Why then should we become infatuated with one another through these relative ties? Thinking thus, we shall abandon our attachment to relatives. The wise person should know: 'This is external; this is even more transitory,' namely: my hands, my feet, my arms, my thighs, my belly, my head, my virtue, my life-span, my strength, my complexion, my skin, my shadow, my hearing, my eye, my nose, my tongue, and my sense of touch are cherished by me. Yet they decay: the life-span, strength, complexion, skin, shadow, hearing, eye, nose, tongue, and sense of touch. The well-knit joints become loose; the body becomes covered in wrinkles; the black hair becomes grey..."

That is to say: even this very body, which is substantial and nourished by food, must also be gradually abandoned by me. Having reflected upon this, that monk, having set out for the practice of alms-gathering, should understand the world from two perspectives: namely, living beings and non-living things; and mobile beings and immobile beings.

In this world, indeed, householders have violence and possessiveness; and there are even some ascetics and brahmins who likewise have violence and possessiveness. They themselves initiate violence against these mobile and immobile living beings, they cause others to initiate such violence, and they approve of others who are initiating such violence.

In this world, indeed, householders have violence and possessiveness; those sensual enjoyments, whether animate or inanimate, they themselves appropriate, cause others to appropriate, and approve of others appropriating them. In this world, indeed, while some householders have violence and possessiveness, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who likewise have violence and possessiveness. [Thinking: "I, however, shall live in non-violence and without possessiveness," [one reflects: "Since there are certain ascetics and brahmins who have violence and possessiveness, just like householders, it is for their sake that we shall live the life of celibacy. For what reason? Because as it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before. These [conditions] are straightforward, continuous, unceasing, and persisting; once again, they are exactly of the same nature.

Indeed, some householders who possess violence and attachments, as well as certain ascetics and brahmins who likewise possess violence and attachments, perform sinful deeds in both ways. Having understood this, a mendicant should wander while not being seen by either of these two extremes. This I declare: whether toward the east, the west, the north, or the south—thus he is one whose karma is fully understood; thus he is one whose karma is cast off; thus he becomes one who has brought an end to action. So it is proclaimed.

In this regard, the Blessed One has declared six classes of living beings as the basis [for non-violence], namely: the earth-body, and so on, up to the mobile-body. Just as if I were being struck with a staff, or with a bone, or with a fist, or with a clod of earth, or with a shard; or being beaten, or threatened, or flogged, or tormented, or exhausted, or destroyed—even to the extent of the pain caused by the plucking out of a single hair—I experience suffering and fear resulting from such violence; know that it is even so for all breathing things, all beings, all souls, and all creatures: when they are struck with a staff, or [with the other instruments] up to a shard; or being beaten, or threatened, or flogged, or tormented, or exhausted, or destroyed—even to the extent of the pain caused by the plucking out of a single hair—they experience suffering and fear resulting from such violence.

Having understood this, all living beings, down to all creatures, must not be killed, must not be subjected to violence, must not be imprisoned, must not be tormented, and must not be destroyed. This I declare: those Arhats, Blessed Ones, who have passed away, those who are present, and those who will come in the future—all of them proclaim thus, speak thus, teach thus, and explain thus: "All living beings, down to all creatures, must not be killed, must not be subjected to violence, must not be imprisoned, must not be tormented, and must not be destroyed. This Dharma is eternal, constant, and everlasting; having perceived the world, it has been proclaimed by those possessed of knowledge. Thus, that monk should abstain from injury to living beings, down to abstaining from possession. He should not clean his teeth with a tooth-stick, nor use collyrium, nor emetics, nor purgatives, nor fumigations, nor should he practice such [medicinal] treatments.

That monk—free from action, free from impurity, free from anger, free from pride, free from deceit, free from greed, tranquil, and fully extinguished—should not form expectations for the future, thinking: "By this which has been seen by me, or heard, or thought, or known; or by this practice of good conduct, austerity, restraint, and the life of celibacy; or by this Dharma characterized by the overcoming of birth and death—having passed away from here, may I become a god after death, a master over sensual enjoyments; or may I be a perfected one (siddha), free from suffering and pain. He should not think: "May it be so," or "May it not be so. That monk is uninfatuated with sounds, uninfatuated with forms, uninfatuated with smells, uninfatuated with tastes, and uninfatuated with touches; he is restrained. He is free from anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, aversion, strife, slander, calumny, backbiting, likes and dislikes, deceitful falsehood, and the thorn of false view. Thus, having stilled himself regarding that great undertaking, having turned away from it, and having desisted from it—that is the monk.

Regarding those living beings that exist as either mobile or immobile—himself he does not initiate violence against them, nor does he cause others to initiate it, nor does he approve of others who are initiating it; thus, from that great undertaking, he is tranquil, established [in restraint], and desisted.

That monk—whatever these sensual enjoyments are, whether animate or inanimate—does not himself take possession of them, does not cause others to take possession of them, and does not approve of another who is taking possession of them; thus he is calmed, established, and abstinent from that great grasping. That monk—whatever this karma for future lives is being performed—he does not himself do it, does not cause others to do it, and does not approve of another who is doing it; thus he is calmed, established, and abstinent from that great grasping.

If that monk should know: "This food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy—was intended for this purpose, specifically for one fellow-monk; it was acquired by harming living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings; it was prepared specifically for him, bought, borrowed, taken by force, ungiven, brought from elsewhere, or specially set aside"—and if that [food] should be such, then that monk, if he further knows: "There exists among them the effort for whose sake it was prepared, namely: for oneself, for sons, daughters, daughters-in-law, nurses, kinsmen, kings, male servants, female servants, laborers, laborers' wives, messengers, or for separate refreshments, snacks, and morning meals, or for the accumulation and hoarding of provisions here for the eating of these people"—then he does not eat it himself, nor cause others to eat it, nor approve of another who eats it. Thus, out of great consideration, he remains calm, established in restraint, and abstains.

Therein, a monk—having sought and received food placed in his bowl that was prepared by others, finished by others, pure in its procurement and search, beyond reproach, dedicated by the giver, obtained without causing injury, sought and solicited, gathered from various sources, moderate in quantity, serving as a support for the body like a medicine for a wound or an ointment for a sore, and conducive to self-restraint, vitality, and freedom from debt—should take his nourishment with himself as one who has become like a snake in a hole: food at the time for food, drink at the time for drink, clothing at the time for clothing, shelter at the time for shelter, and bedding at the time for bedding.
