That monk, being mindful, having taken up a certain direction or sub-direction, should preach the Dharma, analyze it, and proclaim it; whether to those who have approached or those who have not approached, and to those who are desirous of hearing, he should declare it—peace, renunciation, tranquility, Nirvana, self-restraint, rectitude, gentleness, lightness, and non-violence. He should proclaim the Dharma after due consideration for all breathing things, all beings, all living beings, and all creatures. That monk, while proclaiming the Dharma, should not preach the Dharma for the sake of food, nor for the sake of drink, nor for the sake of clothing, nor for the sake of shelter, nor for the sake of bedding, nor for the sake of various other sensual pleasures. He should preach the Dharma without weariness, and he should preach the Dharma for no other purpose than the wearing away of karma.

Indeed, in this world, having heard the Dharma from that monk and having reflected upon it, those heroes who have risen through right exertion and established themselves in this Dharma—those heroes who, having heard the Dharma from that monk and having reflected upon it, have risen through right exertion and established themselves in this Dharma—they are thus freed from all bonds, they are thus withdrawn from all things, they are thus tranquilized in all respects, and they are thus completely extinguished in every way. Thus I say.

Thus that monk, established in the Dharma, knowing the Dharma, and having entered upon the path of liberation, is as described: whether it be the lotus with its petals or the lotus without its petals. In this way, that monk—having fully understood karma, having fully understood attachments, and having fully understood household life—is tranquil, self-controlled, steadfast, and ever-vigilant. He is worthy of these designations: namely, a *śramaṇa*, or a *brāhmaṇa*, or patient, or self-restrained, or guarded, or liberated, or a sage, or a silent seer (*muni*), or a doer, or a knower, or a monk, or one who is austere, or one who stands on the shore, or one who has mastered conduct and practice.
Thus I say.

[The Chapter on the Stances of Action] This was heard by me, O venerable one, as it was thus spoken by the Blessed One: "In this world, indeed, the chapter named 'The Stances of Action' has been taught; its meaning is as follows: here, indeed, two stances are thus declared in brief: namely, the righteous and the unrighteous, the tranquil and the non-tranquil."

In this regard, as for the first section concerning the side of unrighteousness (*adhammapakkha*), its meaning is declared as follows: Indeed, here in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain human beings—namely, some who are noble and some who are ignoble; some of high birth and some of low birth; some tall and some short; some fair-complexioned and some dark-complexioned; some handsome and some ugly. And having reflected upon this kind of undertaking of violence (*daṇḍasamādāna*) by them, [which leads] to states among hell-beings, or animal births, or humans, or gods—whatever living beings of such a nature experience conscious sensation...

And for them also, these thirteen bases of action (*kriyāsthāna*) are declared to exist, namely: the infliction of punishment for a purpose, the infliction of punishment without a purpose, the infliction of punishment through violence, the infliction of punishment unintentionally, the infliction of punishment due to perversion of view, the basis of false speech, the basis of taking what is not given, the internal basis, the basis of pride, the basis of malice toward friends, the basis of deceit, the basis of greed, and the basis of movement (*iryāpathika*).

The first undertaking of violence is described as "engaged in violence for a specific purpose. For example, suppose some man, for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of his house, or for the sake of his family, or for the sake of his friends, or for the sake of a *nāga*, a *bhūta*, or a *yakṣa*, himself discharges that violence against mobile and immobile living beings, causes another to discharge it, or approves of another discharging it. Thus, indeed, on account of that, it is described as blameworthy; thus is the first undertaking of violence described as "engaged in violence for a specific purpose."

Furthermore, the second form of adopting violence is described as "inflicting violence for no purpose. Suppose, for example, there is a certain man who, regarding these mobile living beings, does not [kill them] for the sake of skin, nor for hide, nor for meat, nor for blood, nor for heart, nor for bile, nor for fat, nor for feathers, nor for tails, nor for hair, nor for horns, nor for tusks, nor for fangs, nor for bathing, nor for sinews, nor for bones, nor for marrow; nor thinking, "They have harmed me," nor "They are harming me," nor "They will harm me"; nor for the sake of nourishing his sons, nor for nourishing his cattle, nor for the maintenance of his household, nor for the sake of supporting ascetics or brahmins; and who does not cause any transformation whatsoever to that body—yet he kills, cuts, pierces, lops off, tears apart, destroys, and abandons them. Such a fool becomes a partaker of enmity through violence inflicted for no purpose.

Suppose, for example, there were a man who [takes] these stationary living beings, namely: reeds, or hard wood, or jantuga plants, or paragā plants, or mokkhā plants, or grass, or kuśa grass, or kucchaga grass, or parvaga plants, or straw; and he does not use them for the nourishment of his children, nor for the nourishment of his cattle, nor for the maintenance of his household, nor for the support of ascetics and brahmins—yet by subjecting that body to various forms of transformation, that fool, having killed, cut, split, torn, plundered, destroyed, and cast it away, becomes a partaker in enmity through groundless violence.

Suppose, for example, some man were to repeatedly pile up grass in a marsh, a lake, water, a river, a whirlpool, a hollow, a thicket, a dense forest, a mountain, or a mountain ravine, and himself set fire to it, cause another to set fire to it, or approve of another setting fire to it—this is a purposeless infliction of harm (*anaṭṭhā-daṇḍa*). Indeed, on account of that, this is declared to be a blameworthy act for him; thus is the second undertaking of violence described as consisting in purposeless infliction of harm.

Furthermore, the third undertaking of the rod is explained as being concerned with the rod of violence. For example, suppose some man thinks: "He has harmed me, or my mother, or another person, or another woman; he is harming them, or he will harm them. Because of that, he himself inflicts the rod upon mobile and stationary living beings, causes another to inflict it, or approves of another who is inflicting it—this is the rod of violence. Thus, indeed, on account of that, it is explained as being blameworthy; this is declared as the third undertaking of the rod, concerned with the rod of violence.

Furthermore, the fourth form of taking up violence is described as "unintentional violence" (*akammhā-daṇḍa-vattiyā*). Suppose, for example, some man goes into a marsh, or even into a mountain fastness, with the intent of hunting deer, the purpose of hunting deer, and the aim of hunting deer, in order to kill deer. Thinking, "These are deer," he draws his arrow and shoots it at one particular deer, thinking, "I shall kill that deer. But having instead struck a partridge, a quail, a *caḍaga*, a *lāvaga*, a *kavōyaga*, a *kavi*, or a *kavijala* bird, he kills it. In this case, he touches one thing for the sake of another; this is unintentional violence.

Suppose, for example, a certain man, while gathering rice, or barley, or millet, or *kaṅgu* grain, or *paraga*, or *rālā*, were to discharge a weapon for the sake of some other grass, thinking, "I shall cut the grass that is *sāmaga*, or *taṇaga*, or *kumudaga*, or the straw of the rice, or the *kalēsuya* grass. Having cut the rice, or the barley, or the millet, or the *kaṅgu*, or the *paraga*, or the *rālā*, it happens thus: he touches another thing for the sake of another; this is an unintentional offense (*akamhā-daṇḍa*). Thus, indeed, his transgression arising from that is declared to be blameworthy (*sāvajja*). This fourth undertaking of violence (*daṇḍasamādāna*), consisting of unintentional violence, has been explained.

Furthermore, the fifth application of force is described as the application of force resulting from a perversion of vision. For example, suppose a certain man, while living together with his mother, father, brothers, sisters, wives, sons, daughters, or daughters-in-law, perceives a friend as an enemy; thus, through the application of force resulting from a perversion of vision, he comes to have slain a friend.

Suppose, for example, that a certain person, during a raid on a village, or a city, or a market-town, or a hamlet, or a port, or a camp, or a settlement, or a town, or a capital city, were to strike one who is not a thief while believing him to be a thief—being one who has previously struck those who are not thieves due to a perversion of vision. Thus, indeed, his action is declared to be blameworthy because it originates from that [perversion]; this is declared as the fifth undertaking of violence, characterized by a perversion of vision.

Furthermore, the sixth station of action is described as being rooted in falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*). For example, suppose some man, for his own sake, for the sake of another, for the sake of his household, or for the sake of his family, speaks a lie himself, causes another to speak a lie, or approves of another speaking a lie. Indeed, on account of that, it is described as being blameworthy for him; thus is the sixth station of action described as being rooted in falsehood.

Furthermore, the seventh station of action is described as being concerned with taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). For example, suppose some man, for his own sake or for the sake of his family and retinue, takes what is not given himself, causes another to take what is not given, or approves of another who is taking what is not given. Truly, on account of that, it is described as a blameworthy act for him; thus is the seventh station of action described as being concerned with taking what is not given.

Furthermore, the eighth station of action is described as "internal" (*ajjhattha-vattiyā*). For example, suppose there is a certain man who does not deceive anyone at all; yet he himself is base, wretched, wicked, dejected, with his mind and intentions overwhelmed, plunged into an ocean of anxiety and grief, his face resting in his palms, fallen into the meditation of distress (*ārtadhyāna*), and brooding with his gaze fixed upon the ground. In him, four internal and unconfessed states are thus described: namely, anger, pride, deceit, and greed. These—anger, pride, deceit, and greed—are indeed internal to him. Thus, on account of these, it is described as a blameworthy state; this eighth station of action is described as being internal.

Furthermore, the ninth station of action is explained as "arrogance": Suppose, for example, there is a certain man who, being intoxicated by some ground for intoxication—whether by pride of birth, or pride of family, or pride of strength, or pride of beauty, or pride of austerity, or pride of learning, or pride of gain, or pride of power, or pride of wisdom—despises, reviles, scorns, censures, humiliates, and disregards another, thinking: "This person is insignificant; I, however, am distinguished by my superior birth, family, strength, and qualities."

Thus one exalts oneself; upon the dissolution of the body, being subject to the second type of karma, one passes from womb to womb, birth to birth, death to death, and hell to hell—becoming fierce, stubborn, fickle, and full of pride. Indeed, this is declared to be the transgression arising therefrom; thus the ninth station of action is called "arising from pride."

Furthermore, the tenth station of action is explained as being characterized by malice toward friends: Suppose, for example, there is a certain man living together with his mother, father, brothers, sisters, wives, daughters, sons, or daughters-in-law, and because of some very slight offense committed by any one of them, he himself inflicts a severe punishment upon them; namely—

He may scrub his body with cold water, or he may sprinkle his body with hot water; he may scorch his body with a fire; or he may tear out his side-hair with a hook, a comb, a needle, a blade of grass, a knife, a creeper, or any other kind of instrument. Or he may strike his body with a staff, a bone, a fist, a clod of earth, or a potsherd. When such a person lives among them, they become dejected; when he departs, they become joyful...

A person of such a kind—who relies on punishment, holds punishment dear, and places punishment foremost—is harmful in this world and harmful in the next world; he is full of burning passion, prone to anger, and even backbiting. Thus, indeed, on account of that, it is declared to be a blameworthy action; this is explained as the tenth ground of action, characterized by malice toward friends.

Furthermore, the eleventh station of action is explained as being characterized by deceit (*māyā-pratyaya*). Those who are thus described are those of hidden conduct, belonging to the darkness, light as a bat’s wing but heavy as a mountain; though they are teachers (*ācāryas*), they employ un-Aryan speech.
Being one way themselves, they consider themselves otherwise; when asked about one thing, they explain another; when something must be told in one way, they tell it in another...

Just as, for example, a certain man with an internal arrow neither extracts that arrow himself, nor causes it to be extracted by another, nor causes it to be destroyed; rather, he conceals it, and while not confessing it, he suffers internally within his inner self—even so, a deceitful person, having committed a deception, does not disclose it, does not repent, does not blame himself, does not censure it, does not turn away from it, does not purify it, does not resolve to refrain from it in the future, and does not undertake the appropriate penance and expiation.

The deceiver is reborn in this world; the deceiver is reborn in the next world. He censures and blames, he praises and flatters; he does not desist, he does not turn back; he conceals his own misconduct. The deceiver also possesses a mental disposition that is not established in happiness. Thus, indeed, on account of that, it is declared to be a blameworthy action for him; this eleventh station of action is declared to be characterized by deceit (*māyā*).

Furthermore, the twelfth station of action is explained as being characterized by greed (*lobhavattiya*): namely, those who are forest-dwellers, village-dwellers, or town-dwellers, and who are sometimes secretive; they are neither very restrained nor very abstinent toward all living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings. They formulate such true-and-false propositions for themselves: "I am not to be killed, but others are to be killed; I am not to be enslaved, but others are to be enslaved; I am not to be imprisoned, but others are to be imprisoned; I am not to be tormented, but others are to be tormented; I am not to be destroyed, but others are to be destroyed..."

In exactly the same way, those who are infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and obsessed by sensual pleasures—for four, five, or even up to sixteen years, or for a shorter or longer duration—having enjoyed various objects of enjoyment, at the time of death, pass away and are reborn in certain demonic and sinful states. When they are eventually released from there, they are reborn again as blind, as deaf, or as mentally deficient.

Thus, indeed, on account of that, it is declared to be blameworthy; this is declared as the twelfth place of action (kriyāsthāna), characterized by greed. These twelve places of action must be thoroughly and correctly understood by a wise ascetic or brahmin.

Furthermore, the thirteenth station of action is taught as that which pertains to movement (*iryāpathika*). Here, indeed, for a homeless monk who is self-restrained, who is restrained in movement, restrained in speech, restrained in seeking alms, restrained in the taking up, laying down, and handling of his bowl, robes, and other requisites, restrained in the disposal of excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, and sweat, who is restrained in mind, restrained in speech, and restrained in body; who has guarded his mind, guarded his speech, and guarded his body; whose senses are guarded and who is a guardian of celibacy; who moves with careful attention, stands with careful attention, sits with careful attention, lies down with careful attention, eats with careful attention, speaks with careful attention, and takes up or lays down his cloth, bowl, blanket, or broom—even when there is merely the flicker of a glancing eye—a subtle action pertaining to movement (*iryāpathika*) is produced.

That [karma] is bound and touched in the first moment, experienced in the second moment, and exhausted in the third moment. That which is bound, touched, raised, experienced, and exhausted becomes "without karma" at a later time. Thus, indeed, that which arises from it is designated as blameworthy; this is declared as the thirteenth station of action, namely, *īryāpathika*.

I say this: all those Arhats, Blessed Ones—those of the past, those of the present, and those yet to come—have spoken, do speak, or will speak of these very same thirteen places of action; they have explained, do explain, or will explain them; and likewise, they have practiced, do practice, or will practice this thirteenth place of action.

Furthermore, I shall explain the unsurpassed analysis of the conquest of men: here indeed, for those of various understandings, various inclinations, various conducts, various views, various tastes, various undertakings, and possessed of various resolutions, there exist various kinds of evil scriptural studies.

Namely: earth-omens, portents, dream-interpretation, celestial phenomena, bodily marks, voice-analysis, physiognomy, the characteristics of women, the characteristics of men, the characteristics of horses, the characteristics of elephants, the characteristics of oxen, the characteristics of rams, the characteristics of cocks, the characteristics of partridges, the characteristics of quails, the characteristics of pigeons, the characteristics of wheels, the characteristics of umbrellas, the characteristics of hides, the characteristics of staffs, the characteristics of swords, the characteristics of gems, the characteristics of coins, the arts for making one fortunate, the arts for making one unfortunate, the arts for causing pregnancy, the arts for causing delusion, the magical incantations of Ātharvaṇa, the magical incantations of Pākaśāsana, the ritual oblations of substances, the Kṣatriya-science, the movements of the moon, the movements of the sun, the movements of Venus, the movements of Mercury, the fall of meteors, the burning of the quarters, the circles of deer, the circles of crows, showers of dust, showers of hair, showers of flesh, showers of blood, the Vētāla-spells, the half-Vētāla-spells, the spells for inducing sleep, the spells for opening the palate, the Sōvāgī-spells, the Sāvarī-spells, the Dāmili-spells, the Kāliṅgī-spells, the Gōrī-spells, the Gandhārī-spells, the spells for descending, the spells for ascending, the spells for opening the jaw, the spells for paralyzing, the spells for piercing, the spells for causing disease, the spells for removing poison, the spells for flight, the spells for invisibility, the spells for stretching out the limbs...

Such spells as these they employ for the sake of food, they employ them for the sake of drink, they employ them for the sake of clothing, they employ them for the sake of shelter, they employ them for the sake of bedding, or they employ them for the sake of various other sensual pleasures. They practice those spells like beasts of prey; those ignoble ones, having fallen into error, at the time of death pass away and are reborn in certain places of the Asuras, in states of sinful misery. Even when they are eventually released from there, they return once more to a state of extreme stupidity and blinding darkness.

If one person, for his own sake or for the sake of another, for the sake of a bed, for the sake of a house, or for the sake of a retinue; relying upon a leader or a fellow resident; or as a follower, or as an attendant, or as a traveling companion; or as a burglar, or as a cutpurse, or as a butcher of sheep, or as a fowler, or as a hunter, or as a fisherman, or as a catcher of iguanas, or as a cowherd, or as a thief, or as a maker of golden ornaments, or as a woman who makes golden ornaments...

If one person, having formed the intention to follow [another], kills that very person, cuts him, pierces him, plunders him, destroys him, and consumes him as food, then by thus proclaiming himself through great sinful deeds, he becomes one who has proclaimed himself [guilty] of great sins. Or, if one person, having formed the intention to serve [another], serves that very person and then kills him, cuts him, pierces him, plunders him, destroys him, and consumes him as food, then by thus proclaiming himself through great sinful deeds, he becomes one who has proclaimed himself [guilty] of great sins.

If someone, intending to act as a highwayman, stands right there on the road and kills, cuts, pierces, plunders, loots, and destroys [another], taking their food for himself—thus he makes himself known by great evil deeds. Or if someone, intending to act as a housebreaker, breaks and pierces that very wall—and so on until—he makes himself known by great evil deeds.

Some one, having resolved upon the state of a "knot-cutter," having cut and split that very knot, and so on until he has proclaimed himself [as such] through great evil karmas; some one, having resolved upon the state of a sheep-slayer, having killed a sheep or some other breathing creature, and so on until he has proclaimed himself [as such]—this same formula applies everywhere.

Some, adopting the state of a hunter, becomes one who kills or causes others to kill a buffalo or some other breathing being, up to and including deceiving them; some, adopting the state of a trapper, becomes one who kills or causes others to kill a deer or some other breathing being, up to and including deceiving them; some, adopting the state of a fowler, becomes one who kills or causes others to kill a bird or some other breathing being, up to and including deceiving them.

In one case, having been reborn in the state of a fish, he becomes a killer of a fish or some other mobile being, and so on, up to one who deceives himself; in another case, having been reborn in the state of a cow-killer, he becomes a killer of a cow or some other mobile being, and so on, up to one who deceives himself; in yet another case, having been reborn in the state of a cowherd, he repeatedly harasses that very same cowherd or [another] mobile being, and so on, up to one who deceives himself.

In some cases, having formed the intention to kill, he becomes one who kills that very same auspicious being or another mobile creature, up to and including deceiving others; in some cases, having formed the intention to kill, he becomes one who kills that very same human or another mobile creature, up to and including consuming food [obtained thereby]; thus, by deceiving himself through great evil karmas, he becomes one who has deceived himself.

If one person rises from the midst of the assembly and, thinking "I shall kill this," kills a partridge, a quail, a *caḍaga*, a *lāvaga*, a *kavōyaga*, a *kaviñjala*, or any other living being with a breath, and so on, up to becoming one who causes others to slaughter them.

If, out of some motive, or through malice, or even for the sake of a wine-vat, a person himself burns the crops of householders or their sons with fire, or causes them to be burned by another with fire, or even approves of another burning the crops with fire—thus he makes himself out to be possessed of great evil deeds.

If, on account of some grievance, or because of a harsh word, or even because of a wine cup, he himself yokes the oxen, cows, horses, or donkeys of householders or their sons to the plow, or causes another to yoke them, or approves of another doing so, then by such great evil deeds he makes himself a participant in [the resulting] suffering.

If, on some occasion, being provoked by some cause—whether by harsh speech or by the giving of wine—a person burns, or causes to be burned, or approves another burning, the stables for camels, oxen, horses, or donkeys belonging to householders or their sons, using a bundle of thorns and fire himself, then he becomes greatly subject to rebirth.

If a certain person, being provoked by some offense—whether by a harsh word, or by a vessel of wine, or by a bowl of liquor—himself steals, causes another to steal, or approves of another stealing, the earrings, jewels, or pearls of householders or their sons; thus he incurs great [demerit], and so forth.

If a certain person, when in conflict with someone over some matter—whether through malicious intent, or through a dispute over wine-vats—himself takes away, or even consents to the taking of, a staff, an umbrella, a vessel, a bowl, a walking stick, a water-strainer, a cloth, a floor-cover, a leather mat, a leather shoe, a leather case, or anything else belonging to ascetics or brahmins; thus he becomes one who proclaims himself a great [man], and so forth.

If he, being alone, does not hesitate, but himself burns medicinal herbs with fire belonging to householders or the sons of householders, and even approves of another burning them—thus he becomes one who proclaims [himself] as a great [ascetic], and so forth.

If he alone does not hesitate—namely, if he himself cuts the noses of householders, or householders' sons, or of oxen, or horses, or donkeys; or causes another to cut them; or approves of another cutting them—then by this he makes himself out to be possessed of great evil karma.

If he alone does not hesitate—namely, having observed that the goats' sheds or even the donkeys' sheds belonging to householders or the sons of householders have been set on fire with a bundle of thorns, he himself burns them with fire, or even approves of it.

In some cases, he does not hesitate—namely, when he himself steals, or even consents to the theft, of earrings, gems, or pearls belonging to householders or their sons; and in some cases, he does not hesitate—namely, when he himself steals, or even consents to the theft, of umbrellas, staffs, or even leather bags belonging to ascetics or brahmins. Thus, he becomes one who is greatly [blamed] up to being a slanderer.

If one person, having seen a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, makes himself known through various kinds of evil deeds; or if he slaps him with his fingers; or if he speaks harshly to him; or if, even when the time has come for him to enter, he does not give him food, drink, soft food, or delicacy.

Those who, being wearied by existence, burdened by their load, indolent, base, and miserly, go forth as ascetics—they merely sustain this very life of a disgraceful livelihood; they do not cling to anything for the sake of the world beyond. They suffer, they grieve, they burn, they bleed, they are tormented, they are distressed; they remain unceasing in their suffering, burning, grieving, bleeding, tormenting, and distressing, and in their afflictions caused by slaughter, imprisonment, and bondage. Through great exertion, through great mobilization, and through great exertion and mobilization combined, by means of various kinds of evil deeds, they become enjoyers of magnificent human pleasures.

That is to say: food at the time for food, drink at the time for drink, clothing at the time for clothing, shelter at the time for shelter, and bedding at the time for bedding; and furthermore, having bathed earlier and later, performed his sacrificial offerings (*balikamma*), and completed the auspicious rites and purificatory ceremonies (*kautuka-maṅgala-pāyacchitta*); having bathed his head, wearing a garland on his neck, adorned with jewels and gold, his body decorated with fashioned wreaths and crests, his limbs bound with ornaments, his waist-cord and clusters of flower-garlands hanging down, dressed in unwashed garments, his body sprinkled with sandalwood paste; seated upon a great, massive lion-throne within a vast, grand peaked-roofed hall, surrounded by a troop of women, while a great lamp burns all night long, amidst the sound of loud singing, dancing, instrumental music, strings, cymbals, clapping, and the resonance of drums, gongs, and various musical instruments—he dwells enjoying sublime human pleasures.

When he gives even a single command, four or five men rise up even before being told, saying: "Speak, O Lord! What shall we do? What shall we bring? What shall we offer? What shall we prepare? What is desired by your heart? What will satisfy your palate? Seeing him, the ignoble ones say: "This man is surely a god; this man is surely one who has bathed like a god; this man is surely one who lives like a god; others indeed depend upon him. But seeing him, the noble ones say: "This man is one whose actions are exceedingly cruel; he is excessively arrogant and excessively guarded; he goes toward the right [path] only to go to hell; he belongs to the dark faction, and for him, enlightenment will be difficult to attain in the future..."

Thus, those who have arisen from this state are seized by greed; those who have not arisen from it are seized by greed; and those who are consumed by greed are seized [by it]. This state is ignoble, incomplete, imperfect, unrighteous, impure, not leading to the highest good, not the path to success, not the path to liberation, not the path to nirvana, not the path to final deliverance, and not the path to the destruction of all suffering; it is exclusively false and unwholesome. This, indeed, is declared to be the analysis of the first position, the side of non-dharma.

Furthermore, in the analysis of the second point regarding the side of righteousness (*dhammapakkha*), it is said as follows: Here indeed, in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain men who are such as this—

There are noble beings and ignoble beings; those of high lineage and low lineage; those possessing bodies and those possessing laughter; those of beautiful complexion and ugly complexion; those of handsome form and deformed form. And their fields and lands are possessed as property. This entire discourse is to be understood just as in the case of the *Puṇḍarīka* (White Lotus) Sūtra, with the same terminology, up until: "having extinguished all [passions], they have attained final liberation in every respect. Thus I say.

In this state, the noble one is solitary, [proceeding] until the path that leads to the destruction of all suffering; he is a sage of absolute rightness. Thus has the analysis of the second state, the side of righteousness, been declared.

Now, the analysis of the third state, the mixed state, is declared as follows: those who are forest-dwellers, village-dwellers, or town-dwellers, who are somewhat secretive, and so forth—they, being released from there, are reborn again into a state of dullness and darkness.

This state is ignoble, incomplete, and not the path for the destruction of all suffering; it is exclusively false and unrighteous. This, indeed, is declared to be the analysis of the third mixed state.

Furthermore, regarding the analysis of the first point, the side of unrighteousness, it is declared as follows: Here indeed, in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain householders who are full of great desire, engaged in great undertakings, possessing great property, unrighteous, followers of unrighteousness, devoted to unrighteousness, proclaimers of unrighteousness, living by unrighteous means, looking toward unrighteousness, taking pride in unrighteousness, whose conduct is characterized by unrighteousness, and who live their lives solely by unrighteous means.

They kill, cut, pierce, and dismember; they are blood-stained, fierce, cruel, wicked, and violent; they abound in deception, fraud, guile, trickery, hypocrisy, and deceit; they are immoral, of evil conduct, difficult to appease, and unrighteous. They refrain from all killing of living beings for as long as life lasts; they refrain from all anger up to the thorn of false views for as long as life lasts. They refrain from all bathing, massaging, perfumes, scents, ointments, sounds, touches, tastes, forms, fragrances, garlands, and ornaments for as long as life lasts. They refrain from all carts, chariots, vehicles, yokes, palanquins, sedan-chairs, litters, carriages, beds, seats, conveyances, enjoyments, food, and modes of dress for as long as life lasts. They refrain from all buying and selling, and from transactions involving coins and half-coins for as long as life lasts. They refrain from all gold, silver, bullion, grain, gems, pearls, conchs, stones, and corals for as long as life lasts. They refrain from all false weights and false measures for as long as life lasts.

They do not desist from all undertakings and preparations for life as long as they live; they do not desist from all acts of doing and causing to be done as long as they live; they do not desist from all acts of cooking and causing to be cooked as long as they live; they do not desist from all acts of crushing, pounding, threatening, beating, killing, binding, and tormenting as long as they live; and they do not desist from whatever other such sinful, unrighteous occupations that cause suffering to other living beings and are practiced by the ignoble, as long as they live.

Suppose, for example, that a certain man, being uncontrolled and cruel, inflicts wrongful punishment upon partridges, quails, pigeons, francolins, wild fowl, deer, buffaloes, boars, crocodiles, rhinoceroses, tortoises, porcupines, and so forth; even so, such a person inflicts wrongful punishment upon those same creatures. Furthermore, regarding his external retinue—consisting of slaves, messengers, servants, laborers, wage-earners, or hired men—if they commit even the slightest offense, he himself inflicts a heavy punishment upon them.

Namely: "Punish him! Shave him! Threaten him! Beat him! Bind him with fetters! Bind him with shackles! Bind him in stocks! Bind him in prison! Bind him with both shackles and chains, twisting and breaking his limbs! Cut off his hands! Cut off his feet! Cut off his ears! Cut off his nose! Cut off his lips! Cut off his head! Cut off his face! Subject him to forced labor! Mutilate his limbs! Have his wings torn out! Pluck out his eyes! Pluck out his eyeballs! Pluck out his testicles! Pluck out his tongue! Hang him! Grind him! Crush him! Impale him on a stake! Pierce him with a stake! Subject him to the ordeal of caustic lye! Subject him to the ordeal of execution! Subject him to the 'lion's tail' torture! Subject him to the 'bull's tail' torture! Burn him with a flaming sword! Force him to eat pieces of his own flesh like a crow! Deprive him of food and drink! Bind him for life! Or kill him with some other cruel and wicked method. And whatever his inner circle of attendants may be...

Whether it be a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, a wife, a son, a daughter, or a daughter-in-law—if one of them commits even a very slight offense, he himself inflicts a severe punishment upon them. That is to say: he causes them to be immersed in cold water; he acts as one who harbors malice toward friends, and so on, until he becomes harmful in the next world. They suffer, grieve, waste away, pine, are tormented, and are consumed by distress; they do not desist from these sufferings, sorrows, wasting, pining, tormenting, and consuming, nor from killing, binding, and the afflictions thereof.

In exactly this way, those who are infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and obsessed by sensual pleasures—for four, five, six, or even more years—having indulged in various enjoyments, having accumulated causes of enmity, and having committed many sinful deeds, through an abundance of karma consisting of such accumulations: just as a ball of iron or a ball of stone, when thrown into water, sinks to the bottom of the water and comes to rest upon the surface of the earth; even so, a person of that kind—who is full of faults, full of deceit, full of mud, full of enmity, full of lack of trust, full of hypocrisy, full of guile, full of self-aggrandizement, full of infamy, and who is excessively a slayer of living beings—when his time has come and he dies, sinks below the surface of the earth and comes to rest upon the surface of hell.

Those hells are circular within and square without; below, they are shaped like a razor; they are perpetually shrouded in darkness, devoid of the light of planets, moon, sun, constellations, or other celestial bodies; their floors are smeared and plastered with a mire of fat, marrow, flesh, blood, and layers of pus; they are impure, putrid, and of an extremely foul odor; black, with the appearance of glowing embers; harsh to the touch, difficult to endure, and unpleasant; the hells are foul, and the sensations within the hells are foul.

Indeed, the hell-beings in the hells do not sleep, nor do they nod; they obtain neither hearing, nor sight, nor mindfulness, nor intelligence. There, experiencing intense, vast, deep, bitter, harsh, fierce, painful, miserable, sharp, and unbearable hellish sensations, they remain.

Suppose, for example, there were a tree grown on a mountain peak; its roots having been severed and it being heavy at the top, it would fall from that very place—downward, toward the uneven, toward the inaccessible. In the same way, such a type of person goes from womb to womb, from birth to birth, from death to death, from hell to hell, from suffering to suffering. He is destined for the right [side], a denizen of hell, belonging to the dark faction, and for him enlightenment will be difficult to attain in the future. This state is ignoble, not leading to absolute knowledge, and so forth, until it is not the path for the destruction of all suffering; it is exclusively false and unrighteous. Thus has the analysis of the first position, the side of non-dharma, been declared.

Furthermore, regarding the second point of the righteous side (*dhammapakkha*), the analysis is explained as follows: Here indeed, in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain men who are as follows—they are non-violent (*anārambha*) and without possessions (*aparigraha*); they are righteous, followers of the Dharma, established in the Dharma, and even maintain their livelihood solely through the Dharma; they are well-disciplined, well-vowed, well-established in faith, and true ascetics. They abstain from all taking of life for as long as life lasts, and so on, up to: whatever other such sinful, unrighteous actions that cause affliction to other living beings are performed, from those they abstain for as long as life lasts.

Just as, for example, the venerable *anagāras* (homeless ascetics) are restrained in their movement (*iriyā-samiya*), restrained in speech (*bhāsā-samiya*), restrained in seeking alms (*esaṇā-samiya*), restrained in the taking up, handling, and setting down of requisites and utensils (*āyāṇa-bhaṇḍa-matta-nikkhēvaṇā-samiya*), restrained in the disposal of excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, and sweat (*uccāra-pāsavaṇa-khēla-siṅghāṇa-jalla-pāriṭṭhāvaṇiyā-samiya*); restrained in mind, restrained in speech, and restrained in body; guarding the mind, guarding the speech, and guarding the body; self-guarded, with senses guarded, practicing celibacy with guarded conduct; free from anger, pride, deceit, and greed; peaceful, tranquil, serene, extinguished (*parinivvuḍa*); free from the influxes (*anāsava*), unattached, with the stream of rebirth severed, free from defilement; like a bronze vessel that has shed its water, like a conch shell that is stainless, like a living soul whose movement is unimpeded, like the expanse of the sky that is without support, like the wind that is unobstructed, like autumnal water that is pure-hearted, like a lotus leaf that is undefiled, like a tortoise with guarded limbs, like a bird that is liberated, like the horn of a rhinoceros that is solitary, like a *bhāruṇḍa* bird that is vigilant, like an elephant that is majestic, like a bull that is full of vigor, like a lion that is invincible, like Mount Mandara that is unshakable, like the ocean that is deep, like the moon that has a gentle luster, like the sun that is radiant with splendor, like refined gold that is of noble form, and like the earth that endures all touch—blazing with the brilliance of a well-kindled fire...

For those Blessed Ones, there is no obstruction whatsoever. That obstruction is declared to be fourfold, namely: attachment to eggs, or attachment to boats, or attachment to acquisitions, or attachment to possessions. Yet, in whichever direction they desire, they travel unhindered, serene, light, and free from knots, dwelling while cultivating themselves through self-restraint and austerity.

The venerable ones had this kind of mode of life and conduct, namely: they took food on every fourth meal, every sixth meal, every eighth meal, every tenth meal, every twelfth meal, every fourteenth meal, every fortnight, every month, every two months, every three months, every four months, or every five months; furthermore, they were wanderers who had set out [on their rounds], wanderers who had withdrawn [from them], wanderers who had both set out and withdrawn, wanderers in remote areas, wanderers in secluded places, wanderers on coarse food, wanderers who gathered [food] themselves, wanderers who accepted invitations, wanderers who did not accept invitations, wanderers who accepted invitations from those of similar status, those who received what was seen, those who received what was not seen, those who received what was touched, those who received what was not touched, those who received alms-food, those who did not receive alms-food, wanderers who did not recognize [the donor], those who lived on what was placed [in their bowls], those who ate by counting [mouthfuls], those who limited their alms-food, those who practiced pure search for food, those who ate only the remnants, those who ate only the refuse, those who ate tasteless food, those who ate bitter food, those who ate coarse food, those who ate empty food, those who lived on remnants, those who lived on refuse, those who subsisted on *āyambila* (sour gruel), those who ate only the first half [of the bowl], those who abstained from fermented foods, those who abstained from meat, those who did not enjoy savory flavors, those who stood [while meditating], those who stood in specific postures, those who sat in the *ukkuḍuka* posture, those who sat cross-legged, those who sat in the *vīrāsana* posture, those who stood with arms raised like a staff, those who remained naked, those who did not rub [their bodies], those who did not scratch [themselves], those who did not spit, those who shook out their hair, beard, and body hair, and they remained entirely free from grooming the whole body.

Wandering by means of this mode of life, they complete the course of the ascetic life for many years. Having completed it, when many afflictions have arisen or are about to arise, they renounce many meals; having renounced them, they terminate many meals through fasting. For the sake of that purpose for which nakedness, shaving the head, not bathing, not cleaning the teeth, not using an umbrella, not using shoes, sleeping on the ground, sleeping on a plank bed, sleeping on a wooden bed, plucking out the hair, living a life of celibacy, entering the houses of others, and receiving what is obtained or not obtained—namely, honor and dishonor, insults, censures, reproaches, condemnations, threats, beatings, and various hardships and village persecutions, as well as the twenty-two types of trials and obstacles (parīsaha-uvassagga) are endured—they fulfill that purpose. Having fulfilled that purpose, with their final inhalations and exhalations, they produce infinite, unsurpassed, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and perfect supreme knowledge and vision (kevala-vara-ñāṇa-dasaṇa). Having produced it, they thereafter attain perfection, awaken, are liberated, reach final nirvana, and make an end to all suffering.

Furthermore, some venerable ones become [liberated], while others, by virtue of the remainder of their past karma, at the time of death, pass away and are reborn in certain celestial realms as gods—namely, in those who possess great power, great splendor, great prowess, great fame, great strength, great majesty, and great happiness. There they exist as gods of great power, great splendor, and so on, up to great happiness; their chests adorned with necklaces, their arms resplendent with bracelets and armlets, wearing earrings that grace their cheeks and ears, possessing various hand-ornaments, various garlands, and crests upon their heads, clothed in auspicious and excellent garments, bearing auspicious and excellent perfumes and ointments, with radiant bodies and long hanging flower-garlands. With divine form, divine color, divine fragrance, divine touch, divine stature, divine configuration, divine prosperity, divine excellence, divine radiance, divine luster, divine effulgence, and divine brilliance, illuminating and shining forth in the ten directions, they are auspicious in their gait, auspicious in their station, and destined for future welfare. This state is noble, leading to the destruction of all suffering, entirely right, and wholesome. Thus has the analysis of the second section concerning the side of Dharma been declared.

Furthermore, regarding the analysis of this third mixed category, it is declared as follows: Here indeed, in the east, west, north, or south, there are certain men who are thus: having few desires, few undertakings, and few possessions; righteous, followers of the Dharma, maintaining their livelihood by the Dharma alone; living with good conduct, good vows, well-established in faith, and being true ascetics; they abstain from some forms of taking life for as long as life lasts, yet do not abstain from others; and as for other such blameworthy, unrighteous occupations that cause injury to the lives of others, they abstain from some of those for as long as life lasts, but do not abstain from others...

For example, there are lay followers (*śramaṇopāsaka*) who have understood the nature of the soul (*jīva*) and the non-soul (*ajīva*); who have discerned merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*), as well as the influx of karma (*āsrava*), its stoppage (*saṃvara*), its experience (*vedanā*), and its shedding (*nirjarā*); who are skilled in action (*kriyā*), transgression (*adhikaraṇa*), bondage (*bandha*), and liberation (*mokṣa*); and who are incapable of being led away from the Nirgrantha doctrine by hosts of gods such as the Asuras, Nāgas, Suvarṇas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Kinnaras, Kiṃpurusas, Garuḍas, Gandharvas, and Mahoragas. They are unshakable in this very Nirgrantha doctrine; they are free from doubt, free from hesitation, and free from uncertainty; they have attained the goal, grasped the goal, questioned about the goal, determined the goal, and fully understood the goal. With their very marrow, they are devoted with love and affection for this Nirgrantha doctrine, thinking: "O venerable one! This Nirgrantha doctrine is the truth, this is the supreme truth; all else is falsehood. With their ramparts raised and their doors closed, they do not enter the inner apartments of others or the houses of strangers. On the fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, and the full moon days, they properly observe the complete *poṣadha*. They provide for the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas wholesome and suitable food, drink, snacks, and delicacies; clothing, bowls, blankets, and brooms; and medicines and remedies; as well as seats, beds, couches, and bedding. They dwell adorning themselves with many vows, restraints, virtues, abstentions, *poṣadha*, and fasts, according to their means, through ascetic practices.

Living in such a manner, they fulfill the status of lay disciples for many years. Having fulfilled it, when affliction has arisen or has not yet arisen, they renounce many meals; having renounced them, they terminate many meals through fasting. Having terminated them, and having confessed and repented, they attain meditative absorption and, at the time of death, passing away at the proper time, they are reborn as gods in various celestial realms, as follows:

Among those of great power, great splendor, and even great happiness—the rest is exactly as before—up to: "In this state, one is an *ārya*... up to: 'an absolutely right (*egantasamma*) ascetic (*sāhu*). Thus has the analysis of the third state, the mixed state, been declared. With reference to non-restraint (*avirati*), one is designated as a fool (*bāla*); with reference to restraint (*virati*), one is designated as a wise man (*paṇḍita*); with reference to both restraint and non-restraint (*virayāvirati*), one is designated as a fool-wise man (*bālapaṇḍita*). In that regard, whatever constitutes total non-restraint—that state is a state of undertaking (*ārambha*), it is un-noble (*anārya*), up to: "not the path for the destruction of all suffering; it is absolutely wrong (*egantamiccha*) and not an ascetic. In that regard, whatever constitutes restraint—that state is a state of non-undertaking (*anārambha*), it is noble (*ārya*), up to: "the path for the destruction of all suffering; it is absolutely right (*egantassama*) and an ascetic. In that regard, whatever constitutes both restraint and non-restraint—that state is a state of both undertaking and non-undertaking; in this state, one is noble, up to: "the path for the destruction of all suffering; it is absolutely right and an ascetic."

In this very way, when followed out, they converge upon these two positions: namely, the righteous (*dharma*) and the unrighteous (*adharma*), or the tranquil (*upaśānta*) and the non-tranquil (*anuśānta*). Now, regarding the first position, that side of the unrighteous, which has been thus explained, there are therein three hundred and sixty-three types of sinful doctrines, so it is declared. Namely: those who maintain the doctrine of action (*kriyāvādins*), those who maintain the doctrine of non-action (*akriyāvādins*), those who maintain the doctrine of ignorance (*ajñānikavādins*), and those who maintain the doctrine of chance (*vainayikavādins*). They too have proclaimed *nirvāṇa*; they too have proclaimed liberation; they too say, "O lay disciples! and they too say, "O practitioners of the vows! (*śrāvakas* and *śrāvikās*).

All those Pāvadukas, founders of various doctrines, possessing diverse understandings, diverse inclinations, diverse conducts, diverse views, diverse tastes, diverse undertakings, and endowed with diverse resolutions, having formed a great circle, all stood together. Then a man, taking a bowl completely filled with glowing coals with an iron pair of tongs, addressed all those Pāvadukas, founders of various doctrines, possessing diverse understandings and diverse resolutions: "Oho, Pāvadukas, founders of various doctrines, possessing diverse understandings up to diverse resolutions! First, take this bowl completely filled with glowing coals and hold it in your hand for a moment—do not frequently use the tongs, do not frequently stoke the fire, do not frequently perform services for your own fellow-religionists, and do not frequently perform services for those of other religions; being upright, committed to the path of liberation, and acting without deceit, stretch forth your hand. Having said this, that man, taking that bowl completely filled with glowing coals with an iron pair of tongs, placed it in their hands.

Then those founders of doctrines, possessing various understandings and endowed with various intentions and resolutions, withdrew their hands. Then that man said this to all those founders of doctrines, possessing various understandings and endowed with various intentions and resolutions: "O founders of doctrines, possessing various understandings and endowed with various intentions and resolutions! Why do you withdraw your hands? Let the hand not be burned; what will happen when it is burned? You withdraw [your hands] thinking, 'It is suffering, it is suffering'? This is the standard, this is the measure, this is the assembly; for each there is a standard, for each a measure, for each an assembly. In this regard, those ascetics and brahmins who thus declare, and so forth, thus propound—"

"All living beings, down to all creatures, should be killed, deprived of life, plundered, tormented, exhausted, and destroyed. They will come to cutting; they will come to piercing; they will come to birth, old age, death, the womb, birth, saṃsāra, rebirth, dwelling in the womb, the cycle of existence, and states of wretchedness. They will partake of many punishments, many shavings [of the head], many reproaches, many beatings, many imprisonments, many whirling [tortures], many deaths of mothers, many deaths of fathers, many deaths of brothers, many deaths of sisters, many deaths of wives, sons, daughters, and daughters-in-law, many miseries, many misfortunes, many associations with the unpleasant, many separations from the beloved, and many sufferings and dejections. They will wander again and again through this beginningless, endless, long-lasting, fourfold wilderness of saṃsāra. They will not attain perfection, they will not awaken, and so on, until they do not make an end to all suffering. This is the balance, this is the measure, this is the convergence; for each individual it is a balance, for each individual it is a measure, for each individual it is a convergence."

In this regard, those ascetics and brahmins who thus proclaim and teach: "All breaths, all beings, all souls, and all living creatures are not to be killed, not to be subjected to violence, not to be imprisoned, not to be tormented, not to be exhausted, and not to be destroyed"—they will not face cutting [of limbs] for the sake of some [transgression], nor will they face dismemberment; they will not be partakers of birth, old age, death, the womb, birth, saṃsāra, rebirth, dwelling in the womb, the cycle of existence, or the state of misery. They will not be partakers of many punishments, nor of many shavings [of the head], up to many sufferings and dejections. They will not wander again and again through the long, beginningless, endless, fourfold wilderness of saṃsāra. They will attain perfection (siddhi), up to making an end to all suffering.

Living beings engaged in these twelve bases of action (*kiriyāṭhāṇa*) have not attained perfection, nor awakened, nor been liberated, nor reached final nirvana; they have not made an end to all suffering, nor do they do so, nor will they do so. However, living beings engaged in this thirteenth basis of action have attained perfection, awakened, been liberated, reached final nirvana; they have made an end to all suffering, they do so now, and they will do so in the future. Thus, that monk—intent on his own welfare, devoted to his own welfare, guarded in his own welfare, possessed of his own welfare, striving for his own welfare, protecting his own welfare, compassionate toward his own welfare, and seeking the fulfillment of his own welfare—should withdraw from [the first twelve] and apply himself solely to his own welfare.

Thus I say. [The Knowledge of Food] It has been heard by me, O venerable one! That it was thus declared by the Blessed One: "In this world, indeed, there is a chapter named 'The Knowledge of Food' (*āhārapariṇṇā*); this is its meaning. Here, indeed, in whatever direction—east, west, north, or south—in every way and throughout the entire world, four types of vegetable bodies (*bījakāya*) are thus described, namely:"

There are plants propagated from seeds, from roots, from joints, and from stems; and according to their respective seeds and according to their respective locations, certain beings there—born from the earth, originating from the earth, and emerging from the earth; born from that source, originating from that, and emerging from that; drawn by karma and conditioned by karma—emerging there, transform into the state of trees within various kinds of earth-born wombs.

Those living beings consume the moisture of those various kinds of earth; those living beings consume the bodies of earth, the bodies of water, the bodies of fire, the bodies of air, and the bodies of plants. They render the bodies of various kinds of mobile and immobile creatures insentient and discarded. That body—having been previously consumed, having been consumed at that time, transformed, and integrated into their own form—[is thus assimilated].

Furthermore, it is declared that the bodies of those earth-born trees are of various colors, various odors, various tastes, various textures, and are established in various shapes; they are produced from various kinds of corporeal matter (poggala) and are beings reborn through the power of karma.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings have trees as their womb, are born from trees, and emerge from trees; having that as their womb, being born from that, and emerging from that, they enter [the state] through karma and are subject to karma. By the causal condition of karma, they emerge there and transform into the state of trees within trees whose womb is earth. Those living beings consume the moisture of those trees whose womb is earth.

Those beings consume the bodies of earth, the bodies of water, the bodies of fire, the bodies of air, and the bodies of plants that have been discarded; that body, having been previously consumed, consumed at that time, transformed, and integrated into their own form, exists as such.

Furthermore, there are other bodies belonging to those trees born from the womb of trees—possessing various colors, various smells, various tastes, various textures, and established in various shapes—which are produced from the matter of various kinds of bodies; it is declared that those beings are reborn through the power of karma.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings are born from trees, originate from trees, and emerge from trees; having that [tree] as their womb, originating from it, and emerging from it, they enter through the power of karma and, by the causal condition of karma, emerge there to be reborn as trees within those tree-wombs. Those living beings consume the sap of those trees which have tree-wombs as their source.

Those living beings consume the bodies of earth, the bodies of water, the bodies of fire, the bodies of air, and the bodies of plants; they render the bodies of mobile and immobile creatures inanimate and discard them. That body—previously consumed, then consumed at that time, transformed, and integrated into their own organic form—[is thus assimilated].

Furthermore, it is declared that the bodies of those trees born from the womb of trees are of various colors, various smells, various tastes, various textures, and established in various shapes; they are produced by the transformation of various kinds of bodily matter, and those living beings have descended there due to their karma.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings are born from trees, originate from trees, and emerge from trees; having that [tree] as their source, originating from it, and emerging from it, they enter through the influence of karma and, by the causal condition of karma, emerge there among those tree-born trees. They develop as roots, as bulbous roots, as trunks, as bark, as sapwood, as shoots, as leaves, as flowers, as fruits, and as seeds. Those living beings consume the moisture of those trees which are born from trees.

Those living beings consume that body of earth, body of water, body of fire, body of air, and body of plants, as well as the bodies of various kinds of mobile and immobile creatures; they render those bodies insentient, having discarded them until they have become assimilated with their own organic matter.

Furthermore, it is declared that the bodies of those plants—whether roots, bulbs, trunks, bark, branches, shoots, or even seeds—are of various colors, various odors, and so forth, being produced from various kinds of bodily matter; those living beings have descended there due to their karma.

Furthermore, it has been declared: here, certain beings have trees as their womb, are born from trees, and proceed from trees; having that as their womb, being born from that, and proceeding from that, they are reborn there by reason of their karma, with karma as the cause, and having proceeded there, they transform themselves into climbing plants upon trees that have trees as their womb. Those living beings consume the sap of those trees that have trees as their womb.

Those living beings consume that body of the earth, which has been transformed into their own form; furthermore, the bodies of those creepers belonging to the womb of trees are said to be of various colors and so forth.

Moreover, it has been declared: here, certain beings whose womb is the creeper, who originate from the creeper, and who—due to the causal condition of karma—migrate there and are reborn as creepers within the womb of trees; those beings consume the sap of those creepers belonging to the womb of trees.

Those living beings consume the body of the earth until it has become assimilated with their own form; furthermore, the bodies of those plants born from the womb of plants are said to be of various colors and so forth. Again, another thing has been declared: here, certain beings whose womb is the plant, who originate from the plant, and who—due to the causal condition of karma—having transmigrated there, are reborn as plants within those plants that have plants as their womb; those beings consume the moisture of those plants that have plants as their womb.

Those living beings consume the bodies of earth and the bodies of water, up until they have assimilated them as their own form. Furthermore, the bodies of those creepers that originate from the womb of creepers are of various colors, and so forth, as it has been declared.

Moreover, this has been further explained: here, certain beings whose womb is the creeper and who originate from the creeper—driven by the causal necessity of karma—descend there and transform into roots, and so forth, up to seeds, within those creepers whose womb is the creeper.

Those living beings, having the climbing plants as their place of birth, consume the sap of those climbing plants; furthermore, the bodies of those born from climbing plants—ranging from roots to seeds—are described as being of various colors and so forth.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings born from the womb of earth, originating from earth, and proceeding from earth—even those of various kinds of wombs—transform into the state of grass within various types of earth. Those living beings consume the moisture of those various types of earth-wombs; thus it is declared that those beings are reborn through their own karma.
In this way, they transform into the state of grass among plants born from the womb of earth; thus it is declared.
Thus, they transform into grass within grass-born wombs and consume a grass body born of grass; thus it has been declared.
Likewise, there are four discourses concerning herbs (*ōsahī*).
Likewise, there are four discourses concerning plants (*hariyā*).

Furthermore, another [point] has been declared: here, certain beings born from the womb of the earth, originating from the earth, and driven by the cause of their karma, enter into various kinds of wombs within the earth—becoming *āyatta*, *vāyatta*, *kāyatta*, *kuhaṇa*, *kundaka*, *uvvēhaniyatta*, *nivvēhaniyatta*, *sachatta*, *chattagatta*, *vāsāniyatta*, and *kūra*—and they transform there;
those living beings consume the moisture of those various kinds of earthly wombs as their food.

Those beings consume the body of the earth while it still exists; moreover, the bodies of those born from the womb of the earth—whether they be dependent or even cruel—are of various colors, as has been declared. There is but one formula for trees born from the womb of the earth, consisting of four sections; the same applies to climbing plants (*ajjhāruha*). For grasses, medicinal herbs, and greenery, four formulas each are to be recited.

Furthermore, it is declared: here, certain beings born from a watery womb, originating in water, through the causal condition of karma, having transmigrated there, are manifested in various kinds of aquatic births as water, as algae, as moss, as *kalambuga*, as *haḍa*, as *kasēruka*, as *kacchabhāṇiya*, as blue lotus (*utpala*), as red lotus (*paduma*), as white lotus (*kumuda*), as *nalina*, as *subhaga*, as *sōgandhika*, as white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), as great white lotus (*mahāpuṇḍarīka*), as hundred-petaled, as thousand-petaled, likewise as *kalhāra*, as *koṅkaṇaya*, as *aravinda*, as *nāmarasa*, as *bhisā*, *bhisamuṇāla*, and *pukkhalacchima*. Thus they are manifested.

Those living beings consume the moisture of those various kinds of water-born organisms; those beings consume the body of earth as long as it exists. Furthermore, the bodies of those water-born organisms—ranging from those born of water up to the *pukkhalacchibhaga* species—are of various colors, as has been declared; this is the only discourse [to be applied], while the remaining three do not exist.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings born from water, originating in water, and so on up to "due to the cause of karma," having passed away there, are reborn as trees within waters of various kinds of origins. Those living beings consume the moisture of those waters of various origins. Those beings consume the body of the earth, and so on until it is exhausted. Moreover, the bodies of those trees born from water are of various colors, and so on, as has been declared.

Furthermore, another [teaching] has been proclaimed: here, certain beings [are born] from those very earth-born trees, from tree-born trees, from tree-born roots, up to tree-born seeds; from tree-born creepers, from creeper-born creepers, from creeper-born roots, up to creeper-born seeds; from earth-born grasses, from grass-born roots, up to grass-born seeds; from earth-born grasses, from grass-born roots, up to grass-born seeds. In the same way, there are three discourses regarding herbs (*osadhī*). Likewise, there are three discourses regarding shrubs (*hariya*).

By means of earth-born bodies, even those that are cruel, up to water-born trees, tree-born trees, and tree-born roots up to seeds—and likewise for epiphytes—there are three discourses each; for annual plants there are three, and for grasses there are three; and by means of water-born waters, pools, up to lotus-beds, they transform into the state of mobile beings.

Those living beings consume the moisture of those earth-born, water-born, tree-born, vine-born, grass-born, herb-born, and green-plant-born entities—of the trees, vines, grasses, herbs, and greens; of their roots up to their seeds; of their trunks up to their branches; and of the waters, including the *avagas* and up to the *pukkhalacchibhagas*.

Those living beings consume the bodies of the earth while they still exist; furthermore, there are the bodies of mobile creatures born from trees, born from creepers, born from grass, born from medicinal herbs, born from greenery, born from roots, born from bulbs, [and so on] up to those born from seeds; born from water, born from moisture, [and so on] up to those born from the *pukkhalacchibhaga* plant—these have various colors, as it has been declared.

Furthermore, another [point] has been declared regarding the various abodes of humans—namely, those of the lands of action (*kammabhūmi*), the lands of non-action (*akammabhūmi*), and the intermediate islands; those who are noble (*ārya*) and those who are barbarian (*milakkhu*). For them, according to their respective seeds and according to their respective conditions, there arises here a union called "sexual intercourse" within the womb of a woman or a man that has been prepared by karma. Therein, both of them accumulate moisture (*sineha*); and therein, living beings transform into the state of femininity, masculinity, or neuter-ness.

Those beings first take as food the mother’s blood, the father’s semen, and the mixture of both—impure and defiled. After that, they consume by degrees the various kinds of flavorful foods that their mother eats; thus, partaking of her nourishment, they gradually grow and reach maturity. Then, emerging from that body, they are born as females, or are born as males, or are born as neuter.

Those living beings, being young, consume mother’s milk and clarified butter; as they gradually grow up, they consume rice, groats, and both mobile and immobile creatures. Those living beings consume the body of the earth, up to that which is derived from its essence. Furthermore, it is declared that the bodies of those various kinds of human beings—whether belonging to the lands of action (*karmabhūmi*), the lands of non-action (*akarmabhūmi*), or the intermediate islands; whether noble (*ārya*) or barbarian (*milakkhu*)—become of various colors and so forth.

Furthermore, another [category] has been declared: the various kinds of five-sensed aquatic animals belonging to the animal realm, namely, from fish up to crocodiles. According to their respective seeds and according to their respective habitats, through the karma performed by a female and a male, [the embryo develops] just as previously described, until they take nourishment in part. Growing gradually and reaching maturity, when emerging from that body, some produce an egg, others produce a live birth. When that egg is hatched, it produces a female, a male, or a neuter. Those beings, while still young, take in warm moisture as food; growing gradually, they consume the vegetable kingdom and mobile and immobile living beings. Those beings consume the bodies of the earth element, as long as they exist. Moreover, the bodies of those various kinds of five-sensed aquatic animals belonging to the animal realm—from fish up to crocodiles—are of various colors, as has been declared.

Furthermore, another [category] has been declared: the various kinds of four-footed terrestrial five-sensed beings of the animal realm, namely—those with solid hooves, those with cloven hooves, those with webbed feet, and those with claws. Through their respective seeds and through their respective environments, a union arises between a female and a male for the purpose of sexual intercourse. Both of them accumulate *sneha* (moisture/affection). Therein, living beings transform into the state of female, male, or neuter. Those beings take the mother’s blood and the father’s semen; thus, as in the case of humans, they sometimes give birth to a female, sometimes to a male, and sometimes to a neuter. When those beings are young, they consume the mother’s milk and clarified butter (*sappi*). Gradually growing up, they consume the vegetable kingdom and mobile and immobile living beings. Those beings consume the body of the earth, and so on, until it exists. Furthermore, the bodies of those various kinds of four-footed terrestrial five-sensed beings of the animal realm—with solid hooves, cloven hooves, webbed feet, and claws—are declared to be of various colors and so forth.

Furthermore, another [category] has been declared: the various kinds of five-sensed terrestrial reptiles that move by crawling on their bellies (*uraparisappa*), such as snakes, pythons, *āsāliya* lizards, and great serpents (*mahōraga*). According to their respective seeds and according to their respective environments, for a female or a male—[as previously described] up to the matter of sexual union—it is exactly the same; however, there is this difference: sometimes they produce an egg (*aṇḍa*), and sometimes they produce a live birth (*pōya*). When that egg is hatched, it sometimes produces a female, sometimes a male, and sometimes a neuter (*napuṁsaga*). Those beings, while still young, consume air as food; as they gradually grow, they consume the vegetable body and mobile and immobile living beings. Those beings consume the bodies of the earth, and so on, until they exist. Furthermore, the bodies of those various kinds of five-sensed terrestrial reptiles that move by crawling on their bellies—from snakes up to great serpents—are declared to be of various colors and various odors, and so forth.

Furthermore, another [category] has been declared: the various kinds of five-sensed terrestrial reptiles (*bhujaparisarpa*) among the animal births (*tirikkhajōṇiya*). Namely: lizards (*gōha*), mongooses (*naula*), lions (*sīha*), *saraḍa* snakes, *salla* snakes, *sarava* snakes, *khara* snakes, domestic pigeons (*gharakōiliya*), *vissambhara* snakes, rats (*mūsaga*), *maṅgusa* fish, *payalāiya* snakes, *birāliya* snakes, and four-footed beasts (*cāuppāiya*). Regarding these, according to their respective seeds and according to their respective space, the birth of females and males should be described just as for the belly-crawling snakes (*uraparisappa*), up until the point where they have attained their own form (*sārūvikaḍa*). Moreover, other [details] regarding those various kinds of five-sensed terrestrial reptiles among the animal births—namely, from the lizards up to what has been declared—should also be understood.

Furthermore, another [category] has been declared: the five-sensed aerial beings of various kinds belonging to the animal realm, namely—the leather-winged, the feather-winged, the shell-winged, and the spread-winged. Regarding them, according to their respective seeds and according to their respective spaces, the female [reproduction] is as described for the belly-crawlers. The distinction is this: those beings, while still young, take nourishment from the moisture of the mother's body; gradually grown up, they consume the vegetable kingdom and mobile and immobile living beings. Those beings consume the bodies of the earth, and so on, until they exist. Moreover, this has been declared regarding those other various kinds of five-sensed aerial beings of the animal realm, starting with the leather-winged, and so forth.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings belonging to various kinds of wombs, having various modes of birth, and undergoing various types of transmigration—born from those same wombs, originating from those same sources, and subject to those same transitions—driven by karma and rooted in karma, transmigrate there into the bodies of various mobile and immobile organisms, whether they be conscious or unconscious, for the purpose of becoming food.

Those living beings consume the moisture of those various kinds of mobile and immobile creatures; those beings consume the body of the earth while it still exists. Furthermore, the bodies of those born from the wombs of mobile and immobile creatures, which are not parasitic, are of various colors, and so forth, as it has been declared. Thus, by way of their origin from foul substances; thus, by way of having two hooves.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings of various kinds of birth, up to being conditioned by karma, having transmigrated there, [reside] within the bodies of various mobile and immobile living beings, whether conscious or unconscious. That body—whether self-produced, held together, or encompassed by wind—becomes an upward-mover in upward winds, a downward-mover in downward winds, and a lateral-mover in lateral winds. Namely:

In dew, frost, hoarfrost, greenery, and pure water, those living beings consume the moisture of various kinds of mobile and immobile creatures. Those living beings consume the bodies of the earth as long as they exist; furthermore, the bodies of those dew-dwellers and others belonging to the wombs of mobile and immobile creatures—ranging from those in dew to those in pure water—are declared to be of various colors and so forth.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings born from water, originating in water, [and so on] up to "due to the cause of karma," having transmigrated there into waters of mobile and immobile origin, are transformed into the state of water. Those living beings consume the moisture of those waters of mobile and immobile origin. Those beings consume the body of earth, and so on, as far as existing. Moreover, the bodies of those beings born from water are of various colors, and so on, as has been declared.

Furthermore, this has been declared: here, certain beings born from water, up to [driven] by the cause of their karma, having transmigrated there, are transformed into mobile creatures within those waters that are of a watery origin. Those living beings consume the moisture of those waters that are of a watery origin. Those beings consume the body of earth, and so on, until it is present. Moreover, the bodies of those other mobile creatures born from water are of various colors, and so forth, as it has been declared.

Furthermore, it has been declared: here, certain beings of various origins, driven by the causal necessity of their karma, transmigrate there into the bodies—whether conscious or unconscious—of various kinds of mobile and immobile living beings, and they transform into the nature of fire. Those beings consume the moisture of those various mobile and immobile living beings; those beings consume the bodies of earth, and so on, as far as [the bodies of] water. Moreover, the bodies of those mobile creatures born from water are said to be of various colors, and so forth.

Furthermore, it has been declared: here, certain beings of various origins, up to being conditioned by their karma, having transmigrated there, transform into the nature of fire within the bodies—whether conscious or unconscious—of various mobile and immobile living beings. Those beings consume the moisture of those various mobile and immobile living beings; those beings consume the body of earth, as far as it exists. Moreover, the bodies of those fires born from mobile and immobile sources are said to be of various colors, and so forth. The remaining three discourses are as those concerning water.

Furthermore, another [teaching] has been proclaimed: here, certain beings, due to various wombs and up to the cause of their karma, having passed away from there, transform into the state of the air-body within the bodies—whether conscious or unconscious—of various kinds of mobile and immobile living beings. As it is for fire, so should the four permutations (gamā) be recited.
