Furthermore, it has been declared: here, certain beings belonging to various classes of birth, driven by the causal necessity of their karma, transmigrate there into the bodies of various kinds of mobile and immobile living beings, whether those bodies be conscious or unconscious—namely, as earth, gravel, sand, stones, rocks, salt, alkaline soil, iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, gold, and diamond. These verses are to be understood: Earth, gravel, sand, stone, rock, salt, alkaline soil, iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, gold, and diamond. (Sūyagaḍa 694)

In Hariyāla and Hiṅguluma there are Manosilā, Sāsagañjana, and Pavāla; in Abbhapaḍala and Abbhavāluya, there are various kinds of jewels in their gross form. [Sūy. 695] There are also Gōmējja, Ruya, Aṅka, Phaliha, and Lōhiyakkha.
Emerald, masāragalla, bhuyamōyaga, and idanīla;
// Sūy.696 // Sandalwood, geruka, haṃsagarbha, pula, and saugandhika should be known;
as well as candraprabha, vaiḍūrya, jalakānta, and sūryakānta. // Sūy.697 //
These verses should be recited regarding these [beings] up until they transform into sun-crystals (*sūrakanta*).

Those living beings consume the moisture of those various kinds of mobile and immobile creatures; those beings consume the body of the earth as long as it exists. Furthermore, the bodies of those earth-beings born from the wombs of mobile and immobile creatures—up to the sun-crystals—are of various colors, as has been declared. The remaining three sections are as in the case of water.

Furthermore, this has been declared: all living beings, all creatures, all souls, and all sentient beings—born of various wombs, originating in various ways, migrating through various states, having bodies as their womb, originating from bodies, migrating through bodies, nourished by bodies, under the influence of karma, dependent on karma, following the course of karma, abiding in karma—it is through karma alone that they undergo transformation. Know this; having known this, one should be restrained in food, self-controlled, steadfast, and always disciplined. Thus I say. [The Action of Renunciation]

I have heard, O venerable one, that it was thus declared by the Blessed One: "In this very chapter on the practice of renunciation (*paccakkhāṇakiriyā*), this is its meaning: the self (*āyā*) may be one who does not renounce; the self may also be one unskilled in action (*akiriyākusala*); the self may also be one established in falsehood (*micchāsaṇṭhiya*); the self may also be one who is exclusively harmful (*ēganta-daṇḍa*); the self may also be one who is exclusively foolish (*ēganta-bāla*); the self may also be one who is exclusively asleep (*ēganta-sutta*); the self may also be one whose mental, vocal, and physical activities are undiscerning; and the self may also be one whose sinful karma has neither been checked nor renounced."

Indeed, this has been declared by the Blessed One: one who is unrenounced, unrestrained, who has not desisted from nor confessed evil karma, who acts with purpose, who is impure, who is exclusively harmful, exclusively foolish, and exclusively asleep—that fool, whose speech and actions of mind, speech, and body are devoid of discernment, does not see even in a dream; yet evil karma is produced by him.

Thereupon, the questioner spoke thus to the proponent: "If one does not kill with an evil, non-existent mind, nor with evil speech, nor with an evil, non-existent body, being without thought, without mental activity, without vocal or bodily expression, and not seeing even in a dream—does evil karma not get produced? For what reason is that so?"

The Cārvāka speaks thus: "By means of some sinful mind, a sinful karma is produced that follows from the mind; by means of some sinful speech, a sinful karma is produced that follows from speech; by means of some sinful body, a sinful karma is produced that follows from the body. Even for one who is killing, who is intent on slaughter, whose mind, speech, and body are active with movement—even in a dream—sinful karma is produced for one of such a nature."

Furthermore, he speaks thus: "In that regard, those who say: 'By an evil mind that is non-existent, by evil speech that is non-existent, and by an evil body that is non-existent—though one does not kill, does not cause others to kill, and has no mental, vocal, or physical activity—yet even while not seeing even in a dream, evil karma is produced'—those who speak thus speak falsely."

Thereupon, the wise questioner spoke thus: "Is it correct that which I previously stated—that even for one who does not kill, who is without malice, whose mind, speech, and body are free from deliberation, and who does not see even in a dream, evil karma is produced by means of an unwholesome, evil mind, an unwholesome, evil speech, and an unwholesome, evil body? Is that correct? For what reason?"

The Teacher said: "In this regard, the Blessed One has declared six classes of living beings as the causes [of violence], namely: the earth-bodied, up to the mobile-bodied. Through these six classes of living beings, one whose sinful karma is neither restrained nor renounced possesses a mind that is constantly harsh and violent toward the rod [of punishment]. That is to say, regarding killing of living beings, up to possession; and from anger, up to the thorn of false view."

The Teacher said: "In this regard, the Blessed One has indeed set forth the example of a hunter. Suppose there were a hunter belonging to a householder, or a householder’s son, or a king, or a king’s officer, who thinks: 'I will enter at a moment when he is asleep; having found a moment, I will kill him. While he is thus plotting—thinking, 'I will enter at a moment when he is asleep; having found a moment, I will kill him'—would that hunter, day or night, whether sleeping or waking, be an enemy, one of wrong intent, and one whose mind is constantly intent on violent assault? When [the disciple] had explained it thus, [the Teacher] asked: "Is it so? [The disciple] replied: "Yes, it is so."

The Teacher said: Just as that thief, thinking to himself, "I will enter when this householder, or householder’s son, or king, or king’s official has momentarily fallen asleep; having found an opportunity, I will carry off [the goods],"—whether by day or night, whether sleeping or waking—is an enemy, wrongly disposed, and possesses a mind constantly harsh with the infliction of violence; even so, the fool is an enemy to all living beings, down to all creatures, whether by day or night, whether sleeping or waking, being wrongly disposed and possessing a mind constantly harsh with the infliction of violence, namely: in the matter of killing living beings, up to the thorn of wrong view.

Thus, indeed, has it been declared by the Blessed One: one who is unrestrained, lacking self-control, who does not abstain from evil, who has not renounced nor rejected sinful karma, who acts with purpose, who is impure, who is exclusively violent, exclusively foolish, and also exclusively asleep—he is a fool whose speech regarding mind, voice, and body is devoid of reflection; he does not perceive even in a dream, and thus sinful karma is produced by him.

Just as that hunter, or that householder, or even that king’s officer, having adopted a distinct intention toward each [being], whether by day or night, while asleep or awake, becomes an enemy, wrongly disposed, and possesses a mind of constant, violent, and harmful intent; even so, the fool, having adopted a distinct intention toward every living being, down to every single creature, whether by day or night, while asleep or awake, becomes an enemy, wrongly disposed, and possesses a mind of constant, violent, and harmful intent.

This is not possible: for indeed, here there are many living beings—whether seen, heard, conceived, or known—who, within this aggregate of a body, have not been individually approached by one who, whether by day or night, asleep or awake, harbors a hostile and wrongly directed mind, constantly possessing a cruel intent to harm through the rod of the mind; namely, [the transgressions] from killing living beings up to the thorn of wrong view.

The Teacher said: "In this regard, two types of analogies have been taught by the Blessed One, namely: the analogy of the conscious being (*sannidṛṣṭānta*) and the analogy of the unconscious being (*asannidṛṣṭānta*). What is the analogy of the conscious being? It refers to those five-sensed beings with fully developed faculties (*paryāptaka*) who, with respect to the six classes of living beings—namely, from the earth-body up to the mobile-body—perform an action themselves or cause it to be performed by another, and it occurs to them thus:"

"In this way, indeed, I perform and cause to be performed actions with the earth-body; yet it does not occur to him: 'By this or by that [specific means] he performs and causes to be performed actions with this earth-body. And he remains with respect to that earth-body unrestrained, undisciplined, and without having turned back from or renounced sinful karma. This should be stated for each body up to the mobile (trasa) body."

If one person performs or causes to be performed an action involving the six classes of living beings, it occurs to him: "I indeed perform or cause to be performed this action involving the six classes of living beings. Yet, it does not occur to him: "By these or by those [specific ones]. He performs or causes to be performed that action by means of those six classes of living beings; and by means of those six classes of living beings, he remains un-restrained, un-disciplined, and without having renounced or turned away from evil karma—namely, from the destruction of life up to the thorn of false view.

Indeed, this has been declared by the Blessed One: one who is uncontrolled, lacking restraint, and who has neither halted nor renounced evil karma, does not see even in a dream; yet evil karma is still being produced for him. This is the illustration regarding the conscious [soul].

What, then, is the illustration of those lacking consciousness (*asaññi*)? It refers to these non-conscious beings (*asaññi-pāṇā*), namely: the earth-bodied beings up to the plant-bodied beings, and sixthly, the mobile beings (*tasa-pāṇā*). For them there is no thought, nor perception, nor intelligence, nor mind, nor speech, whether for performing an action themselves, for causing others to perform it, or for consenting to another’s performance. Yet even they, being foolish, are enemies to all living beings, down to all sentient beings (*sattā*), by day or night, while asleep or awake; they are established in falsehood, possessing minds of constant, violent injury, such as in the case of violence against living beings up to the thorn of false view. Thus, although they possess neither mind nor speech, they do not refrain from causing suffering, grief, exhaustion, distress, beating, and torment to living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings; they remain unceasing in their infliction of suffering, grief, and so forth, up to torment, killing, binding, and affliction.

Thus indeed, even those beings who are unconscious (*asaññin*) are exhorted day and night toward the destruction of living beings, up to being exhorted day and night toward possessiveness, and up to being exhorted toward the thorn of false view (*micchā-damsaṇa-salla*). Furthermore, all beings of every womb—having been conscious become unconscious, having been unconscious become conscious; having been conscious, they become either conscious or unconscious. Therein, they are not separated, not shaken off, not destroyed, and not transformed; they pass from the group of the unconscious to the group of the conscious, from the group of the conscious to the group of the unconscious, from the group of the conscious to the group of the conscious, or from the group of the unconscious to the group of the unconscious.

Whether they be sentient or non-sentient, all those who act with wrong conduct are constantly characterized by violent mental violence (*cittadaṇḍa*), namely: from killing living beings up to the thorn of false view (*micchādamsaṇasalla*). Thus has it been declared by the Blessed One: one who is unrenounced, unrestrained, who has not repudiated or renounced evil karma, who acts with purpose, who is unguarded, who is exclusively violent, exclusively foolish, and exclusively asleep—that fool, whose speech and actions of mind, speech, and body are devoid of discernment, does not perceive even in a dream; and yet, evil karma is produced for him.

Cōyaga asked: "What does one do, what does one cause to be done, and how does one become one who has ceased, restrained, destroyed, and renounced evil karma? The Ācārya replied: "In this regard, the Blessed One has taught six classes of living beings as causes [of harm], namely: the earth-bodied, and so on, up to the mobile-bodied.

Just as if I were being struck with a staff, or with a bone, or with a fist, or with a clod of earth, or with a shard of pottery, or being beaten, or even being tormented—just as I experience pain and fear, even to the extent of the plucking out of a single hair, which is caused by violence."

Know this: all living beings, down to every single creature, when beaten with a staff or even with a clod of earth—whether being struck, beaten, threatened, flogged, or even afflicted by calamities—experience pain and fear caused by violence, even to the extent of having a hair torn out.

Knowing this, all living beings, indeed all creatures, must not be killed and must not be harmed. This is the eternal, constant, and everlasting Dharma, proclaimed by the knowers of the field after having examined the world. Thus, that monk is abstinent from the taking of life up to the thorn of wrong belief. That monk does not clean his teeth with tooth-sticks, nor does he use collyrium, emetics, or incense.
That monk is inactive, untainted, free from anger, pride, deceit, and greed; he is tranquil and fully extinguished.
This indeed has been declared by the Blessed One: one who has restrained, desisted from, obstructed, and renounced evil karma is non-doing, fully guarded, and truly solitary wise.
Thus I say.
[The Discourse on Conduct]
Having undertaken the holy life, O wise ones, one should never practice such unrighteous conduct within this Dharma. (Sūy.
705) Having fully understood it as beginningless or, alternatively, as endless...
One should not hold the view that "it is eternal" or "it is non-eternal. (Sūy.
706) Through these two positions, worldly convention does not exist; through these two positions, one should recognize [the doctrine] as improper conduct. (Sūy. 707)
"Teachers will be completely cut off; all living beings will become either free from passion or possessed of knots, or there will be no eternal [state]. (Sūy.
708) Through these two positions, conventional practice is not found.
By these two points, one should recognize what is improper conduct. (Sūy.
709) Whichever living beings there may be, whether they be small or large, one should not say of them, "The enmity toward them is equal," nor "It is unequal. (Sūy. 710)
In these two cases, no legal proceeding is found; in these two cases, one should recognize improper conduct.
They consume food that has been prepared for them, each according to their own karma.
One should know whether [the body] is smeared or, on the other hand, not smeared. (Sūy.
712) Through these two positions, no legal transaction is possible; through these two positions, one should recognize improper conduct. (Sūy. 713)
Regarding this physical food and that which is produced by karma—
vital energy exists in both of these, yet vital energy does not exist everywhere.
Through these two positions, conventional practice (vyavahāra) is not found.
One should know that through these two positions one follows improper conduct:
"There is neither world nor non-world"—one should not entertain such a view; rather, "There is a world and there is a non-world"—in this way one should establish one's conviction. (Sūyagaḍa 715–716)

"There are no living beings (jīvas) or non-living beings (ajīvas)"—one should not establish such a notion; rather, one should establish the notion that "there are living beings and non-living beings. (Sūy. 717) "There is no Dharma or Adharma"—one should not establish such a notion.
One should not establish the notion that "there is dharma or non-dharma";
one should not establish the notion that "there is neither bondage nor liberation. One should establish the notion that "there is bondage or liberation. (Sūy. 718–719)
"There is neither merit nor evil"—one should not establish such a view; "there is merit and there is evil"—one should establish such a view. (Sūy.
720) "There is neither influx nor restraint"—one should not establish such a view.
One should not establish the notion that "there are influxes or their restraint.

One should not establish the notion that "there is neither feeling nor the wearing away [of karma]. One should establish the notion that "there is feeling and there is the wearing away [of karma]. (Sūyagaḍa 721–722)
"There is neither action nor non-action"—one should not establish such a view.
"There is action or there is non-action"—one should establish such a view. (Sūy.
723) "There is neither anger nor pride"—one should not establish such a view.
"There is anger or pride"—one should not establish such a perception.
"There is no deceit or greed"—one should not establish such a perception. "There is deceit or greed"—one should establish such a perception. (Sūyagaḍa 724–725)
"There is neither affection nor aversion"—one should not establish such a perception; "there is affection or aversion"—thus one should establish the perception. (Sūy.
726) "There is no four-cornered cycle of existence"—one should not establish such a perception.
"There is no end to this saṃsāra"—one should not entertain such a notion.
"There is no god or goddess"—one should not entertain such a notion.
"There is a god or a goddess"—one should entertain such a notion. (Sūyagaḍa 727–728)
"There is neither perfection nor non-perfection"—one should not establish such a notion.
"There is perfection or non-perfection"—one should establish such a notion. "Perfection has no fixed place"—one should not establish such a notion. (Sūyagaḍa 729)
"There is success and its own place"—one should not establish such a notion.
"There is neither the virtuous nor the non-virtuous"—one should not establish such a notion.
"There is both the virtuous and the non-virtuous"—one should establish such a notion. (Sūy. 730–731)
"There is neither merit nor evil"—one should not establish such a view; rather, one should establish the view that "there is merit and there is evil. (Sūy.
732) For otherwise, the distinction between merit and evil would not exist in worldly convention.

Foolish ascetics do not understand what is enmity; they do not perceive it in its entirety, nor as something imperishable, nor as "all is suffering," nor do they utter such speech as "living beings are to be slain" or "they are not to be slain. (Sūy. 733–734)
One should not hold the view: "These monks, who practice equanimity and live as virtuous men, are living by wrong means of livelihood.
Furthermore, one should not think that there is either gain or lack of gain from alms-offerings. (Sūyagaḍa 735)
The wise one should not dispute, but should cultivate the path of peace.
By these points seen by the Jina, O self-restrained one, maintaining yourself, you should wander as a mendicant until liberation.
Thus I say.
[The Second Lesson] O Āḍā! Listen to this which was done in the past: formerly, there was a śramaṇa who wandered alone.
Having brought together many monks, he explained to them individually in detail:

"This way of life was established by the Steadfast One; proclaiming it among the assembly of monks in the midst of the community, he taught the goal for many people, not connecting the later with the earlier. (Sūy. 738–739)
Whether it be exclusively one way or even now,
since the two opposing views do not coincide regarding the past, the present, and the future, one must adhere strictly to that single [truth].
Having understood the world of mobile and immobile beings, the ascetic or the brahmin is the bringer of security.
Even while preaching in the midst of a thousand people, he maintains his solitary state just as before. (Sūy.
741) There is no fault for one who proclaims the Dharma—provided he is patient, self-controlled, has subdued his senses, avoids the faults of speech, and employs the virtues of speech. (Sūy. 742)

The five great vows and the five minor vows, as well as the five influxes and their restraint—having understood these renunciations within this ascetic life, one who has cast off even the slightest faults is called a "shramana," so I say. (Sūy.
743) One should avoid cold water, the body of seeds, food prepared for oneself, and likewise women.
In our Dharma here, those who practice solitary wandering and are ascetic do not incur evil. (Sūy.
744) Cold water, as well as the body of seeds, food-preparation, and likewise women—know that those householders who indulge in these things are not ascetics. (Sūy. 745)
There may be women who consume seeds and water; let them be ascetics, and even householders let them be ascetics—for they too practice in such a manner.
And as for that monk who consumes seeds and water, he wanders about seeking alms, intent on living.
Having abandoned improper attachments, they become free from the body and bring about an end to rebirth.

(Sūyagaḍa 747) But you, proclaiming this doctrine, censure all those who profess sinful views; yet those who profess sinful views, each separately setting forth their own position, maintain their respective dogmatic perspectives. (Sūyagaḍa 748)
Censuring one another, those ascetics and brahmins declare:
"The existent exists, and the non-existent does not exist. We do not censure their views, nor do we censure anything at all.
We do not define anything by means of form; rather, we follow the path of our own vision. (Sūy. 749)
These paths have been proclaimed as straight by the noble ones, the unsurpassed true men. (Sūy.

750) Above, below, and across the quarters, toward whatever beings there may be—whether moving or stationary—one who is filled with apprehension for living creatures and feels revulsion [toward harming them], does not find anything in the world to criticize. (Sūy. 751)
In a guest-house or a park, a monk who is afraid does not take up residence;
for there are indeed many people who cause suffering—those who are deficient, those who are excessive, and those who are frivolous.
But the wise and intelligent ones, having trained themselves, are certain knowers through both the scriptures and their meanings.
“They asked me, ‘Are you not another ascetic? Fearing this, he did not go there. (Sūy.

753) “Neither out of desire for pleasure nor out of childish duty, nor by royal compulsion, nor out of fear—would he explain the question, or even not explain it, here among the noble ones, out of his own personal desire? (Sūy. 754)
Whether one goes there or does not go, let him explain [this] to those who are composed and wise;
for the ignoble are limited in their vision. Suspecting this, he does not approach them.
Just as a merchant seeking profit makes an investment for the sake of gain, so does he exert effort for the sake of his own spiritual advancement.
"Taovame (equal to the self) is the Śramaṇa, the son of the Jñātṛs"—such indeed is my thought and reflection.
One should not create new [karma], one should shake off the old, and having abandoned delusion, the sage (*sādhu*) is thus a *tāyin* (protector).
It is said that by this much one becomes a *brahmavat*; he who strives for its arising is a *śramaṇa*. Thus I say. (Sūy. 756–757)
Merchants indeed exert themselves toward the community of living beings, clinging to possessions as their own;
not having abandoned excessive attachment, they increase their bondage for the sake of wealth. Seeking riches and deeply immersed in sexual desire, those merchants go about for the sake of food.

But we are addicted to sensual pleasures, ignoble and greedy for the flavors of affection. Engaged in violence and possessiveness, unrestrained and dependent on worldly things, they inflict injury upon themselves; and as for what you have said regarding their origin—that leads here to suffering and to endless, boundless misery. (Sūy. 759–760)
Like dancers on a stage, those two [the soul and karma] dance; when that rise of karma occurs, both of them proceed toward the manifestation of qualities.
When that rise has attained its limit, those wise ones assist in bringing about its cessation.
Being compassionate toward all beings and practicing non-violence, they remain established in the Dharma for the sake of the dissociation of karma.
Those who employ deceptive punishments—even though this [act] is not appropriate for them—[are at fault]. (Sūy.

762) If someone were to cook a lump of sesame paste on a spit, thinking, "This is a man," or roast a gourd, thinking, "This is a child," he would be stained by the sin of taking life according to our [view]. (Sūy. 763)

Or again, having pierced a barbarian with a stake, one might cook a man or even a child, thinking them to be *pinnāga* (a type of grain); we [hold that] one is not tainted by the killing of living beings.
Some, having pierced a man or a child, cook them on a stake while they are still alive.

Having ascended the pinnacle and offered a morsel of food, that is permissible for the Buddhas as their breaking of the fast. (Sūy. 765) But he who constantly feeds two thousand bathed [brahmins] gains a very great mass of merit; having acquired it, those great beings become established in the higher realms. (Sūy. 766)

"O Sañjayas, it is unwholesome here for those who, having committed sin by inflicting harm upon living beings, do not see the error of their ways; both those who speak of such acts and those who listen to them are said to be unskillful.
Having understood the signs of the mobile and immobile beings above, below, and in the horizontal directions," (Sūyagaḍa 767)
One who is full of apprehension and feels disgust [toward worldly things], how could he possibly speak or act [in such a way]? (Sūy.
768) The designation "man" does not apply to him in this sense; such a person is ignoble.
For what possibility is there for such a being? Even this speech regarding one who eats lumps of food is said to be untrue. (Sūy. 769)
Whatever one might bring about through the application of speech, one should not utter such speech;
this statement is no ground for virtues.

One who is initiated should not say, "This is wonderful," even when a purpose has been achieved, for [the result] depends on the destiny of living beings and is well-considered by them. (Sūyagaḍa 770)
Having touched both the eastern and western oceans, [the world] is as clear as if held in the palm of the hand. (Sūy.
771) Those who contemplate the experience of living beings and have purified themselves through various methods of food, do not proclaim their own purification.
Living with their motives concealed, this is the true dharma here for the self-restrained. (Sūy. 772)
But that uncontrolled man, who with blood-stained hands feeds two thousand bathed and learned monks with regular alms, incurs reproach in this very world.
Having slaughtered a fat ram here and having prepared food specifically for them...
Having prepared that meat with salted oil, they serve it seasoned with long pepper.
Eating that abundant minced meat, those who follow the ways of the ignoble and are un-Aryan fools, greedy for flavors, say: "We are not defiled by passion. (Sūyagaḍa 774–775)
Those who consume such [food] and indulge in it are practicing evil without realizing it; the wise do not approve of this mental state, and even this speech that is uttered is false. (Sūy.
776) For the sake of compassion toward all living beings, they should completely avoid what is blameworthy and faulty.
The Nātaputta seers, who are free from doubt, avoid food that has been specifically set aside for them.
Out of apprehension regarding living beings and feeling revulsion, they have laid down the rod toward all creatures;
therefore, they do not eat such food. This is the rule of conduct here for those who are self-restrained.
In this Nigaṇṭha Dharma, these are the concentrations; having stood firm in this, one should wander without attachment.
A sage who is endowed with the virtues of morality attains the highest state of praise. (Sūy. 779) But if one were to feed two thousand bath-ascetics who are Brahmins...
"Having generated a very great mass of merit, they indeed become gods; such is the teaching of the Vedas. (Sūy.

780) "But he who constantly feeds two thousand bathed ascetics belonging to the householders' order goes to the Loluva hell, which is most intense, where he suffers from fierce torment and dwells in that hell. (Sūy. 781)

Those who despise the compassionate Dharma and praise the Dharma that brings worldly prosperity—even if such a person feeds but a single one who lacks virtue, where is the Nirvāṇa for them? How could they attain it through the gods? (Sūy.
782) Both [types of people] have indeed set out upon the Dharma; having remained well-established in this, they shall likewise pass their time.
One should be established in conduct, virtue, and knowledge; there is no distinction in the state beyond rebirth (saṃparāya).
[Yet] the great Person is of indeterminate form, eternal, imperishable, and immutable;
he is present in all beings everywhere, like the moon among the stars, his form being complete.

Thus they do not sink down nor do they transmigrate; neither Brahmins, nor those in the guise of Kshatriyas, nor Peshas, nor insects, nor birds, nor reptiles, nor men, nor all the celestial worlds [are subject to this].
Those who, not knowing the world here through omniscience, proclaim the Dharma while remaining ignorant of it—Sūy. 785.
Having perished, they destroy themselves and others in this terrible cycle of existence, which has neither beginning nor end. (Sūy.

786) Those who, endowed with meditative concentration, perceive the world here through perfect knowledge and proclaim the complete Dharma—they, having crossed over, deliver both themselves and others. (Sūy. 787)
"Those who dwell here in this place, and those in the world who are endowed with conduct—what has been proclaimed by me as equal is, in fact, a complete reversal of the truth.
Even if one were to kill a single great elephant every year with an arrow... (Sūyagaḍa 788)
"For the sake of compassion toward other living beings, we adopt this mode of life as our livelihood" (Sūy.

789). "Even by killing only one single creature per year, those whose faults are unrestrained become involved in the slaughter of other beings; therefore, even householders might [accidentally] kill only a small amount [of them]" (Sūy. 790).
Even if one were to kill a single living being every year, that man who disregards the vows of a śramaṇa is unrighteous; the Kevalins do not describe him as such.
By means of this threefold [restraint], remaining well-established in this meditative concentration according to the command of the Buddha, one is a protector.
Having crossed over the great flood of existence as if it were an ocean, one should proclaim the Dharma of right exertion. Thus I say. [The Chapter on Nālandaiya]

At that time, in that period, there was a city named Rājagṛha, prosperous, peaceful, and flourishing; its description is as follows, up to: it was beautiful. To the north-eastern direction outside that city of Rājagṛha, there was a suburb named Nālandā, inhabited by many hundreds of dwellings, [pleasing, lovely to behold, beautiful,] and symmetrical.

There, in the outskirts of Nālandā, there was a householder named Lēva. He was wealthy, opulent, affluent, and possessed of extensive and abundant dwellings, beds, seats, vehicles, and carriages; he had vast amounts of wealth and gold, was engaged in various business enterprises, provided an abundance of food and drink, owned many female and male slaves, cattle, buffalo, and goats, and was beyond reproach among the people.

Now, that householder named Lēva was also a lay follower of the ascetics; he had understood the nature of living beings and non-living beings, and so on, up to: he lived [in this way]. He was free from doubt, free from hesitation, and free from uncertainty regarding the teaching of the Nirgranthas; he had attained the goal, grasped the goal, questioned about the goal, discerned the goal, and fully comprehended the goal; he was colored by a love for the teaching as deep as the marrow of his bones.

"Venerable one! In this Nigaṇṭha dispensation, this is the goal, this is the supreme goal; all else is not the goal. With its ramparts raised, its gates secured and closed, with few openings and restricted entry to the inner apartments, the ascetic Nigaṇṭha dwells there, properly observing the complete *poṣadha* on the fourteenth, the eighth, and the full-moon days; providing for himself food, drink, snacks, and delicacies that are fit for alms; and cultivating his self through many vows of morality, restraints, abstinences, renunciations, and *poṣadha* fasts."

To the north-eastern quarter of that householder Lēva’s residence outside Nālandā, there was a water-hall named Sēsadaviyā; it was supported by many hundreds of pillars, beautiful to behold, and so forth, up to "exquisite. To the north-eastern quarter of that Sēsadaviyā water-hall, there was a forest grove named Hatthijāma; as for the color of the forest grove, it was black.

And in that part of the house, the Blessed One Gautama was staying; while the Blessed One was in the park, Udaya Pēḍhālaputta—the Nirgrantha disciple of the Blessed One, of the Mēḍhya clan—approached where the Blessed One Gautama was, and having approached, he spoke thus to the Blessed One Gautama:

"Venerable Gautama! I have indeed certain points that ought to be asked about; regarding those, venerable one, explain them to me with their context, according to how you have heard and seen them. The Blessed One Gautama spoke thus to Udaya Pēḍhālaputta: "Furthermore, venerable one, having heard and reflected upon it, we shall understand it with its context. Udaya Pēḍhālaputta spoke thus to the Blessed One Gautama:

"O venerable Gautama! There are indeed recluses, the Nigaṇṭhas called the Kummāraputtiyas, who proclaim your own doctrine and cause a householder lay-disciple who has taken it up to renounce [violence] in this way: 'Except for the purpose of releasing a householder who has been seized by thieves through the use of force, one should abandon the infliction of harm upon mobile living beings. For them, thus renouncing, it is a difficult renunciation; for them, thus causing others to renounce, it is a difficult thing to be caused to renounce. In this way, while causing others to renounce, they transgress their own vow. For what reason? Because all living beings are subject to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra); stationary beings are reborn as mobile beings, and mobile beings are reborn as stationary beings. Those being released from the stationary body are reborn in the mobile body, and those being released from the mobile body are reborn in the stationary body. And for those who have been reborn in the stationary body, this is the established rule."

"In this way, for us who renounce, the renunciation is well-renounced; in this way, for us who cause others to renounce, the causing of renunciation is well-caused. Thus, while causing others to renounce, they do not transgress their own vow, except in the case of compelling force or the liberation of a householder from being seized as a thief, having laid down the rod toward living beings endowed with consciousness. Likewise, when one's own speech is available for another's task, those who—out of anger or greed—cause others to renounce, this too is not a proper instruction. Is it not beneficial for us? Moreover, O venerable Gautama, does this also seem right to you?"

Then the Blessed One said this to Udaya Pēḍhālaputta: "O venerable Udaya, it is certainly not pleasing to us that those ascetics or brahmins who thus declare and explain—[as you have]—are indeed not speaking the speech of true ascetics or Nirgranthas; they speak a speech that is self-contradictory. They deny the ascetics or lay-disciples of the ascetics, and they even deny those other living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings with whom they practice restraint. For what reason? Because all living beings are subject to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Mobile beings are reborn as stationary beings, and stationary beings are reborn as mobile beings. When released from the body of a mobile being, they are reborn in the body of a stationary being; when released from the body of a stationary being, they are reborn in the body of a mobile being. And for those who have been reborn in the body of a mobile being, this state is impermanent."

Then Udaya Pēḍhālaputta spoke thus to the Blessed One Gōyama: "Venerable Gōyama, what do you mean when you say 'mobile beings' (*tasā pāṇā*)? Do you speak of those who are currently mobile, or otherwise? The Blessed One Gōyama spoke thus to Udaya Pēḍhālaputta: "Venerable Udaya, those whom you call 'beings that have become mobile' (*tasabhūyā pāṇā*), we call 'mobile beings' (*tasā pāṇā*). And those whom we call 'mobile beings,' you call 'beings that have become mobile. These two positions are equivalent and have the same meaning. Venerable sir, which of these is more well-said for you: 'beings that have become mobile are mobile beings,' or 'mobile beings are mobile beings'? Therefore, venerable sir, reject one and accept the other; this distinction will lead you to liberation."

And the Blessed One said: "There are some people who have previously thought thus: 'Indeed, we are not able to go forth from the home life into homelessness after shaving our heads; rather, we shall serve our lineage in due succession. They make this resolve, they establish this intention, except for the purpose of releasing a householder who has been seized by thieves, having laid aside violence toward living beings; even that is indeed wholesome for them."

They are called mobile beings (*trasa*) because they have acquired a name through karma produced by the equipment of mobility, and their life-span as mobile beings has been exhausted. Having abandoned that life-span, they leave the state of the mobile body and are reborn into the state of immobile beings (*sthāvara*). They are called immobile beings because they have acquired a name through karma produced by the equipment of immobility, and their life-span as immobile beings has been exhausted. Having abandoned that life-span, they leave the state of the immobile body and are reborn again into the state of the next world. They are called living beings (*pāṇa*), they are called mobile beings, they are of great body, and they are long-lived.

Then Udaya Pēḍhālaputta said this to the Blessed One Gōyama: "Venerable Gōyama! There is no such stage [of spiritual development] where a lay follower (*samaṇōvāsaga*) has laid down the rod of violence even toward a single living being. For what reason? Because beings in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāriyā pāṇā*) are indeed migratory; stationary beings (*thāvarā pāṇā*) are reborn as mobile beings (*tasattāē*), and mobile beings are reborn as stationary beings. Those released from the stationary body are all reborn in the mobile body, and those released from the mobile body are all reborn in the stationary body. And for those who have been reborn in the stationary body, this state is undetermined (*adhattaṃ*). Then the Blessed One Gōyama said this to Udaya Pēḍhālaputta: "Indeed, Venerable sir, it is not according to our doctrine, but rather according to your own assertion, that there is no such stage where a lay follower has laid down the rod toward all breathing things, all beings, all souls, and all creatures. For what reason? Because beings in the cycle of existence are indeed migratory; mobile beings are reborn as stationary beings, and stationary beings are reborn as mobile beings. Those released from the mobile body are all reborn in the stationary body, and those released from the stationary body are all reborn in the mobile body. And for those who have been reborn in the mobile body, this state is determined (*dhattaṃ*). They are called 'living beings' (*pāṇā*), they are called 'mobile beings' (*tasā*)."

Those [beings] belonging to the earth-body are large in size and long-lived; they are the greater number of living beings for whom the lay follower’s vow is well-renounced, while they are the smaller number of living beings for whom the lay follower’s vow is not renounced. Therefore, for one who has become tranquil, established, and restrained regarding the large-bodied mobile beings, if you or another should say, "There is no stage of religious life for him in which even a single living being has been spared from harm," this too is not a valid argument for you.

And the Blessed One said: "Indeed, the Nigaṇṭhas should be questioned thus: 'O venerable Nigaṇṭhas, there are indeed certain men here who have previously declared: "For those who have become shaven-headed and gone forth from the home to homelessness, the taking up of the rod has been laid down for life; but for those who dwell in a household, the taking up of the rod has not been laid down for life. Now, could any such ascetics—having spent four, five, six, ten, or even fewer or more years [in the order]—go back to their country and dwell as householders? 'Yes, they could. 'In that case, while he is living as a householder, would his vow of renunciation be broken? 'No, that is not the case. 'In the very same way, for a lay follower (śramaṇopāsaka), the taking up of the rod has been laid down regarding mobile beings (trasa-prāṇa), but the taking up of the rod has not been laid down regarding immobile beings (sthāvara-prāṇa). While he is killing that immobile body, his vow of renunciation is not broken. Do you understand this, O Nigaṇṭhas? This is how it must be understood.'"

The Blessed One said: "O Nigaṇṭhas, you should certainly be asked: 'Venerable Nigaṇṭhas, would a householder or a householder’s son, having come from such families for the purpose of hearing the Dharma, approach [you]? [They would reply: 'Yes, he would approach. [The Blessed One continued: 'And should the Dharma be taught to such people? [They would reply: 'Yes, it should be taught. [The Blessed One continued: 'Having heard and reflected upon that Dharma, would they say: "This very Nigaṇṭha doctrine is the truth, supreme, absolute, perfect, leading, pure, a remover of thorns, the path to success, the path to liberation, the path to deliverance, the path to Nirvana, unerring, free from doubt, the path to the destruction of all suffering; established in this, living beings attain perfection, awaken, are liberated, become completely cooled, and make an end to all suffering"? Would they say: "By that command, we shall proceed thus, stand thus, sit thus, lie down thus, eat thus, speak thus, rise up thus, and by exerting ourselves, we shall rise up; we shall restrain ourselves with restraint toward living beings, creatures, souls, and sentient beings"? [They would reply: 'Yes, they would say so.'"

"Are such persons as those permitted by you to be ordained? Yes, they are permitted. Are such persons as those permitted by you to be shaven? Yes, they are permitted. Are such persons as those permitted by you to be instructed? Yes, they are permitted. Are such persons as those permitted by you to be initiated? Yes, they are permitted. Are such persons as those permitted by you to be initiated? Yes, they are permitted. And has the laying down of the rod toward all living beings, up to all sentient beings, been performed for such persons as those? Yes, it has been laid down."

If they were to wander in such a manner for four, five, six, or ten years—or for a shorter or longer period—and having traveled through various regions, were to return to the household life? Yes, they might. Is the infliction of punishment toward all living beings, down to all creatures, renounced by him? No, that is not the case; for there remains that being toward whom the infliction of punishment toward all living beings, down to all creatures, has not been renounced.

That living being for whom, in the past, the infliction of violence (*daṇḍa*) toward all living beings, up to all sentient beings, had been laid down—that same living being, for whom now the infliction of violence toward all living beings, up to all sentient beings, has not been laid down; who was formerly un-restrained and is currently restrained, yet is presently un-restrained—for such an un-restrained one, the infliction of violence toward all living beings, up to all sentient beings, has not been laid down. Do you understand this thus? O Nigaṇṭhas, it must be understood thus.

And the Blessed One said: "Indeed, the Nigaṇṭhas should be asked: 'Venerable Nigaṇṭhas, would wandering mendicants or wandering mendicant women come here from other religious orders for the purpose of hearing the Dharma? [They would reply: 'Yes, they would come. [Then one should ask: 'Should the Dharma be explained to them in such a manner? [They would reply: 'Yes, it should be explained. [Then one should ask: 'Is it appropriate to initiate them [into the order], and so on, up to [whether] it is appropriate [to ordain them]? [They would reply: 'Yes, it is appropriate.'"

"Are such things as those allowable for you to sweep up? "Yes, they are allowable. "If, by living in such a manner, they were to live on, would they eventually return to the household life? "Yes, they would return. "Are such things as those allowable for you to sweep up? "No, that is not possible."

Whatever living being is beyond [the community], it is not permissible for them to be shared with; whatever living being is within [the community], it is permissible for them to be shared with. Whatever living being is at present not permissible to be shared with—being a non-ascetic (assamaṇa) beyond [the community] and an ascetic (samaṇa) within [the community]—it is not permissible for the Nigaṇṭha ascetics to share with a non-ascetic. Do you understand this thus, O Nigaṇṭhas? This must be understood thus.

And the Blessed One said: "There are some lay followers of the ascetics (*śramaṇopāsaka*) who have previously thought thus: 'Indeed, we are not able to go forth from home into homelessness by shaving our heads; however, on the fourteenth, the eighth, the full moon, and the new moon days, we shall dwell properly observing the complete *poṣadha*. We shall renounce gross violence against living beings (*sthūla-prāṇātipāta*), and likewise we shall renounce gross falsehood, gross taking of what is not given, gross sexual misconduct, and gross possession. We shall set limits to our desires. By means of two ways and three kinds [of action], let no one whatsoever do anything for my sake, nor cause it to be done; therein too we shall renounce. Having not eaten, not drunk, and not rinsed their mouths, they descend from their couches and seats. When they have thus passed away, what should be said of them? That they have passed away rightly?"

It might be said: "Those living beings are indeed called 'living beings,' they are called 'mobile' (trasa), they are large-bodied, they have long lifespans, and they are the more numerous living beings for whom the lay follower's renunciation is complete; whereas those are the fewer living beings for whom the lay follower's renunciation is not complete. Thus, that which you say regarding the great [number of beings]—that very point, up to this distinction—is not a valid principle.

And the Blessed One said: "There are indeed some lay followers of the ascetics (*śramaṇopāsaka*) who have previously thought thus: 'Truly, we are not able to go forth from the home to the homeless state by shaving our heads; nor are we able to dwell properly observing the complete *poṣadha* on the fourteenth, eighth, and full-moon days. However, having practiced the terminal purification through fasting (*apacchima-māraṇantiya-saṃlehaṇā-jhūsaṇā*), having renounced food and drink, and dwelling without longing for life, we shall renounce all killing of living beings, up to renouncing all possession, in a threefold way by means of a threefold [action]. Let nothing whatsoever be done on my account, up to [the prohibition of] chairs and couches. Having stepped down from these, when they have thus passed away, what should be said? Should it be said, "He has died a proper death"? Yes, it should be said. They are also called "living beings" (*prāṇa*), and so on; even this distinction is not considered a valid [logical] conclusion. "

And the Blessed One said: "There are some people who are as follows: they have great desires, great undertakings, and great possessions; they are unrighteous, [and so on] up to being difficult to satisfy; they do not desist from all forms of possession for as long as life lasts—those by whom a monk’s disciple has laid down the rod for as long as death ends. When they cast off their lifespan, having cast it off, they again go toward their own acquisition and become destined for an evil state of existence. They are called 'beings' (pāṇā), they are called 'mobile creatures' (tasā), they are large-bodied, they have long lifespans, and they are more numerous in terms of acquisitions. Thus, that which you say is indeed great; even this distinction of yours does not lead to liberation."

And the Blessed One said: "There are some people who are as follows: they are non-violent, without possessions, righteous, followers of the Dharma, and so forth, up to being completely abstained from all possessions for as long as life lasts. For them, the monk’s lay follower has laid down the rod [of violence] from the taking up of [the vows] until the end of life. They abandon that lifespan; having abandoned it, they again, according to their own undertaking, become those going to a happy destination. They too are called living beings, up to: 'it does not lead to a state of misery.'"

And the Blessed One said: "There are some people who are as follows: they have few desires, little exertion, and little possession; they are righteous, followers of the Dharma, [and so on] up to those who are not yet fully abstinent from all forms of possession. For them, the monk’s lay follower has laid down the rod for as long as life lasts. When they abandon that lifespan and pass away, they then go again to their own respective state and become destined for a happy rebirth. They are called living beings, and so on, until it does not lead to a state of woe."

And the Blessed One said: "There are some people who are as follows: forest-dwellers, village-dwellers, town-dwellers, or those who live in secret. For them, the householder lay follower has laid down the rod of violence toward all living beings from this life until death; yet they are neither very restrained nor very abstinent regarding all breathing things, beings, and creatures. They themselves employ both truth and falsehood, saying: 'I am not to be killed, but others are to be killed,' and so forth. Having passed away at the time of death, they are reborn in various demonic and miserable states. When they eventually escape from there, they return again to a state of dullness and darkness. They are called 'living beings' (pāṇā), and so on, until it is said that they do not attain the path to liberation."

And the Blessed One said: "There are certain living beings who are long-lived, for whom a lay follower has renounced violence from the taking up [of the vow] until the end of life; yet they die first, and having died, they are reborn in another world. Those beings are called 'beings,' they are called 'mobile creatures,' they are large-bodied, they have a long duration of life, they are long-lived, and they are numerous—those for whom the lay follower’s vow is well-renounced and does not become a source of negligence."

And the Blessed One said: "There are certain living beings of equal lifespan, for whom the lay follower has laid down his staff from the moment of taking it up until the end of life; they die naturally and, having died, are reborn in the next world. They are called 'living beings,' they are called 'mobile creatures,' they are large-bodied, they are of equal lifespan, and they are very numerous—those for whom the lay follower’s vow is well-renounced, such that he does not incur sin."

And the Blessed One said: "There are certain living beings with short lifespans for whom a lay follower has laid down the rod from the moment of taking up the vows until the end of life; yet they die beforehand and are reborn in another world. They are called living beings, they are called mobile creatures, they are large-bodied, and they have short lifespans. These are the many living beings for whom a lay follower’s vow is well-renounced, such that it is not considered deficient."

And the Blessed One said: "There are indeed some lay followers of the ascetics who have previously thought thus: 'We are certainly not able to go forth by shaving our heads and so on; we are certainly not able to observe the complete *poṣadha* on the fourteenth, eighth, and full-moon days; we are certainly not able to dwell [in the practice] until the very end. However, having undertaken the *sāmāyika* and the *deśāvakāśika*, whether toward the east, west, south, or north, for this much distance, we have laid down the rod against all living beings, down to all creatures, and we are bringers of security unto all living beings, souls, and creatures.'"

In that regard, those mobile beings in the distance from whom the lay follower has renounced violence for as long as life lasts—having cast off their lifespan there, they are reborn among those very same mobile beings in the distance from whom the lay follower has renounced violence, and so on, until he is fully committed to his vows toward them. Those living beings, too, [are included] until this distinction of his is not considered a transgression.

In that regard, those mobile beings (*trasa*) within that distance from whom the lay follower has renounced violence for as long as life lasts—they abandon their lifespan there; having abandoned it, they are reborn among the stationary beings (*sthāvara*) within that same distance from whom the lay follower has not renounced violence for his own sake, but has renounced violence for no purpose. Those beings toward whom the lay follower has not renounced violence for his own sake, but has renounced violence for no purpose, are also called "beings" (*pāṇā*); they are mobile and have a long duration of life. Even this distinction does not lead to certainty.

In that regard, those mobile beings beyond that point—toward whom the lay follower has renounced violence from the moment of undertaking the vow until the end of life—they abandon their lifespan there; having abandoned it, they are reborn among those other mobile or stationary beings toward whom the lay follower has renounced violence from the moment of undertaking the vow until the end of life. Toward them, the lay follower’s vow is well-renounced. They are also called "living beings," and so on, up to: "this distinction is not to be disregarded."

In that regard, those stationary beings (*sthāvara*) from afar for whose sake the lay follower (*śramaṇopāsaka*) has not laid down the rod of violence, and for whom he has laid down the rod for no purpose—they abandon their life-span there; having abandoned it, they are reborn among those mobile beings (*trasa*) from afar for whose sake the lay follower has laid down the rod until the end of his life. For them, the lay follower’s vow is well-renounced. Those beings, too, [are protected], and this distinction of his is not to be considered a transgression.

In that regard, those stationary living beings (*sthāvara*) who are far away—toward whom the lay follower (*śrāvakasamaṇovāsaga*) has not directed violence for their sake, but has directed violence against others for no purpose—they abandon that life-span; having abandoned it, they are reborn right there among those very stationary living beings toward whom the lay follower has not directed violence for their sake, but has directed violence against others for no purpose. Toward them, the lay follower has not directed violence for their sake, but has directed violence against others for no purpose. These living beings, too, [remain so] until this distinction is no longer to be understood.

In that regard, those stationary beings beyond that point for whose sake the lay follower has not laid down the rod, but for whose sake he has laid down the rod—they abandon their life-span there; having abandoned it, they are reborn among those mobile and stationary beings beyond that point for whose sake the lay follower has laid down the rod for as long as life lasts. For them, the lay follower’s renunciation is well-renounced. Those beings also [are included], and thus this distinction is not to be disregarded.

In that regard, those mobile and stationary living beings beyond which the lay follower has renounced violence from the moment of taking the vow until death—when they abandon their life-span there and pass away, they are reborn among those mobile beings within the same range toward whom the lay follower has renounced violence from the moment of taking the vow until death. Toward them, the lay follower’s vow is perfectly fulfilled. Those living beings [are thus protected], and even this distinction is not to be considered a transgression for him.

In that regard, those mobile and stationary living beings beyond [the boundary] from whom the lay follower has renounced violence for as long as life lasts—they abandon their lifespan there; having abandoned it, they are reborn among those stationary living beings within [the boundary] from whom the lay follower has not renounced violence for his own sake, but has renounced violence for the sake of others. Because he has not renounced violence for his own sake but has renounced it for the sake of others toward those beings, even this distinction does not lead to his spiritual ruin.

In that regard, those other mobile and stationary living beings for whom the lay follower has renounced violence from the moment of undertaking the vows until the end of life—they abandon their current lifespan; having abandoned it, they are reborn among those very same other mobile and stationary living beings for whom the lay follower has renounced violence from the moment of undertaking the vows until the end of life. For them, the lay follower’s vow is well-renounced. Those living beings also [are not killed], and thus this distinction is not to be considered a transgression.

And the Blessed One said: "This has not happened, this cannot happen, and this will not happen—that mobile beings should be annihilated and only stationary beings should remain; or that stationary beings should be annihilated and only mobile beings should remain. Since mobile and stationary beings are never annihilated, it is impossible for you or anyone else to say: 'There is no such stage [of spiritual development]... nor does it lead to final liberation.'"

And the Blessed One said: "O venerable Udaka! He who indeed reviles a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, yet considers them as friends—having attained knowledge, having attained vision, and having attained conduct through the non-performance of evil karmas—he indeed stands as an obstacle to the next world. But he who indeed does not revile a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, yet considers them as friends—having attained knowledge, having attained vision, and having attained conduct through the non-performance of evil karmas—he indeed stands for the purification of the next world. Then that Udaka, son of Peḍhāla, disregarding the Blessed Gautama, departed in the very direction from which he had appeared.

And the Blessed One said: "O venerable Udaka! Indeed, whoever, having heard and reflected upon even a single noble and righteous word from the presence of such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, and having attained for himself through subtle discernment the unsurpassed state of security in yoga, would honor, recognize, revere, pay homage to, respect, and show hospitality toward that [teacher], regarding him as auspicious, a source of blessing, a deity, and an object of veneration—even he, first and foremost, honors [the teaching]. Then Udaka, the son of Pedhāla, spoke thus to the Blessed One Goyama:

“Venerable sir, formerly, due to ignorance, lack of hearing, lack of awakening, lack of comprehension, because these points were unseen, unheard, unlearned, unknown, unpenetrated, unhidden, undiscerned, unexpounded, and unmastered, I did not believe, did not trust, and did not find pleasure in this matter. Venerable sir, now, through knowledge, hearing, awakening, and so on up to mastery, I believe, trust, and find pleasure in this matter; it is exactly as you say.”

Then the Blessed One Goyama said this to Udaka Pēḍhālaputta: “Believe it, O Venerable One! Trust it, O Venerable One! Be convinced of it, O Venerable One! It is exactly as we say. Then Udaka Pēḍhālaputta said this to the Blessed One Goyama: “I wish, O Blessed One, to dwell having adopted the Dharma consisting of the five great vows with confession, from the Dharma of the fourfold restraint in your presence...”

Then the venerable Goyama, taking Udaka Pēḍhālaputta with him, went to where the ascetic, the venerable Mahāvīra was; having arrived, Udaka Pēḍhālaputta performed three circumambulations, keeping the ascetic, the venerable Mahāvīra, to his right; having performed them, he paid homage and saluted him. Having paid homage and saluted him, he spoke thus: "Venerable sir, I desire to dwell having adopted, in your presence, the Dharma consisting of the five great vows along with the practice of confession, in place of the Dharma of the four restraints."

Then the ascetic Bhagavān Mahāvīra said this to Udaya: "As is agreeable to you, dear one; do not hesitate. Then that Udaya, son of Peḍhāla, having adopted the Dharma consisting of the five great vows with confession in place of the fourfold Dharma from the presence of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, lived [accordingly].
Thus I say.
